en: The Twelfth Chapter.
Vyāsa said:
O best of brāhmaṇas, [this concerns] Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is saluted by the gods, during the month of Phālguna.
A Vaiṣṇava person should worship [the Lord] every day with a spirit of devotion.
I shall declare the fruit for him who bathes the Son of Devakī with clarified butter in the month of Phālguna; listen to it correctly from me. 1-2.
Having obtained the fruit of all sacrifices as well as the fruit of all gifts,
and being freed from all sins, he goes at the end to the abode of Hari; having enjoyed the pleasures in the house of Hari for thousands of crores of yugas.
In that very state, having attained supreme knowledge, one thus attains liberation.
He who offers to Kṛṣṇa, who has the form of a cowherd boy in the cool season,
a divine sweetmeat made of sesame seeds, shall go to the abode of Hari.
O Jaimini, he who gives milk-based sweetmeats (laḍḍukas) to the high-souled Keśava shall drink nectar in heaven for the duration of a hundred manvantaras.
He who offers delicious sugar-candies (khaṇḍa) to Hari [attains the same].
Viṣṇu, with a gracious soul, severs his bondage to worldly existence.
O twice-born one, he who offers this divine fruit, laden with various wonders, to the Blessed Lord,
shall go to the city of Śakra at the end [of his life] and become honored by the gods.

O Brahmin, what indeed cannot one who is devoted to Vāsudeva obtain through his grace— just as one obtains pure sugar from the cutting of a sugarcane stalk? In the month of Phālguna, the jujube fruit is well-ripened and sweet.
Listen now to the fruit that he who gives to Kṛṣṇa obtains:
endowed with sons and grandsons, he enjoys every happiness here in this world; and at the end, having ascended a magnificent chariot, he goes to the abode of Hari. 10–11.
O best of Brahmins, one should not offer a jujube fruit mixed with molasses to Hari; if one should offer it out of ignorance, he will become a denizen of hell.
He who offers a pomegranate fruit to Hari in the month of Phālguna [attains great merit].
O Brahmin, listen attentively as I describe that perfectly ripe fruit:
as many seeds as there are within the pomegranate fruit, for so many Manvantaras does the fortunate one reside in the abode of Viṣṇu. 13–14.

O best of the twice-born, he who offers guḍa-piṣṭaka (molasses-cake) to Hari in the month of Phālguna should be known as one who has performed a thousand horse-sacrifices. O best of the twice-born, [he who worships] Madhusūdana with honey in the month of Caitra...
The mortal who bathes [the deity] attains that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Whoever bathes the flawless Nārāyaṇa with honey, no obstacle shall ever be raised against him by the son of the Sun (Yama). 16–17.
For one who worships him, there is indeed no further birth on this earth.
A person who worships the crest-jewel of all gods with a black *vañjula* flower is never overtaken by calamity anywhere. (19–20)
He who, with a tranquil soul, worships the Blessed One in the springtime with fragrant *vāsantī* flowers, is honored even by the gods.
Likewise, he who would worship Hari with divine, unbroken sprouts [attains the same].
Rising up from his seat or even his throne, he himself should pay homage to Him.
That person who worships Hari with fresh, tender leaves of the *dhātrī* tree attains every desire without delay. (22-23)
He who worships Viṣṇu and the Lord with Śāṇḍilya leaves, unbroken petals, Dhattūra flowers, and Arka blossoms, shall cross to the further shore of the ocean of worldly existence.
He who offers an excellent plantain fruit to Viṣṇu through a Brahmin [attains the same].
All the thirty gods, headed by Śakra, praise him day and night.
O Brahmin, he who with devotion offers wheat flour to the one in the form of Gopāla during the month of Caitra is liberated from all sins. 25–26.
O beloved Mādhava, in the pure month of Mādhava,
a devotee of Viṣṇu should renounce meat, sexual intercourse, and oil. Having arrived [in this month], the Vaiṣṇava should indeed perform his ritual bath during the month of Mādhava.
One should renounce the food of others and should not eat twice;
O twice-born one, at dawn one should worship Viṣṇu according to the previously mentioned rite.
In the month of Vaiśākha, one should bathe Viṣṇu with water scented with flowers.
One should bathe Acyuta in cool waters until the time of twilight,
and worship the Lord with devotion at the three junctions of the day with various kinds of food offerings.
In the month of Vaiśākha, the Lord of Lakṣmī is adorned with garlands of *damana* flowers.
O brahmin sage, what will the gratified Supreme Lord not bestow?
O wise one, who is capable of calculating the merit of him who, in the month of Vaiśākha, offers barley-rice to the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu)? 31-32.

Whatever is given in the month of Mādhava for the sake of pleasing Mādhava, all that offered to Mādhava himself becomes inexhaustible (33). Whatever other meritorious deed is performed in the month of Mādhava, [that too becomes inexhaustible].
For one who acts for the pleasure of Mādhava, there is no destruction of that [merit].
That man who, in the month of Vaiśākha, provides a water-station (prapā) for the satisfaction of Mādhava, obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice day after day. 34–35.
The month of Vaiśākha is difficult to obtain and bestows the fruits of all actions;
there, Hari should be worshipped even while setting aside hundreds of other duties.
He who performs the worship of Hari for even a single day in Vaiśākha [attains the supreme goal].
Whatever fruit one constantly obtains by worshipping Hari for six years,
that same fruit a Vaiṣṇava person attains every day in the month of Vaiśākha by worshipping Viṣṇu in the form of the Aśvattha tree, for the sake of attaining the fruits of the four aims of life.

O brahmin sage, even he who performs the service of the Aśvattha tree with merely a mouthful of water goes to the supreme abode, liberated from ten million sins. He who binds the root of the Aśvattha with stones and the like—
What does the Lord, in the form of the Aśvattha tree, bestow upon him?
If one beholds the Aśvattha tree and offers a prostration, he too goes to the supreme abode; there is no doubt that his lifespan increases. (40-41)

O Jaimini, whatever deficiency or excess may occur in the performance of that righteous rite at the foot of the Aśvattha tree, all the sacred fords (tīrthas), such as the Trisrotas and others, are present there. 42. O Jaimini, [all the tīrthas are there].
Wherever even a single Aśvattha tree stands, the best among trees, he who worships that Aśvattha is indeed a worshipper of Viṣṇu,
O twice-born one, because the Blessed Lord himself is present in the form of the Aśvattha. 43-44.

Out of contempt, the fool of deluded intellect destroys the Aśvattha, the best of divine trees; there is no action in this cycle of existence which, having been performed, brings about such purification.
This Aśvattha is the king of trees and is proclaimed to be the very form of Hari.
Therefore, there is no protector whatsoever for those who destroy the Aśvattha tree.
For the Brahmin who beholds the Aśvattha, touches it, stays beyond it,
and likewise bows down to it, Hari removes all the sins residing within his body.
If one who is capable does not prevent someone from cutting down an *aśvattha* tree upon seeing him, his own pair of eyes will be plucked out by Yama using fish-hooks.
(48) Furthermore, he who says to a fool, "Do not cut down the *aśvattha*," [is likewise punished].
The King of the Pretas himself cuts out his tongue with a knife.
That man who destroys even a single small branch of the Aśvattha tree incurs the fruit of ten million murders of Brahmins.
O best of the twice-born, whatever sin exists in the killing of a Brahmin, in sexual intercourse with the wife of a preceptor,
in drinking liquor, in theft, and even in the misappropriation of a deposit;
and whatever sin exists in the killing of an embryo or in the killing of a cow— [all that is destroyed by this].

Whatever sin exists in the killing of a woman, as well as in approaching another's wife; in the killing of one who has sought refuge, and likewise in the killing of a friend; in failing to speak the words of trust, and in the act of harming one's husband—[all such sins are removed]. 52–53.
The terrible sin that people incur by censuring others and by eating on the day of Hari (Harivāsara) is even more severe than the sin obtained from cutting down an Aśvattha tree.
That person who, out of delusion, destroys an Aśvattha tree— the very form of Viṣṇu— [incurs such a sin].
No sinner equal to him has ever been heard of on the circle of the earth.
O best of the twice-born, listen with a concentrated mind, my son, as I recount the majesty of the Aśvattha tree, which destroys all sins along with its ancient histories.

Formerly, in the Tretā Yuga, there was a brāhmaṇa named Dhanañjaya who was a devotee of Hari; he was a learned man always intent on the welfare of all living beings, constantly devoted to honoring his kinsmen, and ever engaged in the offering of lamps. (57)
Truthful in speech, having conquered anger, and free from violence and hypocrisy,
that best of virtuous twice-born men, desiring liberation, always worshipped the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Ishvara, with supreme devotion. 58–59.
Then, perceiving his devotion to be great and very firm, the Lord took away all his wealth by some pretext;
nevertheless, that best of virtuous twice-borns [remained devoted] to the high-souled Keśava.
The wise man performed worship daily with supreme devotion in the *cakra*.
O twice-born one, seeing that all the wealth he had acquired with great difficulty was lost, that brāhmaṇa’s mind became overwhelmed with grief beyond thought.

That brāhmaṇa, a knower of the supreme truth, performed the avoidance of eating while firmly fixing his own mind upon the worship of Mahāviṣṇu. Furthermore, Janārdana, having recognized the devotion of that brāhmaṇa, [bestowed his grace].

Then, Śamadatta, being very firm, brought about the separation from his kinsmen. O best of the twice-born, the relatives of that brāhmaṇa, deluded by the māyā of Viṣṇu, began to commit acts of violence against him at all times.

Then, having become free from all attachments, the brahmin, being constantly delighted, worshipped Puruṣottama with abundant devotion. And that divine man, having set aside his wealth for the worship of Keśava, [continued his practice].
And Mādhava, the Lord of the Universe, abandoned all grief for his kinsmen;
moreover, O Jaimini, Mahāviṣṇu, though full of compassion, was curious and continued to carry away even his sons day after day. 67–68.

Nevertheless, O best of the twice-born, he constantly worshipped Viṣṇu Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions, with devotion twice as great as before. Thereupon, his wife became exceedingly distressed by grief and sorrow.
Having gone to her father’s house, she was utterly deluded by the māyā of Viṣṇu.
Then, that brāhmaṇa, who was solely devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu, being alone,
never at any time contemplated misfortune with his virtuous mind.
Once, that best of the twice-born, a foremost among the devotees of Viṣṇu,
took an axe upon his shoulder and went into the forest for the sake of wood.
That virtuous brahmin would always take wood from the forest in this manner.
At the onset of winter, being destitute of clothing, he sought to ward off the cold.
Once, that best of brahmins was unable to go into the forest;
he struck a branch of an *aśvattha* tree standing in his courtyard. 73–74.
In the meantime, the great Viṣṇu, the best of gods, emerged from that Aśvattha tree with a mind distressed by agony.
Along with the Brahmin, he beheld Viṣṇu before him, four-armed and with eyes as broad as lotus petals.
Wearing yellow garments, with curled hair and beautiful locks, bearing his own weapons such as the lotus and others;
making the fresh clouds crimson at twilight by the flowing streams of extensive blood;
like fire itself, that Supreme Lord, who is invisible even to the hosts of gods, is beheld with ease.
With a pair of eyes beautiful with streams of tears of joy, the Brahmin praised him with gentle words:
The Brahmin said: "O Hari! O Murāri! O sole Lord of the world! O Govinda! O Dāmodara! O Mādhava! (77)
O Lord of Lakṣmī, Keśava, enemy of Keśin, Nārāyaṇa, infinite sovereign, be gracious!
78 What can I say regarding Your incarnation? For without You, there is no one else at all on this earth.
Or rather, what more shall I say? You pervade the entire world with Your qualities, and You are equal toward friends and enemies alike. 79

Having bestowed upon someone devotion to the Lord Viṣṇu—which resides within the body of Hara—and having taken away his prosperity, I shall grant him joy; for devotion granted by the Great One brings great merit. (80) I consider that high-souled one to be like the best among the sinful, O you of infinite forms, who constantly [bestows such grace].
For that very reason, it is a matter of divine mystery that a sinner does not behold your pair of feet.
(81) O Viṣṇu, although I am the foremost among those who suffer, yet today I shall behold you—the very Self of the worlds—with my own eyes, just as Indra beheld his own self. (82)

"Even if my worship at the end were but slight, O Indra, I would never fail to give you the substance; yet even so, You, Keśava, the sole object of worship, have been seen by me in person before me. This very tree of devotion—consisting of the triad of virtue, wealth, and desire—has been granted to me by You."
O Lord, sprinkled today by the rain consisting of the water of Your vision, my head has borne the fruit of absolute liberation (kaivalya).
O Keśava, O Viśvamūrti, may my head become the foremost among all the heads of the worlds; O God of gods, my mind now truly enters into the pair of Your lotus feet. 84–85.
Vyāsa said:
Having thus praised Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World, who is free from all ailment, that virtuous twice-born man spoke to him again with devotion, his hands joined in reverence. 86.
The Brahmin said:
"O God of gods, Lord of the world, you who bestow grace upon the worlds!
This body of yours is drenched in blood from the blows of whips. (87)
"The lineages of all the Daityas have been destroyed by you in battle;
who on earth is capable of slaying you, O Lord? This is a great marvel.
The Blessed One said:
"O child, what you have said is true; there is no doubt in this matter.
Neither a Dānava nor a Rākṣasa is capable of killing me.
I am indeed the very form of the Aśvattha tree, struck down by you with an axe."
"Therefore, O twice-born one, blood has now fallen upon my body.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, that brahmin was overwhelmed with fear.
The twice-born man censured himself in many ways by means of his own mind:
"Fie upon that destiny which, in truth, makes me the foremost among all sinners; though I am the giver of the lord of the three worlds, a great agony remains in my heart. (91-92)
Viṣṇu, the remover of all sins, has been made ill by me;
this boundless sin cannot be remedied by me alone.
For when he is pleased, even sinners become honored by the gods.
"Tormented by the pain caused by her being struck by me, I am now struck with grief. Alas!
Even the gods, led by Brahmā, propitiate her with supreme devotion;
yet I, a sinner, have inflicted this agony upon her heart. (94–95)
"What is the use of austerities, what use of prayers, or what use of houses and livelihoods for me?
He alone is the giver of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, free from all affliction.
Having spoken thus, O best of the twice-born, he [struck] his own axe with [his hand].
He resolved to give it as a necklace for the sake of pleasing Viṣṇu.
Knowing his devotion to be firm, the compassionate Lord of Kamalā, who is kind to His devotees, quickly took that supreme jewel from his hand. 97-98.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O child, why do you perform such an extremely cruel deed?
I am never pleased with those men who commit suicide."
"I am exceedingly pleased by your devotion; do not fear, O best of beings. Choose a boon, O chief of Brahmins, whatever dwells in your mind.
The Brahmin said:
"O Supreme Lord, O Master, let this great [discus] given by me, which causes no pain,
remain within your body as a supreme boon.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O twice-born one, this karma was performed by you out of ignorance;
therefore, this great offense of yours must not be disregarded. Since you are the best among devotees, I am always to be protected by you. (102)
"O child, although I see faults in you day after day, my great devotion to you has always increased. Therefore, O child, I now wish to attain freedom from my debt to you. (103-104)
"O Vāmana, dispel all fear from the sky before me.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"In birth after birth, may you, O best of all gods, [be mine]. (105)
"Let there be firm devotion to Hari while he remains; what is the use of other boons?
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, spoken out of affection for Keśava, [he remained silent]. (106)
Then, being pleased, the Lord gave him the garland that was upon his own neck;
having embraced the brahmin like a father embracing a son, he spoke these gentle words with his four long arms. 107.107-108ab.
The Blessed One said:
"O Brahmin, since you are my devotee, by my grace all that is auspicious shall come to pass for you before long. (108)
"O best of beings, worship me eternally in the form of the Aśvattha tree through the yoga of ritual action;
I shall accomplish every desire of yours.
Having spoken thus to that best of the twice-born and embracing him once more, Keśava—
In that very moment, the abode of compassion became peerless;
having obtained the garland from Viṣṇu’s neck, that brāhmaṇa, the best of Vaiṣṇavas,
considered himself to have accomplished his purpose and remained in his own home.
Then, O brahmin-sage, at the command of Keśava, Kubera himself rained down vast amounts of wealth into the house of that brahmin; furthermore,
a magnificent palace was constructed for him by the artisan Viśvakarman.

By the command of Nārāyaṇa, his excellent palace there, named Vaijayanta, shone forth, accompanied by male and female servants and adorned with various articles; it was crowded with tens of millions of elephants and horses. 114.
Even those kinsmen of his who had been lost became reunited with him.
His wife, having shown him contempt, came to his house herself;
and that wife, whose son was dead, [was restored] through the compassion of Keśava.
The subjects became stable, and the Brāhmaṇas were devoted solely to their master;
having enjoyed all pleasures for a long time together with his sons and grandsons, that best of Brāhmaṇas, along with his wife, attained liberation at the end of his life.
Vyāsa said:
Viṣṇu himself is manifest as the Aśvattha tree, the best of trees;
for those men who practice devotion to it, nothing inauspicious exists anywhere.
O best of men, for him who serves the Aśvattha tree while meditating upon Viṣṇu,
the Lord, being pleased, grants the supreme state.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Aśvattha," in the Kriyāyogasāra of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The Thirteenth Chapter.
Vyāsa said:
O best of the twice-born, in the month of Jyeṣṭha, [one should worship] the Blessed Janārdana.
One should worship with a spirit of devotion, bathing [the deity] with cool waters;
likewise, fragrant *udvartana* powder and *āmalaka* fruit should be offered,
as well as fragrant oil for Hari, day after day during the summer season.
O best of Brahmins, one should daily install the Lord of Kamala in a very beautiful temple that is well-perfumed and cool,
within a pavilion for the people; however, not in a fierce place, nor in a house of fuel where there is smoke.
And one should place the Lord of Kamalā within the lying-in chamber;
fanned by very long white chowries, O best of the twice-born, what does the Lord of Kamalā not bestow when he is well-pleased in the month of Jyeṣṭha?

O best of beings, Hari, fanned by long-handled yak-tail whisks and by the wind from palm-leaf fans and the breeze from pure garments, grants everything desired in no time at all. 6. By the wind from palm-leaf fans and the air from holy raiment.
All those who worship Viṣṇu during the summer go to heaven.
During the summer, one should perform anointing with fragrant pastes and sandalwood for Hari, and one should enter the body of Mādhava.

O best of the twice-born, there is no doubt that one should install Viṣṇu during the twilight hours in a place where the heat has subsided, in a garden of blossoming flowers, or likewise in a grove of tulasī, where the breeze is gentle. 9.

He by whom Viṣṇu is adorned with garlands of *pāṭala* flowers in the month of Jyeṣṭha should be known as one who has performed a thousand horse-sacrifices. Furthermore, that person who gives a string of pearls to the Lord of Śrī during the summer season [attains great merit].
Hari shall grant the status of a sovereign ruler to him in birth after birth, who adorns Śrī Kṛṣṇa with a garland of jewels during the summer;
O brāhmaṇa, listen to me as I describe the fruit of his merit. 12.
As far as Brahmā has created this entire world, O Jaimini,
so long shall he remain in the city of Viṣṇu, adorned with garlands of jewels,
as well as with ornaments of gold and silver. 13–14.
He who adorns Kṛṣṇa during the summer season shall also obtain that same fruit;
and he who offers a variegated couch along with a water-pot to Hari,
the God of gods, shall never be miserable.

During the summer season, O best of Brahmins, one should give garments and other items to Hari; a pure, fine, and delicate cloth should be offered to Him. Furthermore, one who worships Hari with divine, fragrant *acyuta* fruits [attains great merit]. 16–17.
Having gone to the city of Indra at the end [of the world], he shall joyfully drink the nectar of immortality;
whoever worships the Lord of Kamalā with divine priyāla fruits attains that very fruit—what is the use of further words? 18.

O best of Brahmins, that devotee of Viṣṇu who, during the summer heat in the month of Āṣāḍha, with faith offers very cold gruel accompanied by various side dishes to the God of gods, the Teacher of the World, [attains great merit]. 19–20.
Having bathed him with curds, the wise man should worship him with devotion;
thereafter, he does not drink the milk from his mother’s breasts again.
During the onset of the rainy season, one should worship Hari, who is dark as a rain-cloud, with *kadamba* flowers.

O brahmin-sage, he who propitiates [the deity] shall attain the supreme goal. O best of brahmins, for him who adorns a pavilion resembling a blazing fire with garlands of kadamba flowers, there shall be the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
O best of the twice-born, the Lord of Kamalā, when worshipped with fragrant ketakī flowers, removes all the suffering of human beings; likewise,
[he is pleased] by divine jackfruit, well-ripened and mixed with ghee.
When worshipped, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu bestows supreme sovereignty.
O best of the twice-born, a Vaiṣṇava desiring liberation should faithfully offer curd-rice to Hari every day during the month of Āṣāḍha.
The Vaiṣṇava person who indeed offers the butter of Kṛṣṇāyana, being purified of all sins, goes to the world of Brahmā.
[Likewise, one who offers] with Śephālikā blossoms and Yūthikā flowers... 27.
He who worships the Supreme Self shall go to the supreme state.
O twice-born one, may that merit which belongs to him who worships Hari with fragrant, blossoming *mālatī* flowers become our merit as well. (28–29)

A person on earth who worships Janārdana, the kinsman of the world, with *kaṇṭaka* flowers and *vakula* blossoms, attains every desire; likewise, one who worships Hari with great *mahā-mahā* flowers and *kurubaka* flowers [attains the same]. 30.

Hari is always pleased with him who worships Him with full-blown flowers; he who worships Viṣṇu with *sairīyaka* flowers, with jasmine flowers, or with *karavīra* blossoms, attains the presence of Hari. (31-32)

O best of the twice-born, he who offers parched grain mixed with ghee in the month of Śrāvaṇa shall have prosperity facing every direction in the home of that brahmin sage. In the month of Bhādrapada, [one should worship] the healthy Nārāyaṇa.
With faith, the wise man should worship Him who bestows the four goals of human life.
Having constructed a new temple free from all calamities,
he should install therein the lotus-eyed Lord Janārdana.
A human being should not place Hari, the ancient destroyer of the serpent [Kaliya], in a house scattered with gadflies, mosquitoes, flies,
and the like, nor in a house where the door is covered in mud or the walls are crumbling. 36.
O best of the twice-born, the wise man who installs Lord Parameśvara in a temple of Viṣṇu during the rainy season goes to the wonderful Candratapa and the world of the Moon. 37-38.
At night, during the time of worship, one should ward off gadflies and mosquitoes from the Lord of the World with various kinds of incense; and having covered Acyuta,
who is reclining on the couch, with fine muslin cloths.

During the rainy season, one should establish Viṣṇu in a divine temple at night. Furthermore, a mortal desiring liberation should worship the Lord of Gods with fresh, fragrant *kahlāra* petals day after day in the month of Bhādrapada.
In the month of Bhādrapada, the Destroyer of Arjuna (Janārdana) should be worshipped with ketakī flowers;
for in the month of Bhādrapada, the ketakī is equal to wine.
He who worships the Joy of the Yadus (Yadunandana) with the divine, ripe fruits of the palmyra tree [attains great merit].
And he shall not undergo the great suffering of dwelling in a womb again.
That mortal who, with faith, offers a ripe palm fruit accompanied by ghee and milk to the Enemy of Mura (Viṣṇu), shall go to the abode of Hari. 43–44.

O best of the twice-born, in the month of Bhādrapada, a Vaiṣṇava should offer a cake made of *tāla* flour with ghee to Hara for the sake of attaining the Absolute (*kevala*). O Brahmin, during the month of Bhādrapada, one should consume only vegetables.

A Vaiṣṇava person desiring liberation should not eat at night. O best of Brahmins, in the month of Āśvina, people should diligently offer water to Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions, to Hari during the forenoon.
The Lord of Kamalā accepts that water as if it were nectar;

and that water which is offered at midday to the Wielder of the Discus (Cakrapāṇi) should be understood, O best of the twice-born, to be like that [nectar]. 48. He accepts that water just as [the former does].

If water is offered to Govinda in the afternoon, that water becomes like blood; therefore Hari does not accept it. For this very reason, O best of the twice-born, one should worship Hari in the forenoon.
O best of Brahmins, by the compassion of Keśava, one obtains every desire; however, one should not perform the worship of Hari wearing only a single garment,
nor would Keśava accept the worship even if it were performed in such a manner.
If one performs the worship of Hari with an unwashed garment,
that worship shall be fruitless, and Viṣṇu will not be pleased. Likewise,
if worship is performed for the Discus-bearer by people whose topknots are untied, [it is likewise in vain].
One does not obtain the fruit of that worship, and it becomes a mere offering of food;
for when the worship of the Lord of the World is performed in an unrefined house, O best of Brahmins, that worship indeed becomes a mere offering of food. 54.

A wise Brahmin does not perform bathing, worship of the gods, giving of gifts, or honoring the ancestors without a *tilaka*. Whatever meritorious rite is performed without having taken the *tilakas*, [is rendered fruitless]. 55–56.
All that [sin] is reduced to ashes, yet the perpetrator shall become a denizen of hell;
O best of Brahmins, he whose body is seen marked with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus should be known as Acyuta himself. (57)
On the right arm, one should draw a conch and a lotus for a Vaiṣṇava;
on the left, a discus and a mace—he is indeed Viṣṇu, there is no doubt about this.
One should draw a lotus on the right arm above the conch.
O twice-born one, the entire mass of his sins perishes in an instant; he who draws a mace upon a wheel on his left arm is saluted even by the gods,
headed by Śakra, O best of the twice-born.
A wise person should draw the pair of feet of Murāri upon his own forehead;
even a sinful soul, upon seeing that, becomes liberated from sin.
He who holds the great eight-syllable mantra, as well as the Fish and Tortoise incarnations, within his heart—
The best of all Vaiṣṇavas should draw [these symbols], for he purifies the three worlds;
to him whose body is marked day by day with the weapons of Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the Universe, grants the supreme abode.

Whatever action a person performs, whether auspicious or inauspicious, with their body marked by the weapons of Kṛṣṇa, all of that becomes inexhaustible. So too do the Dānavas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, and Vetālas [be affected]. 64–65.
Piśācas, pannagas, yakṣas, vidyādharas,
as well as kinnaras, guhyakas, grahas, and bālagrahas; kūṣmāṇḍas, ḍākinīs, and other such creators of obstacles.
Seeing it marked with the weapons of Kṛṣṇa, all fled in fear;
even the island-dwellers, the forest-dwellers, and other inhabitants of the woods,
upon merely seeing it marked with Kṛṣṇa's weapons, fled away out of terror.
Great diseases such as jaundice and others that afflict the body fall away from the person who,
with devotion, beholds the body marked by the weapons of Kṛṣṇa;
that human being obtains a fruit equal to the sight of Kṛṣṇa himself.
The son of Aśvinī should worship Hari with dūrvā grass blades arranged in groups of three;
his lineage of dūrvā will continue without interruption.
Whoever offers a karkaṭī fruit to Hari in the month of Āśvina, [attains great merit].
O twice-born one, when Kārtika has arrived— the most auspicious of all months— sorrow never arises in the heart of that wise man who worships Dāmodara, the God of gods, with devotion. 72.
O best of Brahmins, in the month of Kārtika, for the sake of pleasing Viṣṇu,
a wise man should perform his morning bath according to the prescribed rules.
Furthermore, he who renounces meat and sexual intercourse during the month of Kārtika [attains great merit].
O best of the twice-born, one who bathes at dawn when the sun has entered the zodiac sign of Libra is liberated from sins accumulated in other births and attains the supreme goal; likewise,
eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) and observing celibacy destroy even the greatest of sins.

O best of Brahmins, he who indulges in meat and sexual intercourse during the month of Kārtika will become a village pig in birth after birth. Furthermore, a devotee of Viṣṇu [should avoid] eating twice a day, food belonging to others, and oil. 76–77.
When the month of Kārtika has arrived, one should diligently abandon [other lights];
O twice-born, listen as I describe in brief the fruit for him who offers a lamp to Dāmodara during the month of Nabhas. 78.
Freed from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and other afflictions,
he shall go to the city of Dāmodara and remain there for ten million yugas; the inhabitants of heaven, led by Indra, behold a lamp burning in the sky.
Seeing this, they were all delighted and said to one another:
"This man is the best among those of meritorious soul, for he is devoted to the worship of Keśava;
he is the one who offers a lamp to the Wielder of the Discus during the month of Kārtika."
O best of Brahmins, Hari is always pleased with him during the month of Kārtika.
That man who offers an imperishable lamp in the temple of Hari day after day throughout Kārtika obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice every single day. 82-83.

He who worships Hari with a hundred thousand Tulasī leaves in the month of Kārtika obtains the fruit that a human being gains from a hundred thousand horse-sacrifices. He who would worship the imperishable Viṣṇu with a hundred thousand Bilva leaves—
O Lord of the World, through [His] grace one attains supreme liberation.
Whatever is given during the month of Kārttika dedicated to Viṣṇu, all that becomes inexhaustible; this which I speak is the truth. 85–86.
He who, in the month of Kārttika dedicated to Viṣṇu, offers a leaf of the *asu* tree smeared with ghee day after day to a Brahmin, shall have his residence in the city of Viṣṇu;
this applies whether the leaf is a full-blown lotus petal, white or even black. 87.
What on earth is difficult for one to obtain who worships the Beloved of Kamalā?
What has that foremost of the twice-born not given to Hari—the conqueror of Daityas and the Lord of Viṣṇu—who has not offered a lotus in the month of Kārtika? 88–89.
Does the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, the husband of Śrī, not grant everything to that enemy of Kaiṭabha who, having offered even a single lotus, gives it to him?
By whom has Hari not been worshipped with lotuses during the month of Kārttika? 90.
In birth after birth, Lakṣmī shall remain in his house.
He who gives lotus seeds to the great-souled Keśava is born into a pure Brāhmaṇa family in every successive birth. 91–92.
Born into a brahmin family, he shall be a friend to the four Vedas,
wealthy, possessed of many sons, and a sustainer of his household.
O Jaimini, it is told as a truth that there is no flower equal to the lotus.
By worshipping Govinda with this, even a sinful soul becomes a partaker of liberation.
O best of the twice-born, I shall now describe in detail the greatness of the lotus flower along with its history; listen attentively. 94-95.
There was once a unique man among people who was not a Brahmin, yet he was a knower of all the scriptures;
his mind, like a bee, always dwelt upon the lotus feet of Hari.
He was ever devoted to the gods, the Brahmins, and his own teachers. (96)
Having performed worship, even hundreds of his duties and non-duties were fulfilled;
he regarded the wealth of others as poison and the wives of others as his own mother, and he behaved in this same manner toward both friend and foe. 97–98.
Seeing a guest approaching, that brāhmaṇa who knew the supreme truth felt no pride at all toward the beggar, even if he were the best of the twice-born.
By him, all sacrifices have been performed and all vows completed.
By one desiring to cross the terrible and shoreless ocean of saṃsāra—
once that best of the twice-born, who was solely devoted to the worship of Hari, reflected in his mind upon his own death and his former birth. (100–101)
"Who was I, or what was my state, and what actions were performed by me in the past?
How was this birth obtained, and where shall I go again?"—
thus reflecting, that Brahmin sighed again and again.
In order to learn the former account, he went to the sacred field of Śiva (Śivakṣetra).
There, with palms joined in reverence and endowed with supreme devotion, the Brahmin praised the god Śaṅkara, Śiva, with sweet words. 103–104.
The Brahmin said:
Salutations to you, O Mahādeva; salutations to you, O Supreme Lord. Salutations to you, O Śaṅkara, O Śāna; salutations to you, O Bestower of Boons, O Sovereign Lord. 105
Salutations to you whose form is knowledge; salutations to the giver of knowledge;
salutations to you who dwell within the lotus-hearts of all beings. 106.
Salutations to you, the creator of the world; salutations again and again to the father of the world.
Salutations to the creator of dissolution, and salutations to the Lord of bound souls (paśu). 107. Salutations to you whose eye is fire; salutations to you whose eyes are fire;
salutations to you whose eye is the moon, and indeed salutations to you whose eye is the sun. 108.
Salutations to you who are adorned with ashes; salutations to you who are clothed in animal skins;
salutations to you who wear a garland of bones; salutations indeed to you, the blue-throated one. 109. Salutations to you, the five-faced one; salutations to you, the wielder of the trident.
Salutations to you who shatter the pride of Kandarpa; salutations to you of terrifying form. 110 Salutations to you, the God of gods; salutations to you, the enemy of Tripura.
Salutations to you, the Lord of Pārvatī; salutations to you of terrifying form. 111
Salutations to you, whose mind is exceedingly satisfied by the devotion of Bāṇa;
salutations to you, who possess many forms, and indeed to you who possess the universal form (Viśvarūpa). Salutations to you, the bearer of the Gaṅgā, the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice.
Salutations to you, the lord of the *pretas*; salutations to you, the wielder of the *pināka* bow.
Salutations to you, the Sovereign (*Īśāna*); salutations again and again to you, the wise one (*Manīṣin*). Salutations to you who are visible; salutations again and again to you who are invisible.
Salutations to you who are conceivable, salutations, salutations to you who are inconceivable.

(114) You alone are Brahmā, you alone are Viṣṇu, the sole lord of the thirty gods, you alone are the Sun, and you alone are the Moon, the remover of all suffering; salutations, salutations to you, the Supreme Lord. (115)

Having heard his hymn of praise, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world, the Supreme Lord, suddenly appeared in person, gracious and serene. Beholding him who had manifested, he who is saluted by all the gods—
That brahmin, possessed of extreme devotion, prostrated at his feet (117).
Once again, that best of virtuous twice-borns, his mind overflowing with joy,
joined his palms in reverence and praised the Lord Mahādeva, the granter of boons (118).
The Brahmin said:
"O Lord of Gods, that very Lord whom even the gods, including Indra, do not behold—I see him directly; this is my great good fortune. (119)

With a mind established in meditation, I behold this invisible Supreme Lord directly; what further goal remains for me to achieve? Even for those who are great sinners, by the mere remembrance of Your name—
They go to the supreme abode; let me behold that Lord.
I have achieved my purpose, I have achieved my purpose, I am blessed and have achieved my purpose!
Salutations to you, salutations to you; be gracious, O Supreme Lord! 121–122.
Mahādeva said: "O best of the twice-born, I am pleased by these words of yours. Choose a boon, O highly fortunate one; indeed, I desire to grant you a boon. (123)
The Brahmin said:
"O Lord, I behold you directly as the Supreme Self, invisible even to the gods; what need have I for other boons? (124)

Nevertheless, O Mahādeva, you who are full of compassion and desirous of granting boons, tell me, O Supreme Lord, whatever I ask: who was he that stood before you in the past, and what deed was performed by him of old? 125.

O Lord, I have fallen into the ocean of saṃsāra; how, O Master, is a body obtained through karma? A living being is smeared with sin, and by the power of that sin, one attains a miserable rebirth. 126–127.

"O Lord, O Śaṅkara, by the power of which karmas was this birth obtained by me, which brings manifold sufferings? Be gracious and tell me, for this birth is rooted in sin and is the cause of suffering in every life. (128)

Therefore, I wish to know the account of my own previous existence. While staying within my mother’s womb, I was tormented by the fire of the stomach and covered in urine and excrement as a result of my past karmas.
O Lord, destroyer of the distress of your devotees, I do not consider any suffering in this saṃsāra to be equal to the pain of dwelling in the womb; how was that experienced by me?
In this saṃsāra, which is most terrible and filled with various miseries...
In this world which is devoid of essence, deluded by the illusion of Viṣṇu, and a refuge for sins;
which is difficult to cross, bereft of kinsmen, and joined with desire, anger, and the like;
and which indeed bestows sorrow and disease, as well as birth and death. (132–133)
"O Lord of the worlds, I have fallen into a state beyond this shore; O Śiva, O All-pervading One, if you have favor toward me, tell me all of this.
Mahādeva said:

Although this great secret, more secret than the secret of the best of the twice-born, is not to be disclosed, nevertheless I shall speak it to you, my devotee. Formerly, you were an excellent Brāhmaṇa born into the Śabara lineage.
Known as Daṇḍapāṇi, he remained there, inflicting suffering upon the world;
having abandoned the fear of the next world and being devoid of discernment, he adopted the conduct of a bandit, which brings misery and supreme affliction to those in distress. (136–137)
Seeing you engaged in the conduct of a bandit and exceedingly merciless,
all your other brothers likewise became bandits.
O best of brahmins, I shall now declare the names of those brothers to you.
With whom you formerly practiced banditry as brothers—
Daṇḍin, Daṇḍāyudha, Dattavān, Dattabhū, Suṇḍa, and Daṇḍaketu— these six are proclaimed to be your brothers. (139-140)
By those most terrible brothers, who were utterly devoid of compassion,
all people were constantly kept in a state of agitation through the use of punishment;
and by you, together with those wicked brothers, this was done out of greed for wealth.
In the forest wilderness, hundreds of thousands were slaughtered by you; O twice-born one, having always slain them with sharp arrows while dwelling in the woods,
you ate their raw flesh along with wine.
Then, out of fear of you, all the merchants abandoned their methods of transport in that forest; thus, misfortune has fallen upon them forever.
For him who has wealth, that is not true wealth; for him who has a home, that is not a true home.
When his wife became a non-wife and you attained the state of a Dasyu,
thus praised by those brothers of his in that very great forest,
he went toward a lake for the sake of bathing, exhausted by the fatigue of the journey.
O best of the twice-born, having bathed there according to custom, those brothers, being hungry, ate lotus stalks and drank water;
then, O most excellent of the twice-born, you too, O virtuous one, did so out of curiosity.
At that very time, many fully blossomed lotus flowers had been consumed. Then, a Brahmin known as Sarvaveda, who wandered in the forest, arrived there for the purpose of bathing. 148–149.
Having bathed there, that virtuous soul, desiring to worship the Blessed Lord Janārdana,
requested a lotus from you with great humility. Then, O best of Brahmins, you gave him a single, perfectly pure lotus.
With supreme devotion, you offered this lotus for the worship of the Lord of Kamalā.
O best of the twice-born, being pleased by the lotus offered by you, he performed the worship of Viṣṇu, the creator of all, right there. 151–152.
Seeing that brāhmaṇa, who was devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu and was well-versed in all the Vedas,
you too laughed and praised Viṣṇu, the granter of all desires.
Then, having worshipped the Supreme Soul, the bestower of the fruits of the four aims of life, [you continued].
Having come from afar according to the prescribed method,
O best of beings, by that offering of a lotus, by that prostration,
and by witnessing the worship of Viṣṇu, all your sins have been destroyed. 154–155.
Then, after some days, O best of the twice-born, you met your end and passed away in that very great forest when your time had come.
The Blessed One, the abode of compassion, was pleased by that very deed.
"I grant you a supreme abode, difficult even for the gods to attain.
For thousands and hundreds of *manvantaras*, various pleasures shall be enjoyed there by the grace of the Lord of Kamalā. (157–158)
Then, O twice-born one, at the conclusion of that karma, having returned to this land of action (Karmabhūmi) by virtue of those fruits of merit, you were born into a lineage of the twice-born;
O best of beings, having obtained birth in a pure family of Brāhmaṇas.
Having attained unwavering devotion to Hari, which is the refuge of all virtues,
you have propitiated the Lord Mahāviṣṇu through the yoga of action; He will grant you supreme realization, and through that knowledge, you shall become liberated.
"Go, O Brahmin; may it be well with you. Return to your own home with joy. You have obtained the sight of me and are liberated from the bonds of worldly existence.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, the Lord of the Universe vanished right there, O Brahmin; and that Brahmin, having achieved his purpose, also went to his own home.
Then, for three days, he worshipped Viṣṇu with beautiful lotus flowers.
With great effort, you propitiated the Supreme Lord for the sake of praise.

Having worshipped Viṣṇu for a long time with various lotus blossoms and beautiful flowers, and having attained knowledge through the grace of the illustrious Garuḍa-bannered Lord, he went to liberation. 164–165.
"If such is the fruit for one who offers even a lotus unintentionally, I know not what would happen for one who offers it with devotion to Viṣṇu!
Truth, truth, again truth—this is indeed the truth as I speak it. (166)

By worshipping Hari with lotuses, the supreme state is attained. (167) He who offers even a single lotus to the enemy of Mura shall have no further birth in this world, which is fraught with fear. (168)
Those who worship the compassionate Nārāyaṇa, the granter of desires, with full-blown lotuses—even if they are burdened by intense sins for a single day—those sinners too attain liberation. 169.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Essence of Kriyā-yoga," in the glorious Padma Purāṇa. 13.
Chapter Fourteen. Vyāsa said:
O best of the twice-born, [one should worship] him who is accompanied by Mahālakṣmī in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.

A Vaiṣṇava should indeed worship the imperishable Viṣṇu with a spirit of devotion. O best of Brahmins, one should not worship Viṣṇu in a land of barbarians (mleccha-deśa), nor in the abode of the fallen, nor in a place pervaded by foul odors.

One should not perform the worship of Viṣṇu in the presence of heretics, those who have committed great sins, or those who speak untruths; nor should one do so in the vicinity of those weeping or engaging in quarrels.
Likewise, one should not perform the worship of Hari in the presence of those who mock;
nor should one worship Viṣṇu in the presence of those addicted to accepting gifts,
nor in the house of misers who covet the wealth of others.
One should not perform the worship of Viṣṇu with deceitful conduct;
rather, in the worship of Nārāyaṇa, one should be a brāhmaṇa devoted to supreme bhakti. Abandoning all other thoughts, one should become intent on the meditation of Hari.
O best of the twice-born, one should not perform the worship of Hari while making cries of distress, sighing,
or expressing wonder, nor in the company of heretics; rather, having become single-minded, one should worship the God of gods, the Teacher of the World.
O twice-born one, even if a flower is offered into ashes, it reaches Lord Hari;
yet the mortal who, exhausted by hundreds of anxieties, offers a flower upon stone discs, does not obtain that same result from the Lord.
Having become single-minded, the wise person should conquer Viṣṇu through devotion.
Whatever action is performed with a deluded mind is fruitless;
all action is dependent on the mind, and the three worlds are dependent on the mind.
Therefore, having made the mind firm, one should worship the Lord of Kamalā;
for if one's mind is elsewhere while the worship is elsewhere, O best of the twice-born,
his undertaking will not bear fruit even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Even if one has performed purification with great effort and is devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu,
if he is devoid of purity of mind, he is regarded as a Cāṇḍāla.
O twice-born one, even if penance is performed for a very long time according to the rules, it is fruitless if it is undertaken without devotion.
All of it would be entirely useless, being merely a purification of the body—
even if gold equal in size to Mount Meru were given to a brahmin householder for the sake of fulfilling a request or even for spiritual welfare, yet without devotion. (15)
Therefore, becoming single-minded and endowed with devotion and faith, one should offer vegetables such as *savāstuka* in the assembly of Viṣṇu;
and whoever offers a divine, well-ripened orange fruit [attains great merit]. (16–17)

O best of the twice-born, Keśava is worshipped by us with great effort; whatever new object is dear to the Lord Hari, that very thing one should offer with devotion to Murāri during the month of Āgrayaṇa. 18.

When the month of Pauṣa has arrived, a Vaiṣṇava person should bathe the divine Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the bestower of boons, with divine sugarcane juices. O best of Brahmins, he who bathes the Lord Viṣṇu with sugarcane juices—

One who enjoys all happiness in this world and, upon death, goes to the ocean of sugarcane juice—he who offers sugarcane as an oblation to Viṣṇu, the God of gods—attains that very fruit; what is the use of further elaboration? (21)
By giving well-milked fresh rice mixed with curds along with betel leaves to the enemy of Mura (Viṣṇu), a mortal shall obtain all desires;
likewise, by discarding all old garments and offering them to the enemy of Mura. 22–23.
On the transit of the sun into Capricorn (Pauṣa-saṃkramaṇa), a man desiring liberation should give a new garment for the purpose of warding off the cold to a Brahmin who is Śrī Viṣṇu;
he should also give a seat of ten colors.
I shall describe the fruit of the merit for one who, having worshipped the Lord of Kamalā, sounds the conch; listen, my child, with a concentrated mind.
Such a person is liberated from all sins, including the sin of approaching those who should not be approached. (25-26)

O best of the twice-born, I shall now describe the merit of him who sounds the bell marked with the *vṛṣabha* (bull) of Hari during the time of worship; having gone to the city of Viṣṇu at the end, he rejoices together with Viṣṇu. (27)
Freed from all sins, such as the eating of forbidden food,
he ascends a beautiful chariot and goes to the abode of Viṣṇu;
there, he enjoys all his desires for a duration of hundreds of crores of kalpas.
Returning again to the earth, that best of the twice-born, learned in the four Vedas,
shall enjoy all desires there for a duration of hundreds of crores of kalpas; then,
having gone once more to the city of Viṣṇu, he attains unsurpassed liberation.

He who plays the lute at the time of worship of the Lord of the World shall become a leader among scholars, honored by mortals in every birth. He who plays the mṛdaṅga drum during the worship of the Enemy of Kaiṭabha [shall likewise attain such status].
The Blessed One, being pleased with him, grants his desired fruit:
the *ḍamaru*, the *ḍiḍima*, the *jharjharī*, and likewise the *madhurī*; as well as the *paṭaha*, the *dundubhi*, the *kāhala*, and the *siṃdhuvāraka*.
Listen to the merit of him who plays the bell-metal gong, the cymbals,
or the flute at the time of the worship of Mahāviṣṇu;
freed from sins such as theft, he goes to the abode of the Wielder of the Discus.
Having attained supreme knowledge, one is liberated right there.
O best of Brahmins, I shall now describe the merit of whoever makes the sound of a *kala* instrument or a wind instrument at the time of worship of the Teacher of the World.
Accompanied by tens of millions upon tens of millions of kinsmen, he goes to the abode of Hari;
having attained knowledge there, he shall obtain imperishable liberation.
He who, endowed with devotion, dances in the temple of Viṣṇu— [37-38]
O best of Brahmins, he who sings the songs of that Viṣṇu with devotion before Nārāyaṇa attains the supreme abode of Viṣṇu;
indeed, he obtains the status of a king in the cities of the Gandharvas. 39.
The Vaiṣṇava person praises the Lord of the World with hymns of praise and devotion;
the Blessed One, being pleased with him, grants all his desires.
He who worships Hari according to this rite month after month— 40–41.

O brahmin-sage, that Acyuta grants grace very quickly to those mortals who desire to cross this ocean of the world, which is exceedingly deep and the source of all suffering; and they all worship the beautiful pair of lotus feet of the Supreme Person, which are served by the hosts of the gods. 42-43.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Worship of the Blessed Lord," in the Kriyāyogasāra of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Fifteen. Vyāsa said:
O twice-born one, listen again as I speak of the majesty of Nārāyaṇa,
by hearing which a human being becomes liberated from all sins. O best of the twice-born, this entire world has arisen from a portion of Viṣṇu.
Therefore, the wise who seek the supreme truth perceive everything as consisting of Viṣṇu.
All the gods, including Brahmā, Śaṅkara, Rudra, and others, are portions of Viṣṇu; therefore, one should take refuge in Viṣṇu alone, the worship of all the deities.
For those who remember the names of Viṣṇu, which remove all sins, no inauspiciousness exists anywhere by whatever means;
O best of the twice-born, every single sin is indeed purified through such action.
This remembrance of Viṣṇu is unfailing and destroys all sin. Whether sleeping, eating, speaking, standing, rising, or walking,
a Vaiṣṇava person seeking liberation should indeed remember Viṣṇu without ceasing.
O brahmin-sages, all the exalted sages have declared that there is no restriction of time for the remembrance of the Lord of Kamalā, which destroys all suffering;
such is the power of the name of the high-souled Keśava.
I shall relate this to you in brief; listen to this historical account.
In former times, during the Kṛta Yuga, there was a pure Vaiśya named Paraśu, the best of the Vaiśya lineage, who had mastered all virtues. 8–9.
O twice-born one, by the turn of fate, that Vaiśya, afflicted by the diseases of cough and asthma, fell into the power of death during his first stage of life.
His wife, named Jīvantī, was slender-waisted and still in the prime of her youth.
When her husband had died, she went to the abode where he resided;
O best of the twice-born, though she was tormented by her kinsmen, that woman, proud of her fresh youth, continued to live and pursued a course with paramours. 11-12.

Blinded by passion, that woman of beautiful hips and full breasts abandoned her vows, her religious observances, and even her domestic duties, for her heart was constantly enamored with her paramour in the prime of her youth.
O best of the twice-born, he never saw the path of dharma. Seeing her to be of such ill character, her father— who was devoted to dharma and fearful of infamy— spoke thus, filled with extreme anger.

O wicked sinner, having obtained birth in my lineage which is free from all defects, why do you commit this sin? If your mind is indeed intent on committing sin, then come, let us eat it together! 16.
"O ill-fated one, go from my presence; leave this house of mine!
Thus addressed by her father, she, with eyes reddened by anger, abandoned her father's home and departed as she pleased.
Then, wandering about by her own will out of a desire for a paramour, she abandoned her shame and took up the profession of a courtesan.
Whether he was a Pulinda, a Śabara, or even a Caṇḍāla, he would go to her house.
That unchaste woman also sported with joy with him as he arrived; furthermore, that courtesan did not, at any time or in her mind, consider the fear of the next world, proceeding in due order. 20–21.
Once, a certain excellent Brahmin who was a hunter arrived at her house, bringing a young parrot for the purpose of selling it;
that courtesan also [saw] that most excellent young parrot.
Having honored the hunter with wealth, she accepted him with supreme affection;
out of constant curiosity, she provided for Śuka’s nourishment by daily giving him suitable food through her courtesan.
Considering that young parrot, which was most difficult for the courtesan to bear,
as her own son, she took upon herself its upbringing.
O best of the twice-born, that bird also, by her command, always [performed its duties].

And he conducted himself with affection for her mind as if she were a kinswoman. Then, having developed an attachment to her, that parrot was constantly taught by the courtesan the name "Rāmā," spelled out in beautiful syllables.
The name of Rāma is the Supreme Brahman, greater than all the gods and most exalted;
it is the destroyer of all sins. Śuka was constantly reciting it.
(28) Merely by the utterance of "Rāma," for both of them—that parrot and that prostitute—[the supreme state was attained].
All that most terrible sin was utterly destroyed.
Once, both that chief of courtesans and that best of brahmins passed away simultaneously;
they both met their end at the same time. (29-30)
Then, in order to bring them back, Dharmarāja dispatched his servants, Caṇḍa and others, who had been assigned the task of seizing all sinners.
Thereupon, all those servants, Caṇḍa and the rest, set out with great speed.
By the command of Yama, those servants of Viṣṇu, possessing the prowess of Viṣṇu and holding nooses and mallets in their hands, all arrived; they came in order to bring them [back],
but seeing the two bound with nooses, the servants of Viṣṇu fell prostrate.
The messengers of Viṣṇu spoke these words to the angry messengers of Yama, who were like unto gods:
"O messengers of Yama, how strange is this speech heard from your mouths! (34-35)
Even while they were devotees of Hari, these two were punished by the son of Bhāskara;
alas, the conduct of the wicked is never noble, for they constantly commit violence against the virtuous even with great effort. 36.
This conduct of the wicked who have committed sins is truly marvelous.
(37) Those of virtuous soul perceive the entire world as free from sin, whereas the sinful do not perceive the whole world as being filled with sin, as if it were their own. (38)
Virtuous people find satisfaction upon hearing of the merit of those whose souls are meritorious;

sinful people find satisfaction upon hearing of the transgression of sinners. Just as sinners find satisfaction upon hearing accounts of sin, so too do the righteous find satisfaction upon hearing of virtue. 39. Upon hearing a discussion of sin, sinners are satisfied.

O twice-born one, they are not satiated even upon obtaining hundreds of loads of gold; alas, such is the powerful illusion (māyā) of the high-souled Mahāviṣṇu, that they commit even sins that cause them self-affliction. 40-41.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, those messengers of Viṣṇu, who were solely devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu, severed the bonds of those two brahmins with the edge of their discus. 42
Then those messengers of Yama, enraged and resembling fire,
suddenly rained down heaps of blazing coals there.
Daṇḍa said:
"I too had already arranged for Śuka and the sinful courtesan to be brought here;
that you have arrived at this very moment is truly wonderful. O most excellent ones, it was surely as if you intended to bring them both when you came.
"Therefore, wage war against us right now!
Having spoken thus, those powerful messengers of Rāma, holding their weapons aloft and full of arrogance, filled all the directions with lion-like roars.
Likewise, the high-souled messengers of Viṣṇu, headed by Supratīka,
made the entire world resound with the melodious blasts of their conchs. Then,
by the great messengers of Yama, arrows were released from their bows.
Those messengers of Viṣṇu, though concealed, were present in that exceedingly terrible battle;
some hurled spears, some [threw] pikes into the great ocean, some [discharged] thousands of arrows, and others, out of rage, [cast] discs. 48–49.
The messengers of Viṣṇu, the great gods, pulverized those great weapons discharged by them with arrows, maces,
clubs, and other weapons. Then, by the edge of their discuses, the followers of the Bhagavat shattered the weapons of the Yāmyas.
The feet of some were severed, and likewise the arms of others;
some had their heads split off, and some had their chests pierced;
with their wounds most extraordinary, some fell down lifeless, their limbs scattered.
Some with one foot severed, some with one hand severed, those messengers of Yama suddenly abandoned the battle and fled. Then, seeing those messengers intent on flight, [he spoke].
Fierce with rage and wielding a mallet,
Caṇḍa, the most eminent among the hosts of Yama’s messengers and possessed of extreme prowess,
entered the battle and struck Viṣṇu’s servants by the hundreds with his mallets.
Then the messengers of Bhagavān, enraged, swiftly rained down a shower of sharp weapons upon Caṇḍa of fierce prowess; thereupon,
Caṇḍa struck the messengers of Viṣṇu individually with his mallet.
His body drenched with flowing blood, he struck them;
thus beaten by Caṇḍa in battle, the messengers of the Lord abandoned their strength and fled toward the back of Suprakāśa. 57–58.
Then Suprakash, enraged, with eyes resembling hibiscus flowers and mace in hand, entered the battle with great strength. Possessing prowess equal to Vishnu, he struck out in his fury.
From the mallet and the fierce hand, which struck terror into the onlookers,
there arose a most terrifying [being] accompanied by smoke and a foul stench,
having been struck by that swift and violent mallet.
Then that furious Caṇḍa immediately released a shower of sparks that caused extreme terror;
with that very mallet, O brahmin-sage, he struck the exceedingly powerful Suprakāśa.
Then, O Brahmin, Suprakash, forgetting his pain and filled with wrath,
struck Chamunaki’s servant Chanda with a mace;
struck by him, Chanda there was drenched in blood.
O Jaimini, he fell unconscious upon the ground like the rising sun;
then those messengers of Yama, seizing the swooning Caṇḍa, fled from the battle while crying out "Alas! Alas! in terror.
Then, O Jaimini, best of the twice-born, all those messengers of Viṣṇu were exceedingly delighted and blew their conchs; meanwhile,
the messengers of Yama remained drenched in streams of blood.
Crying out and overwhelmed by fear, they went into the presence of Yama.
The messengers of Yama said:
"O mighty-armed son of the Sun, we are the executors of your commands."
Nevertheless, such a miserable state has been brought upon us by the messengers of Viṣṇu.
O Lord, although you are indeed the foremost among great sinners,
you have gone to the abode of Nārāyaṇa through the power of the name of Rāma.

"O Lord, even those wicked souls who have committed sins and deserve to be punished by you go to the city of Viṣṇu; what then is your sovereignty? O messengers of Viṣṇu, this humiliation has not been inflicted upon us by them."
"O Lord, this belongs to you alone, since we are your servants.
Yama said:
"O messengers, remember those two syllables of the name of Rāma."

Then the Lord Nārāyaṇa shall punish those two who are to be chastised. O servants, listen: there is no sin in this world that does not immediately reach complete destruction through the remembrance of Rāma, however firm it may be. 73–74.

Those humans who daily remember with devotion the names of Madhusūdana—which destroy the flood of terrible misfortunes—of You who are worshipped by the foremost of the gods, even if they are sinners, O soldiers, they are certainly not to be punished by me.
(75) [They who call out: "Govinda! Keśava! Hara! Jagadīśa! Viṣṇu! Nārāyaṇa! Mādhava, who is compassionate toward those who take refuge in You!"...

Those men who constantly speak thus on earth—"Even these most sinful ones are not to be punished by my soldiers"—O Lord of the gods, destroyer of the distress of devotees, kinsman of the wretched, Lord of Lakṣmī, and remover of all sins; those humans who always speak this on earth, even if they are sinners, are not to be punished by my soldiers. (76-77)
I bow daily to those whose mouths always utter the names Śrī Vāsudeva, Puruṣottama, and Mādhava— names worshipped by hosts of gods headed by Dāmodareśvara—
and to those whose hearts are captivated by discourses on Nārāyaṇa, the sole Lord of the world, and Murāri. 78.
I am always under the command of those excellent warriors who possess the form of lotus-eyed ones; 79.

Those who are devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu, who are devotees of the devotees of Hari, who are intent on the vow of Ekādaśī, and who are free from deceit—even if they are sinners, they are not to be punished by me as my soldiers, provided they carry the water from Viṣṇu’s feet upon their heads. 80.

I bow down to those servants who eat the remnants of the food offerings (naivedya) of the Blessed One Madhusūdana, which destroy the entire multitude of sins; who constantly wear tulasī upon their ears and heads;
and who are devoted to the worship of Kṛṣṇa’s lotus feet, intent on honoring brāhmaṇas, and seekers of virtue.
Those who bestow supreme happiness upon the hearts of the distressed, they are my soldiers; I am perpetually dependent upon them.
(82) Those who are always devoted to speaking truthful words, who are beloved by the world, and who protect those who have come for refuge;
and those men who constantly regard the wealth of others as poison—these are my soldiers and are not to be punished. (83)

Those who are devoted to the gift of food and the giving of water, those who bestow land and desire the welfare of all the world, those who satisfy people deprived of their livelihoods, and those who are peaceful— these messengers are certainly never to be punished. (84) Those who are intent on nourishing their kinsmen, those who speak kindly, and those whose minds are free from pride, anger, hypocrisy, and envy.
"I never engage in conversation with those who are free from evil views and have conquered their senses.
Vyāsa said:
Thus were the servants of Yama enlightened by that Yama.
O best of Brahmins, those who know the incomparable power of Hari, the Lord of the universe,
know that the names of Viṣṇu indeed surpass all other gods;
among them, however, the name "Rāma" is remembered as the most excellent by the knowers of reality.

O twice-born one, this pair of syllables "Rā-ma" is superior to all mantras; by its mere utterance, even a sinner attains the supreme goal. Indeed, the power of the name of Rāma is equal to the worship of all the gods.
O Jaimini, Maheśa alone knows this; no one else knows it.
A mortal obtains that same fruit by merely remembering the name of Rāma as he would obtain from reciting the thousand names of Viṣṇu. 89–90.
"How strange is this conduct of human beings, it is said:
those of evil intent do not remember the name 'Rāma,' which bestows liberation! To speak of it is no small labor, yet it is exceedingly beautiful to hear."
Nevertheless, those of evil intent do not say, "Rāma, Rāma.
Even liberation, which is extremely difficult for men in this world to attain, is obtained by the name of Rāma alone; what action could be greater than this? 92-93.
O best of embodied beings, those sins remain within the bodies of living beings only so long as they do not remember the one who bestows happiness by chanting "Rāma, Rāma.
This applies even during śrāddha rites, water libations (tarpaṇa), offerings to spirits (balidāna), and festivals.
Whether at a sacrifice, in a gift, in a vow, or even in the worship of the deities (95),
or indeed in other Vedic rites,
the wise man who desires their fruit should remember [the Name] with devotion, saying "Rāma, Rāma" (96).
O best of Brahmins, he who recites the six-syllabled mantra "namo rāmāya," preceded by the syllable *oṃ*, attains union (*sāyujya*) with Hari.
A person who performs the worship of Hari with this six-syllabled mantra [attains the same].
Through the grace of the wielder of the discus, one obtains all desires (98).
O best of the twice-born, at the time of death, that man who remembers "Rāma,
Rāma," even if he be the most sinful, attains supreme liberation (99).
Those wise ones who remember the name "Rāma" during this pilgrimage will attain all perfections on their journey; of this there is no doubt.
Whether in the forest, in the wilderness, or even in a terrifying cremation ground—
O twice-born Jaimini, one should remember the name of Rāma;

by that, no calamity shall exist for him—whether at a king’s gate, in a difficult pass, in a foreign land, in the presence of bandits, upon seeing a bad dream, or during afflictions caused by malevolent planets. 101–102.
In times of fear caused by portents, as well as in the fear of wind-related diseases,
a mortal who remembers the name of Rāma never encounters anything inauspicious anywhere.
O best of the twice-born, the name of Rāma is the warder-off of all that is inauspicious.
The wise should constantly remember that which bestows both worldly desires and liberation.
O brahmin-sage, that very moment in which the name "Rāma" is not remembered becomes useless; this is the truth as I speak it. 104–105.
Remembering the names of Hari, human beings do not perish.

(106) A mortal on earth who desires the destruction of the sins of ten million births and seeks prosperity, constantly remembers with devotion the sweet name of Viṣṇu, which bestows liberation upon the world. (107)
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the Kriyāyogāsāra of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Sixteen. Vyāsa said:
O best of the twice-born, listen once more as I proclaim the majesty of Mahāviṣṇu, the Supreme Self, which destroys all suffering.
Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and likewise others born of low origins—
Those who have taken refuge in devotion to Hari have undoubtedly achieved their life's purpose (2). Even a Brahmin who is not a devotee of Hari should be known as worse than a dog-eater;
whereas even a dog-eater who is a devotee of Hari should be known as superior to a Brahmin (3).
How can he be a brāhmaṇa who is devoid of devotion to Hari? And how can he be an outcaste (śvapaca) whose mind is possessed of devotion to the Blessed Lord?
For when Viṣṇu is worshipped even by an outcaste without guile, [he is truly honored].
Then he saw him likewise, superior even to the twice-born learned in the four Vedas.
Formerly, in the age known as Dvāpara, there was a Śabara named Cakrika who attracted the world; though born of noble lineage, he was devoid of proper conduct. 5–6.
One who has conquered anger by avoiding false speech, who refrains from harming others, who is compassionate, free from hypocrisy, and devoted to his father and mother—
yet who has never performed the Vaiṣṇava vow nor heard the scripture of liberation (mokṣa-śāstra). 7.
Nevertheless, unwavering devotion to Hari arose in his mind;
constantly remembering "O Hare! O Keśava! O Govinda! O Vāsudeva! O Janārdana! and other such names of the Wielder of the Discus.
O best of the twice-born, whatever forest fruit he obtained,
that descendant of the royal Śabara lineage would eat and give it back into his own mouth.
Having recognized its sweetness from that, [the king] then drew it out again from his mouth.
Out of devotion, he gave [offerings] to Hari every day with great pleasure;
whether it was leavings or not leavings, he knew neither of the two,
for the innate nature of his own birth constantly resided upon his head.
Once, while wandering within the forest of an excellent brāhmaṇa, he found a single ripe fruit of the priyāla tree; then,
having obtained that fruit, he was filled with joy.
Having recognized him with great agitation, he placed it within his own mouth.
O twice-born Jaimini, listen as to what happened when that fruit entered his throat while he was placing it within his own mouth. 14–15.
O twice-born one, having diligently held the opening of his throat with his left hand and secured it with his right hand,
Cakrika, who was solely devoted to the worship of Hari, began to reflect.
The fruit of this was that when I gave [the offering] to that enemy of Mura, no one else like me, a sinner, has ever been born in this world.
Then, having meditated upon Hari in many ways, he made up his mind. 17–18.
Nevertheless, O twice-born one, that fruit had not emerged from his neck; yet that exclusive devotee of Hari, having cut off his own neck with an axe,
brought that ripe fruit and gave it to the god Viṣṇu.
Having arrived in his presence and contemplating him alone within his heart,
he fell upon the surface of the earth with all his limbs drenched in blood; seeing him lifeless, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu became deeply distressed.
There is no devotee equal to this man even among me;
for he has brought me satisfaction by cutting off his own throat.
Just as this man, possessed of devotion, has performed a virtuous act despite the physical transformation.

"By giving this, I shall attain freedom from debt; what object of value could I possibly have left? (23) This man is blessed, he is most blessed, he is truly blessed—of this there is no doubt—for even at the cost of his own life, he has brought me satisfaction. (24)

"Even if the state of Brahmā, or the state of Śiva, or even the status of Viṣṇu were granted, still the debt owed to this devotee would not be discharged. Having spoken thus, the Lord whose banner is Garuḍa was exceedingly pleased.
Then, with his own lotus-like hand, he touched the head of this Śabara.
From the touch of that lotus-hand, the Śabara— whose suffering had departed, who was possessed of great goodness, and who was devoted to Nārāyaṇa— arose.
Vyāsa said: Then, O twice-born one, Keśava, like a father for his son, sprinkled the dust from his own body upon the limbs of that best of devotees with his own garment.
Beholding Janārdana in embodied form, Cakrika,
with his head bowed and palms joined in reverence, praised him with sweet words.
(29) Cakrika said:

O Govinda, Keśava, Hara, Jagadīśa, Viṣṇu, although I do not know the words of the yoga of praise for You, nevertheless my tongue desires to praise You; O Lord, be gracious and forgive this fault of mine that has increased. 30.
O Lord of All, wielder of the discus, there are indeed men here on earth who, having abandoned You, worship another.
Those very people are the sole abode for the accumulation of misfortunes; yet, O Lord, you are one who bestows grace even upon me.

(31) O Lord, although you know that for men the liberation from the bonds of existence comes only through devotion to you, the sole Master of the world—even so, the Blessed Viṣṇu is well-pleased with me, though I was born into a lineage of Śabaras, who are exclusively sinful. (32)
Even the hosts of gods, including the four-faced Brahmā, do not obtain the touch of Your lotus-hand, which is so exceedingly beautiful;
yet today I have obtained from You that which no one else among Your own compassionate servants has ever received.
O Blessed One, by You the enemy of the gods and others—the demon Kaṃsa, the son of Nimi, who had committed every sin—was destroyed.
Salutations to You, who, together with Indra and the host of gods, formerly acted for the welfare of mortals; salutations to You, the bestower of supreme auspiciousness.

(34) Salutations be to You, who resemble a dark cloud, by whom—O most powerful one, O Supreme God, born as the son of Vasudeva—the two demons Arimardana and Arjuna were slain, as well as the wicked Kālayavana and Dhenuka in battle. (35)
O Śrī Kṛṣṇa Dāmodara, by you, O Ananta, the unshakable glory of the Lord of the Gods was formerly established; salutations be to you, the supreme Lord, the ultimate refuge of the Yadu dynasty.
By you, the Pārijāta tree was taken away and the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra) was conquered.
Salutations again and again to You, by whom Maheśa was conquered in sport!
Having made Vṛkodara the instrument, Jarāsandha was struck down;
and those arms of Bāṇāsura which were struck off were indeed destroyed by You. 37-38.
Salutations again and again eternally to Him by whom the burden of the earth was removed through that great-souled one;
salutations again and again eternally to Him who slew the kṣatriyas by means of His illusory power. 39.
Vyāsa said: Thus praised by the high-souled wielder of the discus, Viṣṇu,
being exceedingly pleased, spoke, "Choose a boon," O Jaimini.
Cakrika said:
O Supreme Brahman, O Supreme Abode, O Supreme Self, O Compassionate One!
I behold You directly; what need have I for other boons, O twice-born one? (41)
No form of yours has been meditated upon, nor has worship ever been performed for you;
no offerings of food, divine flowers, divine incenses, or lamps have been presented, nor have your names ever been remembered by me. (42–43)
O Lord, I have not held the water from your feet upon my head,
nor have I consumed your food offerings (naivedya), nor have I observed your vow;
nevertheless, I have seen you— what need have I for other boons?
"I am born into the lineage of Śabaras and am excluded from all religious duties;
nevertheless, I have today obtained that very lotus-foot of yours which is difficult even for the gods to attain—what need have I for other boons? (45-46)
Nevertheless, O Beloved of Kamalā, since you desire to grant me a boon, may my mind remain steadfast and not sink, through your grace.
(47) The Blessed Lord said:
O noble-minded one, having attained great satisfaction through the rain of nectar from your words, I, a sinful servant, [offer this: that excellent lotus which was given by you to me, your child. 48.
"By this I am exceedingly pleased; filled with joy, I accept your devotion.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, who accepts devotion and is composed of compassion, [departed].
He embraced that devotee with his four long arms.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O best of wheel-turners, I am pleased with your devotion."
"Indeed, O child, this gift that has been given will certainly bear fruit quickly.
(51) Then the Supreme Lord, the Soul of the Universe and Protector of the World, embraced that great devotee once more and vanished right there before the eyes of the Brahmin. (52)
Sacakrika, being exceedingly contented and devoted to the worship of Hari,
abandoned his sons, wife, and other attachments, and went to the city of Dvārakā.
Having arrived there, by the grace of the Lord of Kamalā, he attained [liberation] in this very manner.
At the end of his life, he attains liberation, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Therefore, the God is subject to His devotees; He is pleased by devotion alone, and not by hymns, nor by wealth, nor by austerities, nor by recitation.
O best of the twice-born, although the fruit was given by him as leavings, Viṣṇu was nevertheless pleased, knowing his unwavering devotion.
Therefore, Lord Nārāyaṇa [should be worshipped] in this worldly existence by those seeking liberation. 56–57.
Those men who, with firm devotion, worship the pair of lotus feet of Vāsudeva—
which are indeed worshipped by the foremost of gods such as Indra— truly attain liberation.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter of the *Kriyāyogasāra* in the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
The seventeenth chapter. Jaimini said:
"O Guru, speak once again of the majesty of the Lord of Kamalā."
Who indeed could ever become satiated after drinking the nectar of Hari’s stories?
Śrī Vyāsa said:
Truly, there is no one else in this world as meritorious as you.
Since you desire to hear the majesty of Keśava with devotion, [listen],
for the delightful narrative of Nārāyaṇa thus purifies the three worlds—
the listener, the questioner, and the speaker alike, O best of the twice-born.
Listen, O child, to the greatness of the Lord of Lakṣmī, which destroys all sins; I shall describe it in brief as it bestows the fruits of the four aims of life.
He who worships Viṣṇu with supreme devotion for even a single day—
