Hari instantly removes the sin committed over ten million lifetimes by such a person. How can that mortal be considered virtuous by whom Hari has not been propitiated?
And how can he be considered a sinner who possesses devotion toward the Lord Nārāyaṇa?
There is a city named Puruṣottama, the best among all cities;
it is endowed with every excellence and is the refuge of all the hosts of gods. It is declared to be the most excellent of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Because Keśava himself dwells in that beautiful city,
O Bhadra, there was formerly a certain Brahmin named Tanu;
he was handsome, pleasant of speech, and born of a pure lineage.
Having reached the prime of youth, the handsome brahmin became infatuated with desire;
casting aside the fear of the next world, he became devoted to courtesans. He no longer engaged in the study of the Vedas nor of the Purāṇas in any way.
Due to association with heretical people, he abandoned his noble reputation;
he became a receiver of gifts from those unfit to offer them, a thief of others' property, a reviler of dharma, and that brahmin was devoted solely to sin. 11-12.
That lowest of Brahmins abandoned the conduct of a Brahmin as well as his sense of truthfulness;
he ceased honoring his gurus and guests, and whatever action was most sinful, that alone he performed. 13.
O Jaimini, there is no action more meritorious than that;
yet once, having committed a sin, that Brahmin, overcome by fear of public shame, performed a *śrāddha* devoid of devotion to the *śrāddha*. (14–15)
Having gone to the house of the sharp-toothed one, he addressed the courtesan, saying:
"O lady of broad hips, this is the day of my father's śrāddha ceremony. 16.
Though I have come here bound by your virtues, O beloved, behold this night that brings fear to all the worlds;
the expanse of the sky is pervaded by masses of pouring clouds. 17.17-18a.
With my mind drawn by your virtues,
I have come to your house even on this night whose path is obscured by fresh rain, guided by Kāma— who appears like lightning amidst the clouds— to instruct me in my purpose. (18–19)
O beloved, having come day and night through faith in the meditation upon your virtues,
no joy arises in me even for a moment without seeing you; indeed, O causeless one, it is only through sorrow that I have come to see you.

O beloved, what need have I for bathing in the waters of sacred pilgrimage sites? Sprinkled with the water of the sacred site that is your love, I have attained heaven; what further fruit could there be for me in serving those who grant happiness in the hereafter? 21-22.
"O beloved, by your grace, heaven itself shall be attained by me while I am still alive;
out of fear of ill-repute, the śrāddha rite was performed at home. In this śrāddha, not even the slightest lack of faith on my part is to be found. (23)
"You are my prayer and my austerity; you are my policy, O beautiful one.
O beautiful one, I have sought refuge in you alone with my whole being in this world; command me, for I am ever at your service—what shall I do?"
Sumadhyamā said:
"O son, because of you as a son, our father has become as if sonless; even on the day of the ancestral śrāddha, you desire to engage in sexual intercourse. (26)
If one of evil mind engages in sexual intercourse on the day of the ancestors,
his ancestors shall become eaters of semen, and he too shall be so.
If a fool, out of delusion, engages in sexual intercourse on the day of the ancestors, [the same fate awaits him].
That śrāddha would become graspable by rākṣasas; of this there is no doubt.
(28) If your mind were truly directed toward Viṣṇu with the same affection as you have declared for me, then what indeed would you not attain? (29)
The life of embodied beings dwells between the staff of Yama;
yet, O fool, you always commit sin without fear.
Life, O fool, is as transient as a water bubble, perishing in an instant.

For what purpose would you, with a mind fixed on permanence, always desire that which is inscribed upon your forehead? How can one who has the two syllables "Death" written there commit a sin that brings all suffering?
O twice-born one, since this earth belongs solely to the great Viṣṇu who is free from illusion, a man who constantly commits sin remains delighted; therefore,
O embodied being, give me a place in your own body, which is a refuge for the wicked.
"For the fire of the Aśvamedha sacrifice burns like a blazing Vītihotra.
Vyāsa said:
"And thus it was spoken by that beautiful courtesan because of the sin instigated by fate."
The Brahmin, having committed a sin, reflected in his mind:
"Fie, fie upon me, a great sinner, a fool, the foremost among transgressors! That knowledge belongs only to the prostitute; it does not exist in me, a wicked soul. (35-36)
Having obtained birth in a pure Brahmin family, I have constantly committed great sins that lead to self-destruction;
for when one is born, death is certain, and when one dies, Yama is the master.
Due to my lack of discernment, how then shall I perform [these deeds]?
Recitation, austerity, likewise burnt offerings, and the study of the Vedas; the conduct of a Brahmin, the honoring of guests, devotion to the guru, and the worship of the twice-born. (38–39)

"I have not performed the ancestral rites (pitṛyajña) and other ceremonies, nor have I worshipped the Lord of Kamalā; how then will there be a supreme destination for me? [I shall go to] the high-souled Mārkaṇḍeya, the best among those who know all dharmas."
The wicked Brahmin, having prostrated on the ground like a staff, spoke words of praise:
(41) The Brahmin said: "Salutations to you, O best of the twice-born; salutations to you, O long-lived one!"
Salutations to you, the Great Soul, whose nature is Nārāyaṇa.
Salutations to you, the son of Mṛkaṇḍu, who desires the welfare of all the worlds;
salutations indeed to you, the ocean of knowledge, who is changeless.
Thus praised by that Brahmin, Mārkaṇḍeya,
the great ascetic who has reached the further shore of the meaning of all scriptures, spoke with supreme delight.
(44) Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"I am exceedingly pleased by your devotion; choose a boon, O highly fortunate one. I shall immediately fulfill your desire; it shall not be otherwise.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O best of the twice-born, I am the foremost among the evil-minded, devoid of the conduct of the twice-born,
constantly intent on harming others, and always devoted to the wives of others. O lord of brahmins, great sin has been perpetually committed by me, a fool."
"Merit performed for another is never respected [by them].
In this terrible, sorrow-inducing, and exceedingly fearsome ocean of saṃsāra, how can there be deliverance for me, a great sinner? (47-48)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:

O best of the lords of brahmins, even though you have committed sin, you are indeed the foremost among those of meritorious soul, since this wisdom—so difficult to attain in saṃsāra—has arisen within you. 49
The virtuous vision of those with virtuous souls increases day by day,
while the sinful vision of those with sinful souls increases day after day; yet even by you,
who are of a sinful nature, this sinful vision is being restrained.
Therefore, the Lord of the World appears truly gracious to you.
They say that even a mortal who, having committed a sin, turns away from sin even further, is a superior man who has worshipped Acyuta in a previous birth. 51-52.
Seeing his own devotee engaged in sin, the Lord Mahāviṣṇu bestows upon him a vast intellect so that he may attain a righteous state.
Therefore, O best of brāhmaṇas, you have been a worshiper of Acyuta throughout every birth.
"Before long, may it be well with you;
there is no doubt that you will hear whatever has been asked by you, provided you listen attentively, for the time for my daily rites is now approaching. (54-55)
"There is a certain twice-born man named Dānta who knows the true nature of all things;
he will tell you all that—go to his hermitage.
Thus instructed by the wise Mārkaṇḍeya, that Brahmin [set out].
He quickly went to the holy and exceedingly beautiful hermitage of Dānta,
which was adorned with Aśvattha, Campaka, Bakula, and Priyaka trees, as well as other flowering trees, making it most enchanting. (57-58)

The fragrance of blossoming flowers pervaded every direction, swarms of bees hummed, and the forest resounded with the great noise of falling fruit; the water was likewise cooled by a breeze blowing very gently.
Then the Brahmin, having entered that most enchanting hermitage— which was crowded with hundreds of beasts of prey and teeming with disciples and grand-disciples—
beheld the self-controlled knower of reality surrounded by all his hosts of disciples.
Having praised that best of Brahmins, who was self-controlled and whose very nature was Nārāyaṇa, that most excellent of the twice-born bowed his head at his feet. 62.
Dānta said:
"Who are you, O blessed one, who have arrived here? What is your purpose? Tell me the truth; for what reason have you come to me now? 63.
Bhadra-tanu replied:

"O highly fortunate one, I am a Brahmin, yet devoid of Brahminical conduct; I am known by the name Bhadranu, having committed every kind of sin. How can there be for me, a sinner, the severance of the evils of saṃsāra?"
"O Brahmin, tell me this, for you are a knower of all principles. Dānta said: "Listen, O Brahmin, to this supreme secret; it is spoken by me out of affection for you."

By this, the severance of the bonds of saṃsāra occurs for men. (66) Abandon association with heretics; always cultivate the company of the virtuous. [Abandon] desire, anger, delusion, greed, pride, and envy. (67)
O twice-born one, by constantly remembering the names of the high-souled Mahāviṣṇu, one abandons untruth and violence even without effort.
O best of the twice-born, likewise, the sweeping and the smearing [of the temple] should be performed again.
Adorn the path with five lamps at the temple of Keśava (69).
Always perform service to Brāhmaṇas and service to your kinsmen;
likewise, give gifts of water and constantly perform the five great sacrifices (70).

O best of beings, as you listen to the stories of Hari and chant the twelve-syllable mantra, and perform all these rites, supreme knowledge will arise within you; through that knowledge, you shall attain liberation. 71–72.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
O Brāhmaṇa, please explain the detailed exposition of those auspicious things which have been mentioned by you; what are delusion, hypocrisy, and envy? (73)

What is untruth? What are non-violence, compassion, peace, and self-restraint? What is said to be equanimity? What is the worship of the Lord of Kamalā? (74) What is said to be day and night? And likewise, what is the remembrance of Viṣṇu?
O best of Brahmins, tell me everything regarding the five great sacrifices (mahāyajñas) and which mantra consists of twelve syllables; by your grace, I shall thereby attain the supreme state. (75-76)
Dānta said:
Those who, abandoning the duties approved by the Vedas, perform other actions and are devoid of their own traditional conduct, are proclaimed as heretics (pākhaṇḍas). 77.

Those who adhere to their own proper conduct, act in accordance with the Vedas, and are free from sinful desires are celebrated as virtuous people (sajjana). That desire which is always directed toward women, the acquisition of wealth, and so forth— [is what they lack].
"O best of Brahmins, that which proceeds with desire is called *sakāma* (with desire).
That burning which arises in the heart upon hearing one's own censure should be known as *sakrodha* (with anger), which destroys all dharma. (79-80)
O best of the twice-born, that desire which arises in the heart upon seeing the wealth and other possessions of others, wishing to acquire them, is proclaimed as greed (lobha).
"This is mine, this is my mother, this is my father, this is my wife, this is my house."

This other sense of "mine-ness" is proclaimed as delusion (samoha). "I am a great soul, wealthy; there is no one equal to me on earth"—whatever pride of this kind arises in the mind is called intoxication (mada) by the wise. 82–83.
"He who says of himself, 'People censure me; fie upon my life!'"—this self-reproach is *matsara* (envy).
That which is a truthful statement and bestows happiness upon all people is [the opposite]. 84.
That which is true should be known as such, and its opposite as untrue.
When the thought arises in the mind, "When will sovereignty, wife, children, and so forth, become inexhaustible for me?"—that is proclaimed as non-violence (ahiṃsā). 85–86.

O best of the twice-born, that ground of desire which arises in the heart even with effort to remove the suffering of others is proclaimed as *adaya* (compassion). That satisfaction which arises in the mind is called *śānti* (tranquility) by the wise.
The wise who perceive the truth have declared that self-restraint (*dama*) consists in the non-restraining of the mind from other despicable actions;
O best of Brahmins, you always remain content in both suffering and happiness. 88–89.
Likewise, maintaining an equal vision toward both enemy and friend is indeed declared to be non-violence (ahiṃsā).
O Brahmin, when a person worships Hari with faith using food offerings, perfumes, flowers, and so forth,
that is proclaimed as worship (pūjā).
O best of beings, that fasting which is prescribed at midday and likewise at night should be understood as lasting for a full day and night,
encompassing both the preceding and following days for both oneself and Keśava.
That unification is called the remembrance of Viṣṇu;
O best of beings, the sacrifice to Brahman, the sacrifice to men, the sacrifice to the gods,
the sacrifice to the ancestors, and the sacrifice to all beings are proclaimed as the five sacrifices.

"O best of Brahmins, those who know the truth have declared this great twelve-syllable mantra, preceded by the syllable *oṃ*, to be: *namo bhagavate vāsudevāya*. I have now told you everything that was asked."
O Brahmin, by knowing which all men attain the supreme knowledge,
you shall obtain the difficult-to-attain liberation by reciting one hundred and eight names of the Lord of Kamalā every single day.
Bhadratanu said:
"Recite the one hundred and eight names of Viṣṇu, the Lord of Lakṣmī. Dānta said:
Listen, O Brahmin, I shall proclaim the one hundred and eight names;
having extracted the essence from the thousand names of Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self,
these one hundred and eight names destroy even the greatest of sins.
It should be recited after meditating thus; listen now as the meditation is described by me.
[One should visualize the Lord] having the hue of an *atasī* flower, with eyes like blossoming lotuses, and His entire body adorned with the dust from the hooves of cows. 99–100.
The Lord, whose head was adorned with a noose made of the tail-hair of a cow,
whose beautiful lips were set to the sound of the flute,
and who was surrounded by affectionate children dwelling in the cow-pens. 101.
Having meditated upon the one clad in yellow garments, whose face is like that of Smara (Kāmadeva), yet possessing a most excellent dark countenance. 102.

Oṃ, salutation to Him. For this hymn of one hundred and eight names of Kṛṣṇa, Vedavyāsa is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ), Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is for the purpose of pleasing Śrī Kṛṣṇa through recitation. 103.
Salutations to Kṛṣṇa, Keśava, the enemy of Keśin, the eternal one, the foe of Kaṃsa, the enemy of Dhenuka, the adversary of Śiśupāla, the Lord,
the delight of Devakī, the descendant of Śūra, whose eyes resemble lotuses. 104.
Dāmodara, Jagannātha, the creator of the world, who consists of the world;
105 Nārāyaṇa, the destroyer of Bali, Vāmana, the son of Aditi;
Viṣṇu, the best of the Yadu clan, Vāsudeva, the bestower of wealth. 106
Ananta, Kaiṭabhāri, Mallajit, Narakāntaka, Acyuta, Śrīdhara, Śrīmān, Śrīpati, Puruṣottama,
Govinda, Vanamālī, Hṛṣīkeśa, and Akhilārtihā. 107.
Nṛsiṃha, the enemy of the Daityas, Matsyadeva, who pervades the universe; the Great Tortoise who supports the earth, Varāha, the lord of the earth;
Vaikuṇṭha, the one clad in yellow garments, the wielder of the discus, and the bearer of the mace. 108–109.
The bearer of the conch, the lotus-handed one, the wielder of the Nandaka sword, he whose banner is Garuḍa;
the four-armed one, the great being, the one of great intellect, the one of mighty arms; the great festival, the one of great splendor, the lord who is dear to the long-armed one. 110.
Viṣvaksena, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, Padmanābha, Janārdana;
the beloved of Tulasī, the boundless one, the Supreme Lord, the Highest Sovereign, the remover of supreme affliction, the giver of happiness in the hereafter, the Transcendent. 111–112.
He who dwells in the heart and resides in the ether, who destroys delusion through the syllable Om,
who is the destroyer of all sins, the ender of even the most powerful demons, the beloved of Rukmiṇī, the great breaker of Rukmin’s vow. 113.
Hari, bound by the rope, the remover of afflictions, the upholder of Govardhana;
the enemy of Pūtanā, the enemy of Muṣṭika, the breaker of the Yamalārjuna trees;
Upendra, the universal form, whose feet are the sky, the eternal one. 114–115.
The Supreme Self, the Aparabrahman, the destroyer of the suffering of those who bow before him;
Trivikrama, the Great Illusion, the knower of Yoga, the one whose feet are the seat of the Vedas (Viṣṇu);
the treasure-house of Śrī, the abode of Śrī, the enjoyer of sacrifice, and the bestower of happiness. 116.
The Lord of Sacrifice, the enemy of Rāvaṇa, the slayer of Pralamba, the imperishable, the immutable—
this is the one hundred and eight names from among the thousand names; it brings all pleasure to Viṣṇu and destroys all sins.
It destroys bad dreams and eliminates the afflictions caused by malevolent planets;
it brings about the destruction of all diseases and likewise bestows supreme sovereignty. It is the destroyer of all calamities and the granter of the fruits of all ritual actions.
O best of the twice-born, I have spoken this for the sake of pleasing the Vaiṣṇavas.
He who daily recites these one hundred and eight names with devotion at the three junctions of the day before Hari, Hari is always pleased.
If a devoted Vaiṣṇava person recites this during a Śrāddha ceremony,
his ancestors, being fully satisfied, proceed to the supreme abode.
Likewise, he who recites it at the time of a sacrifice or during the worship of the deities [attains the same].
At the time of giving a gift or during a pilgrimage, one obtains all this fruit (verse 123). By the recitation of this hymn, one who is childless obtains a son, one who seeks wealth obtains wealth,
and one who seeks knowledge obtains knowledge (verse 124).
"Those who recite with devotion the one hundred and eight names of Hari—
no inauspiciousness shall ever be found for them upon the surface of the earth.
Dānta said:
"Go, O Brahmin; may it be well with you. By propitiating Hari with devotion according to the method prescribed by me, you shall attain supreme security.
Thus was he enlightened by that self-controlled man who sought the highest truth.
In that excellent field of merit,
O Jaimini, that brahmin became intent on the worship of Hari; for five days, he constantly performed the worship of Hari with devotion according to the ritual prescribed by Dānta.
Perceiving his firm devotion, Hari, who is full of compassion,
suddenly manifested like the sun with its millions of rays.
Seeing him, the Lord of the worlds, the beloved of Kamalā, the infallible Acyuta—
The brahmin prostrated with his head at the pair of his lotus-like feet. Then that best of brahmins, his mind overflowing with joy,
joined his palms in reverence and praised the Lord of the World, the Consort of Kamalā.
O Lord, you have stolen away my gaze that was fixed upon sin, and you have led me toward my own auspicious devotion to you, O Compassionate One.

Therefore, although I am a rustic man burdened with extensive sins, today you have made me like a true man. When you—whose pair of feet are worshipped by the gods—are angry, the gaze of a human being surely turns toward sin.

Through an abundance of contentment, that very vision toward one who has performed great merit was realized by me alone as being solely the Supreme Lord. O Master, I speak to you of Your power of remembrance, because even though I possessed all manner of accumulated sins, I attained the supreme abode obtainable only by the gods, having ascended a celestial chariot (vimāna) adorned with pure gold.
The hunter Savetrika, though having committed every sin, became forever enriched with virtues by the water from your lotus feet;
and King Yajñadhvaja, saluted by the gods, attained the fruit of sweeping your abode, O sole Lord of the world.
And what of the fruit of smearing your house, O Murāri, the Sovereign who is the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe? || 135 ||
Sumālī, who knows the enemy of the serpent-bannered one (Viṣṇu) and bears the garland of sacrifices, was filled with fear at the sin he had committed;
he circumambulated Hari, and as for the fruit that results from such an act, only Dharma himself knows it, and no one else in the three worlds. 316–317.
O Lord, who on earth is capable of describing the compassion of your heart?
Even a hunter, having pierced you with arrows, attained the supreme state;
and even by censuring you, O Lord of the World, the Lord of the Gods [attained liberation]. 138.
Śiśupāla attained liberation; what then need be said of your devotee? By you, in the form of Brahmā, this world was created;
may my mind take delight in you, that Great Viṣṇu. 139–140.
By you, through this form of Viṣṇu, the destruction of the world is brought about;
and in the form of Rudra within saṃsāra—salutations be to you for that! 141.
Since there is nothing smaller than you, and since there is nothing greater than you...
Salutations to You, by whom the entire world is pervaded.
(142) Salutations to You, from whose two eyes the Sun, the maker of day, was born, and from whose mouth Agni was produced. (143)
O Keśava, to him from whose ears even the winds were born as his vital breaths—
to that best of gods, let there be salutation for me at all times. (144) Lakṣmī is ever perfectly contented upon the lap of his dark-complexioned body.
Salutations to you, who are like a flash of lightning to the cloud;
salutations to you, whose limit of greatness even the gods, beginning with Brahmā, are unable to reach. 145–146.

Salutations to you, who manifest in age after age for the sake of establishing the Dharma and for the destruction of the wicked; salutations to that Great-Souled One by whom this world is deluded through Māyā. 147.
Salutations to that Śambhu who destroys [all things] through his power of illusion;
salutations to you, who are pleased by mere devotion, and not by wealth, nor by praises, nor by gifts, nor by austerities. 148–149.

Salutations to you, who bestows welfare upon cows, Brahmins, and virtuous people, and who likewise exercises compassion toward them; salutations to you who acts as a kinsman to the helpless, to yogis, and to those who suffer. 150.
Salutations be to you, O God, who removes suffering.
Salutations be to you, who abides with equanimity among humans, gods, and all elephants. 151–152.

Salutations to you, in whose satisfaction even a mountain instantly becomes like a blade of grass, and in whose anger even a blade of grass becomes like a mountain; salutations to you who are as dear to me as merit is to the virtuous, and as my own son is to a father. 153.
Just as [the mind] of women without offspring [is fixed], so let my mind be fixed upon you; 154.
Just as the heart of youths is toward women, of the greedy toward wealth, and of the hungry toward food, so let my mind be fixed upon you. 155.
Just as the moon is for those afflicted by heat and the sun is for those afflicted by cold, and just as water is for those afflicted by thirst, so indeed may you be for me;
for by me, devoid of wisdom, the sin of approaching my teacher’s wife was committed. (156)

May that sin go to destruction as I behold you, while the slaughter of those who should not be slain was committed by one deluded by illusion. May that sin go to destruction as I behold you. (157–158)
O Supreme Lord, may that sin of drinking what is unfit for consumption, which was committed by me, come to an end as I behold you.
(159) Likewise, [may the sin of] discharging semen into water while in the water come to an end.
May that sin go to destruction as I behold you.
(160) May the sin committed by the emission of semen upon the earth due to the killing of an embryo go to destruction as I behold you. (611)

May that sin of betraying trust, which was committed through illusion without my knowing it, go to destruction as I behold you; and may whatever false words have been spoken by me at every moment [be likewise destroyed].

May that sin perish as I behold you, while I behold you. (163) May that sin perish as I behold you, while I behold you—the sin committed by reviling the virtuous and by always causing harm to others. (164)

May that sin which I have committed against the mouth of Śleṣmācakra and Kaphaka perish as I behold you; likewise, may the destruction of trees committed when the moon had entered the constellation Vanaspati [come to an end]. 165.
May that sin perish as I behold you, while I am seeing you.
(166) May that sin perish as I behold you, which was committed on a road, in a temple, or in a cow-pen, through the recitation of the root mantra. (167)
O Keśava, may the sin of my lack of devotion toward my father and mother perish as I behold you; for he who was forbidden from going for the sake of bathing or eating [is likewise affected]. 168.
May that sin go to destruction as I behold you,
O best of gods, since I have taken food on the Ekādaśī day— may that sin go to destruction as I behold you. 169–170.
O Lord, whatever sin was committed by me when a guest came to my house and was not honored— that sin may go to destruction as I behold you;
likewise, whatever double meal was consumed on the twelfth or the tenth lunar day.
May that sin perish as I behold you;
may that sin also perish as I behold you, which was committed by obstructing cows as they ran for the sake of drinking water. 172–173.
"May that sin which I have incurred by undertaking a vow and then abandoning it before its completion go to destruction as I behold you;
likewise, may the false testimony I gave out of affection for my friend [be forgiven]. (174)

May that sin perish as I behold you, who have approached your own wife during her fertile season. May that sin perish as I behold you, who have approached your own wife during her fertile season. 175–176.

May that sin which was incurred by me through the food provided by me in the house of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) perish as I behold you; and likewise, O Nṛhari, may that conduct of a village mendicant which was adopted by me [perish].
May that sin perish as I behold you, while I am looking upon you.
O Lord, may that sin of exercising lordship over a king being punished by me perish as I behold you. 178–179.

May that sin which was committed by me as an obstacle during the midst of a Puranic discourse go to destruction as I behold you; for with great reverence, I have listened to the stories of others' meritorious deeds. 180.
May that sin of cutting down the Aśvattha tree and the sin of cutting down the Dhātrī tree go to destruction as I behold you. 181–182.
May the sin committed by me through the sale of curd, milk, and ghee perish as I behold you;
likewise, may that hope which was placed in others by me have been rendered fruitless. 183.
May that sin go to destruction as I behold you;
likewise, may the sin of those brahmins and beggars whom I have looked upon with an angry gaze perish as I behold you. 184–185.

"May the sin of those who gave me the means of livelihood when I rebuked them in anger be destroyed as I behold you. What is the use of saying more here? [May] even the sins accumulated over many births [be destroyed]. 186.
All my sins have come to an end as I behold you;
I am fulfilled, I am fulfilled, I am fulfilled—of this there is no doubt.
Salutations to you, salutations to you, salutations to you, O Lord of the Universe! 187–188.
Having spoken thus, O Jaimini, that twice-born man, his body covered with horripilation due to devotion, fell at the pair of Viṣṇu’s beautiful lotus-feet.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Arise, arise, O Brahmin! I am pleased with your devotion.
Tell me what you desire; I shall certainly grant it to you.
190 Bhadrananu said:
O Supreme Lord Govinda, O Compassionate One, O Supreme Acyuta! By whom else on earth can that which has been obtained by me through Your grace be attained?
(191) Nevertheless, I shall ask for one boon in Your presence, O Enemy of Mura.
O Lord, may this devotion toward You remain very firm for me in birth after birth.
(192) Whatever man recites this hymn composed by me with devotion, You, being pleased, shall grant him all his desires. (193)
The Blessed Lord said: "O Brahmin, this boon has been granted to you; there is no doubt about this.
However, O wise one, I desire to form a friendship with you. (194)
"O twice-born one, those who serve me are worthy; you are such a person here, and therefore friendship has now been fully established between you and me.
Vyāsa said:
Then the god Nārāyaṇa, compassionate and kind toward his devotees,
formed a friendship with that meritorious soul Jaimini;
Hari joyfully gave him the garland that rested upon his own neck.
That brahmin also devoutly offered a garland of tulasī to Hari;
Hari, stretching out his four arms, embraced him,
and that lordly brahmin also joyfully embraced Viṣṇu.
Having thus established friendship with that Brahmin, Hari,
who is compassionate and accepts devotion, vanished right there.
Then, day after day, in that sacred field of Puruṣottama, he remained.
Hari began a game of ball with that Brahmin.
On one occasion, seeing that the brahmin was weak, the compassionate Hari spoke these words out of affection for his friend: "O brahmin-sage! (200-201)
The Blessed One said:
"O friend, why are you so weak? By whom has your wealth been taken? Or what anxiety dwells in your heart? O friend, you ought to tell me that. (202)
Bhadratanu said: "O Lord of the World, for your pleasure I constantly perform such penance; therefore, O Master, my body has become weak. (203)
The Blessed Lord said: O friend, O best of the twice-born, I am not as pleased with anyone else as I am with you; why then do you again subject yourself to physical hardship? 204
Beholding you so weak, a pain arises within my heart; therefore, O best of the twice-born, abandon all bodily affliction.
[He offered] his own upper garments, his own clothes and ornaments, and two beautiful golden buds.

That Brahmin was further adorned by the king’s own bracelets from his own hands, and by the Lord of the Gods himself. Bringing a crown from his own forehead and a pair of anklets from his feet, as well as a golden necklace from his own neck, Kṛṣṇa gave them to that most excellent of Brahmins.
Adorned with those ornaments bestowed by Śrī Hari, this virtuous twice-born man, an expert in the game of ball, would always sport there with Kṛṣṇa, who is as beautiful as a black lotus.

(208) Once, the self-restrained man beheld him there, his limbs adorned with ornaments, his pair of lips charming with the red hue of betel, wearing divine garments and a most excellent upper cloth, and his face smiling. (209)
Dānta said:
"O auspicious one, O auspicious one! Even now you do not abandon your sinful vision, even though your deed has been seen by all people as contemptible. (210)
Since you have been made my disciple, you are indeed everything to me as an ornament; for even one who is arrogant, ill-behaved, merciless, devoted to sin,
and a destroyer of the teacher’s reputation— these five are the dregs among disciples.
One who is devoid of devotion, a talkative chatterer, and likewise one whose mind is fickle;
one who slanders the Guru behind his back—these are declared to be the lowest of disciples.
Having understood this supreme conduct, a disciple should be made wise by those who are discerning.
For that very reason, the ignorance belonging to the wicked— which brings suffering even to teachers—
and the knowledge described by those seers of reality as being conducive to fame, both [types of ignorance] immediately destroy the tree of the teacher’s reputation when residing in the wicked. 214.
Those of virtuous deeds never take pleasure in sinful acts (215).
Just as sandalwood, though fragrant, does not please flies,
so too donkeys are never satiated by even the most delicious food and drink (216).
The wicked are never satiated with thoughts of unrighteousness;
yet, due to the fear of ill-repute, Fortune and Dharma—which grant all desires—never resort to the corrupt, or if they do, they quickly perish. 217.
Through the power of destiny, one may obtain the supreme [state] in every birth;
or sometimes, by the operation of fate, one obtains it even within that very interval. 218–219.
Bhadrananu said:

"You speak the truth, O brahmin-sage; I am not one who is unskilled in the scriptures. No ill repute shall ever come to you through me, your disciple. By your grace, O best of the twice-born, all my desires shall be fulfilled."
"Since you have attained perfection (siddhi), you alone are difficult to find on this earth.
Dānta said: "O Brahmin, tell me what it is that you desire; speak of the perfection you have attained."
"How was the conclusion of these austerities accomplished so quickly?
(222) Bhadrananu replied:
"Even with very little exertion, I have obtained the vision of Hari."
By whose command I abandoned my daily rites and other duties,
as well as my own upper garment, two golden jars, the ring from my own hand, and the crest-ornament from my forehead. (223–224)
O best of the twice-born, the Lord Viṣṇu, being well-pleased, gave me his own anklet and his own pearl necklace;
he, the destroyer of the suffering of his servants, established friendship with me many times. 225.
"I play at handball with him day and night.
(226) "Even though I did not go when I heard these words of yours, I spoke thus out of confidence in you, yet still in your presence. (227)
Dānta said:
"Though I have worshipped Viṣṇu with supreme devotion for seven thousand years, even that all-pervading Lord has not granted me a vision."
"O best of beings, having propitiated Viṣṇu for only five days, you have obtained a vision that is difficult even for the gods to attain!
You are blessed, you have achieved your life's purpose; you are said to be a god in person."
Since you have formed a friendship with the Lord out of love,
O best of the twice-born, and since your affection for Him is free from deceit, tell me, O Brahmin, how the vision of Viṣṇu— which is so difficult to obtain— was achieved.
Vyāsa said:
Having been addressed thus by his preceptor, the wise brahmin, filled with wonder and devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu, returned to his own hermitage in the forest. 232
Then, on another day, having gone there, he played with a ball;
filled with humility, he spoke thus to the compassionate Lord of the World.
233 Bhadra-tanu said:
"O Lord of the Gods, Himavat desires to see you; tell him, 'What is your command? as he stands there, O Lord of pure speech. This brahmin is your exclusive devotee, O lotus-eyed one. 234.
Therefore, O best of gods, you ought to grant him a vision of yourself.
The Blessed One said:
O lord of brahmins, through your supreme devotion over many births, [you have attained this].
"I have been worshipped by you; therefore, I have now granted you my vision. After a few days, that wise brahmin, having honored me—who am invisible even to the gods—desires to see me again."
"Even though he is my great devotee and devoted solely to my service,
he shall obtain a vision of me from time to time.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of his, that brāhmaṇa spoke again with devotion to Keśava, the Lord of Kamalā and destroyer of afflictions.
(239) Bhadra-tanu said:
"O Lord of Gods, O Master of the Universe, when you grant me grace,
then, O lover of your devotees, grant me a vision of yourself face-to-face. Thus did the Guru request from the God the reward of beholding him.
"O Lord, since I have not seen my guru at home, protect me!
(241) The Blessed One said: "Since the fee for the sight of me has indeed been offered by you..."
"Then, having brought that aloe wood, cause me to see it.
Thus commanded by him, Bhadra, with a graceful body, went with joy to the excellent hermitage of his guru; and then his guru returned.
When that best of givers, the self-controlled brāhmaṇa, had arrived, Hari revealed himself to him, endowed with all auspicious marks. Then, beholding Hari, that brāhmaṇa who was devoted to Hari—
With palms joined in reverence and eyes filled with tears of joy, Dānta praised him, saying:
"O Lord whose gaze is compassionate, O Beloved of Lakṣmī, O Protector of those who seek refuge! (245)
Salutations to you, salutations to you, salutations to you, salutations again and again! (246) Today my birth has become fruitful; today my ascetic penance has become fruitful;
today everything has become fruitful for me, as I have obtained the sight of you. (247)
O Lord, Master of Śrī, whatever words were previously contemplated have now been set forth before You, who are as deep as ten million oceans;
yet that hymn does not exist even for Vāgīśa within this world, O Lord of the Universe. (248)
By which hymn of praise I shall generate delight in Your heart; protect, protect me, O Lord! Be gracious, O Master of the World! Accept me as the servant of the servants of Your servants.
Vyāsa said: Then, O Jaimini, the Lord of Gods, who accepts devotion and is composed of compassion, laughed and, placing his lotus-hand upon his head, spoke as follows.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O best of the twice-born, you are my devotee; you have obtained a vision of me.
By my grace, O auspicious one, everything shall indeed come to pass for you. (251)
Vyāsa said:
Then, having affectionately embraced that self-controlled Bhadra and cast off his body, the Supreme Lord suddenly vanished right there, O Brahmin. 252
In that most excellent field, difficult to attain even through merit, having beheld Hari by means of the yoga of action (*kriyā-yoga*) within that Supreme Person, Dānta went to the supreme abode.
That brahmin Bhadrasena as well was solely devoted to devotion for Hari.
At the end of his life, he attains liberation, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
(254) He who worships the Supreme Lord with devotion for even a single day—his sins committed over many births are destroyed, and his love for Hari increases. (255)
Even now, O Jaimini, all the gods, including Brahmā and the others,
do not know the power of a devotee of Hari on this earth;
for this land of action, O Brahmin, is more difficult to attain than even heaven.

O best of the twice-born, there all mortals who have worshipped Viṣṇu become honored by the gods; and all the deities, beginning with Śakra, fearing the exhaustion of their great merit, constantly converse with one another. (257–258)
"When shall we once again go to the land of action?
When shall we there perform worship of the Lord of Śrī-Kamalā?
Most blessed are those people, even greater than we. (259)
In the rare land of Bhāratavarṣa, they worship the Lord Hari. Oh,
who is capable of describing the virtues of Bhāratavarṣa,
where, having previously worshipped Hari, we attained the status of gods?
Thus, O best of the twice-born, all the hosts of gods, headed by Vāsava,
constantly praise the region of Bhārata as the bestower of auspiciousness; for there, having attained birth, one has not failed to propitiate Hari.
No one at all equal to him has been seen or even heard of in this world.
This is true, this is true, and once again it is said: this alone is the truth—that those men who worship the Soul of the Universe even once.

"Even those who, with unwearied and very firm devotion, have performed [their duties] in this land of action (karmabhūmi), are freed from sins easily committed and quickly attain liberation. Thus ends the granting of the boon to Bhadranu in the Puruṣottama-kṣetra, within the Kriyāyoga-sāra of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
The Seventeenth Chapter on Names.
The Eighteenth Chapter. Jaimini said:
"O Guru, if you have favor toward me, please tell me the greatness of that Puruṣottama which has been described by you as the best of sacred fords.
Vyāsa said:
O twice-born one, listen briefly to the majesty of Puruṣottama;
who in this world, other than Viṣṇu, is capable of describing it correctly?
On the shore of the salt ocean lies the place known as Puruṣottama.
That city, O best of Brahmins, is more difficult to attain than even heaven;
for Śrī Puruṣottama himself resides within that city,
and therefore it is called "Puruṣottama" by the wise.
O Brahmin, that sacred field is difficult to attain for ten yojanas all around;
the embodied beings situated there are seen by the gods as four-armed.
Indeed, upon entering that field, all become embodiments of Viṣṇu.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, no deliberation should be made on that matter by the wise;
even food touched by a Cāṇḍāla must be accepted there by the foremost of men,
because Viṣṇu himself is present there in the form of the Cāṇḍāla.
There, the Goddess Lakṣmī herself is the cook of the food, and Janārdana is the eater;
therefore, even for Brahmins and deities, cooked rice is difficult to obtain there.
Whatever remains after Hari has eaten is pure and rare upon this earth.
For those people in this world who eat this food, liberation is not difficult to attain.
All the thirty gods, beginning with Brahmā, come regularly and eat that most rare food; what then need be said of mere mortals? 9–10.
Likewise, that food is a purifier for all and is the destroyer of sin.
O best of the twice-born, although that food was soft and divine, it was as if made of saws within Kṛkaca’s belly; nevertheless, it served to tear away his evil.
Indeed, the sins accumulated in previous lives shall go to destruction for him in whom devotion toward that very rare food arises;
likewise, the merit accumulated over many births shall go to destruction for him [who rejects it]. 14.
O best of the twice-born, devotion to that [Lord] does not arise in one who eats there;
likewise at the lake of Indradyumna, at the Mārkaṇḍeya-hrada, at Rohiṇī, at the ocean, and in the waters of the Śvetagaṅgā. 15–16.
O twice-born one, those mortals who perform their ablutions there endowed with a spirit of devotion,
for them there is no further birth upon this earth;
and by the waters of the salt-ocean, the ancestors are gratified.
Those liberated from all suffering go to the abode of Hari. This ocean is proclaimed as the king of holy places (tīrtharāja) by those who perceive the truth;
therefore, every action performed there becomes entirely inexhaustible. 18–19.

Whatever action a mortal performs in that delightful sacred field— be it the worship of the ancestors, charity, the worship of the Lord’s feet, the sacrifice of recitation (japa-yajña), or anything else— for the purpose of pleasing Viṣṇu, [it becomes inexhaustible]. 20.
All that shall indeed become inexhaustible; there is no doubt in this matter.
(21) For those human beings who behold Balabhadra, Subhadrā, and the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa, nothing whatsoever is difficult to attain. (22)
Without having seen Śrī Jagannātha, Subhadrā, and likewise Balarāma,
a mortal does not attain liberation, even while performing hundreds of meritorious deeds.
There, the body of one who has been struck by a cane becomes red with blood.

O best of the twice-born, all the gods, headed by Śakra, pay homage to him. O brahmin, standing in the intermediate space in their celestial chariots, all the hosts of gods led by Śakra, filled with joy, speak thus to one another. 24–25a.
"When will the Lord of Lakṣmī grant us human birth?
Only as humans shall we go to see the Lord Hari.
When, by the blow of a cane in the sacred field of Śrī Puruṣottama..."
"O best of the twice-born, in that field which grants boons, all the gods, beginning with Vāsava, will always desire the blows of canes upon our own bodies and blood. (27-28)
There, those humans who behold the Akṣayavaṭa with devotion are liberated from the sins accumulated over ten million births and attain the supreme goal;
so too do they who behold Subhadrā, Balabhadra, and the stainless Lord of the World.
Śveta, Mādhava, Deveśa, and likewise Mārkaṇḍeya-hrada;
Jyāmeśvara, Hanumān, and the Akṣayya-vaṭa there—O twice-born one, those mortals who behold these with devotion attain eternal liberation. 30–31.
Listen to the merit of those men who, with devotion, behold Govinda swinging during the three days of the month of Phālguna;
liberated from all sins, they go at the end to the abode of Hari. 32.

Having attained knowledge there, they go to that liberation which is very difficult to obtain. O Jaimini, he who beholds Jagannātha in the month of Caitra or Mārgaśīrṣa shall, upon death, enter the body of Jagannātha himself.

He who beholds the Lord of the World on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, or on the third day, is indeed liberated while still a mortal. Furthermore, that man who enters upon the great ablution of the Lord of the World—
O Brahmin-sage, all his desires shall be fulfilled.
All the gods, beginning with Brahmā, remaining in the sky, behold the great ablution of the Lord of the World, endowed with a spirit of devotion. 36–37.
O brahmin-sage, by beholding the Lord of the World, who is free from all ailment, on the day of Mahājyeṣṭhī, a mortal attains that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
[And likewise] by beholding the Lord of Kamalā proceeding to the Guṇḍikā-maṇḍapa in the month of Āṣāḍha, one attains that same state.
He who beholds Balabhadra is liberated from this; of this there is no doubt.
(39) He who beholds the Lord of the World, the lotus-eyed one, seated upon his chariot, for him there is no rebirth in this saṃsāra which bestows all suffering. (40)
If men behold the auspicious Subhadrā mounted upon her chariot with devotion,
the Blessed One severs for them the bond of worldly existence that causes suffering.
And she who is childless obtains a son if she beholds the auspicious Subhadrā.
O twice-born one, a woman who sees Subhadrā becomes the mother of many children and lives as long as her offspring;
she may otherwise be unfortunate, like a crow, or barren, but she who beholds Subhadrā shall indeed become a woman blessed with a fortunate husband and many children.
The man who beholds Kṛṣṇa, Balabhadra, and Subhadrā while they are situated in the Guṇḍikā-maṇḍapa attains the supreme state.
Even one who is diseased or suffering, if he should behold Hari in the Guṇḍikā-maṇḍapa, [attains that same goal].
O Jaimini, one is suddenly liberated from disease and sorrow.
Furthermore, O best of the twice-born, he who is childless and beholds the Lord of the Universe situated in the Guṇḍikā pavilion indeed obtains a Vaiṣṇava son. 45–46.
One seeking knowledge obtains knowledge; one seeking wealth obtains wealth;
one seeking a wife obtains a wife; and one seeking liberation shall attain liberation.
Even a king who has been deprived of his kingdom, if he beholds Hari with devotion, [shall regain his realm].

O Brahmin, he who beholds Hari with devotion in the Guṇḍikā-maṇḍapa shall regain his own kingdom, freed from enemies; O Brahmin-sage, the enemies of one who thus beholds Hari in the Guṇḍikā-maṇḍapa with devotion perish.
Whoever is severely oppressed by a king should behold [the deity] in the Guṇḍikā pavilion;
he shall immediately bring that king under his own control. Among all processions, the Guṇḍikā is considered the most excellent.
Therefore, even setting aside hundreds of improper deeds, one should perform [the rites] with those of equal status.
That mortal who beholds Hari in that delightful sacred field while sleeping or likewise while rising is honored even by the gods.
Who on earth is able to describe the majesty of Puruṣottama, by the mere entry into which a man becomes Nārāyaṇa? What is the use of saying much here? I shall speak in brief.
The most excellent among all sacred fords is Puruṣottama (54).
He who desires to cross this exceedingly deep ocean of worldly existence— which bestows affliction and is the refuge of multitudes of treacherous evils—
should behold both this [river] and the Supreme Person named Puruṣottama in that field which grants all happiness (55).
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Puruṣottama," in the Kriyāyogasāra of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Nineteen. Vyāsa said:
O best of the twice-born, for those who have taken refuge in Nārāyaṇa and are endowed with devotion, no inauspiciousness ever exists. I shall speak once more of the majesty of the Lord of Kamalā.

Having heard which, all the immortals attain the supreme state. Having heard the majesty of Vāsudeva, the Vaiṣṇavas indeed find satisfaction; the heretics do not find satisfaction, for they are partakers of suffering in hell.

O best of the twice-born, Jaimini, the supreme majesty of Viṣṇu must not be spoken in the presence of heretics; it should indeed be spoken before the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas. Formerly, O Brahmin, in the Tretā Yuga, there was one named Urvīśu.
O best of Brahmins, he was constantly devoted to sin and intent upon censuring the Dharma; he was a stealer of the property of Brahmins, prone to adultery with the wives of others,
an eater of beef, a drinker of liquor, and lustful for the amorous charms of prostitutes.
One who kills those who have sought refuge, one who constantly reviles others,

one who betrays trust, one who slays friends, and likewise one who causes suffering to kinsmen; one who speaks untruths, one who is cruel, and one who associates with heretics— [these are the ones excluded].
He was one who cut off the livelihoods of the twice-born and likewise misappropriated their deposits.
Seeing him to be such a wicked man devoted to sin,
all his kinsmen, filled with anger, went to his own house.
The kinsmen said:
"That established status which was acquired by our ancestors in this stainless lineage—O deluded one, you are now leading that very status toward destruction. (10)
Abandoning the path of dharma, you constantly commit sinful acts;
you have been born as the destroyer of my family’s reputation and the bringer of sorrow to your kinsmen.
O most wonderful one, the Creator’s creation is truly marvelous in you.
In that very river where the moon was born, there also arose the origin of poison (Kṣveḍa).
Alas, the power of wicked sons cannot be measured; they instantly destroy the fame accumulated by many men. 12-13.

"Even if one is born into a low family, if he has an excellent son, that lineage becomes preeminent; but even if one is born into a superior family, if his son is base, the lineage falls into inferiority.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus,
O twice-born one, all those kinsmen, enraged by the fear of infamy, suddenly abandoned that foremost of sinners.
Abandoned by his kinsmen and censured by all people, he was left alone.
Deprived of all his prosperity, the wretched man resorted to the life of a bandit.
While he was performing the deeds of a bandit, mercilessly harming others,
all the people of the countryside seized him and reported it to the king.
O best of the twice-born, because of his affection for his father,
that king did not kill that man of evil conduct, but rather banished him from his own country. Thereupon, that merciless man took refuge in the forest together with bandits.

Once, O Maitreya, while wandering in the forest, he became exhausted and went to the riverbank to bathe, where many arrogant bandits were stationed for the purpose of plundering the property of travelers. 19–20.
On that riverbank, that evil-minded one saw many who were devoted to the service of the Blessed One, appearing in the form of brahmins.
Then all those brahmins, having propitiated Janārdana, [proceeded].
Driven by great curiosity, they spoke to one another:
"Today I have indeed offered these campaka flowers;
someone says that I gave betel-leaf to the enemy of Mura."
"Never in this birth shall betel be consumed by me; today, however, an excellent plantain fruit has been offered to Hari. In birth after birth, the plantain fruit must be eaten by me."
One person said, "I gave a pomegranate fruit to Hari," while another said, "I gave an excellent mango fruit.
Having heard these words as they were speaking to one another, [he understood]. 26.
Urvīśu reflected: "What shall I give to Viṣṇu?
Whatever edible things exist in this world, I am unable to renounce them;
what, then, shall I give to the enemy of Mura?"
"Living constantly within the forest, I am free from fear of thieves or kings;
indeed, I have never at any time had the need to mount a cart.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, O best of the twice-born,
that hunter gave a cart to Hari, the bestower of the four goals of life;
then all those brahmins departed as they had come.
That merchant also went to his own dwelling along with the robbers;
once, however, a certain traveler came alone to that circle by that very same path, carrying a basket of molasses.
Then that fearless bandit, who delighted in harming others,
impetuously seized the jar of molasses from that traveler;
thereupon, the other bandits began to smash the jar of molasses.

O best of the twice-born, having encountered the cart of Urvīśu, which was made of molasses from Śakaṭa-gauḍa, Urvīśu reflected in his mind upon the words [of the sage] preceded by their recollection. (34)
He himself took from Anomayāpura [a portion] for the enemy of Mura (Viṣṇu).
Therefore, in this birth, one should never accept [anything] from Anonama;
having reflected thus in one's heart, one should thereafter take that which is made of jaggery.
O twice-born one, having learned of that devotion of a great sinner who had given [the gift] to some brahmin for the sake of pleasing Mādhava,
Janārdana, being pleased, immediately removed all his sin.
On that very day, having entered the great forest,
the Lord was struck by all the enraged citizens with stones; then, in order to lead him away, he [sent] a celestial chariot fashioned of gold.

Then they dispatched messengers adorned with various ornaments; those messengers of the Blessed One, having placed that lord of the earth, whose sins had departed, upon a celestial chariot, immediately went to the city of Hari.
Then, having attained the presence of Hari, that best of virtuous souls remained in the proximity of Keśava for another hundred manvantaras;
having acquired supreme knowledge, he entered the body of Hari.
Vyāsa said:
By whatever means possible, a man who practices devotion to Hari reaches the further shore of the ocean of worldly existence, just as a royal swan reaches the end of a lake. 43.
Even one whose heart possesses devotion to Hari for but a single moment attains that supreme state; even a sinner goes there.
Having given even a single excellent object to the enemy of Mura, he [attains that state]. 44.
Indeed, one should eat only after [the guests] have eaten, for the pacification of sin.
Whatever object was given that has been taken by Hari, that one should give back to a twice-born; the wise must certainly not eat anything remaining of that themselves. 45–46.

O best of Brahmins, whatever desirable things there may be, those which have not been offered to Viṣṇu must certainly not be consumed by Vaiṣṇavas. (47) Such is the greatness of the food offered to Viṣṇu, which destroys all sins.
I shall relate this history once more; listen, O Brahmin, with a concentrated mind.
(48) There was a Brahmin named Sarvajani, born of a pure lineage, who was peaceful, self-controlled, endowed with compassion, and a worshiper of his gurus and Brahmins. (49)
One who is devoted to the worship of Hari, intent on the remembrance of Hari,
the destroyer of the afflictions of those who have sought refuge, truthful in speech, with senses conquered,
bathing at dawn, adhering to his own conduct, and free from violence; 50.
Devoted to the vow of Ekādaśī and intent upon honoring his kinsmen,
that best of virtuous twice-born men once beheld Keśava in a dream—
dark-hued, with stainless lotus-eyes, a smiling face, and clad in yellow garments.
His body was radiant with golden earrings, anklets, and a crown;
his chest was illuminated by the Kaustubha gem, and he was adorned with a forest garland.
The Lord had four arms, bearing the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus.
Having obtained a vision of the Lord of the World in a dream— He who was endowed with all the auspicious marks and wore a golden sacred thread— that brahmin,
his body thrilled with joy, praised Him with palms joined in reverence. 54–55.

Salutations to You, the sustainer of the entire world; salutations to You, Nārāyaṇa, the beloved of the heart of Kamalā, the bestower of the supreme nectar of dharma, artha, and kāma, and the destroyer of the grief, fear, and disease of these worlds. O Murāri, all the sins committed by me while under the constant influence of delusion—[to You, the destroyer of them, be my salutation].
Therefore, I am afraid of this deep ocean of worldly existence; lift me up by providing the boat of Your own devotion.
(57) O Enemy of Kaiṭabha, although I know that a human being destroys sin, I nevertheless quickly fall into delusion on this earth;
yet even so, I constantly commit evil with joy. Therefore, there is no person as utterly deluded as I am. (58)
"The tree of merit suddenly destroys the fruit of happiness; O Nṛhari, what shall I do? I am one who has committed sin.
I have no wealth for the rite of offering the flowering tree. O Lord, be gracious, O Blessed One, what shall I do?
[59] "Leaving behind the pair of Your lotus feet, which are the abode of supreme nectar, this bee of my mind..."
The face of a woman, which constantly pours forth phlegm, approaches the god [of death] who bestows mortality through the delusion that it is a lotus.
My hand is devoid of giving, my mouth speaks falsehoods, and my two ears are ever intent on hearing evil.
Since you, O Lord, are the destroyer of the faults of those who have come for refuge, may you take away these defects of mine.

O Nṛhari, the boat of devotion to You has once been obtained here by me as something very firm; yet, even so, being under the sway of fate, I am a great evil-souled one who continues to whirl about, and thus my time of suffering persists forever.
(62) Is there a path that leads to the further shore of saṃsāra—a path that is effortless, free from all suffering, compassionate, and gracious?
O Viṣṇu, my vision has never before reached you here, as I have been blinded by the great darkness of delusion.
O Murāri, destroyer of the suffering of ruined people, this mind of mine—even though I am a sinner—is now lost [in devotion] to You, who bring about the destruction of such ruin.
For, O Lord, O Slayer of Keśin, I behold Your lotus feet, which are worshipped by all the gods, even in a dream.
Vyāsa said:
Thus praised by him, the Lord, the Blessed One, the Consort of Kamalā,
who is skilled in speech and the savior from the ocean of worldly existence, spoke these words.
The Blessed Lord said: "O best of Brahmins, I am perpetually pleased by your devotions; therefore, all that is auspicious shall come to pass for you before long."
"O twice-born one, although you were a sinner, I previously liberated you; now that you are my devotee, no calamity shall befall you.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
Who was struck down by Viṣṇu in the past, or what sin was committed by me? How was my deliverance from sin previously accomplished by you?
How was I born in this worldly existence, and how was I brought forth by you?
"O All-pervading Lord, tell me all of this, for you are always compassionate.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O best of the twice-born, although this secret is not to be disclosed,"
Nevertheless, out of affection for you, I shall speak; listen.
O best of brahmins, in former times you were born into a lineage of birds upon the various regions of the earth as a result of the ripening of your own karma. (70–71)
Constantly distressed by hunger and thirst, you wandered about eating insects and drinking from mountain torrents and hot springs;
thus, born as a bird upon a boat, you always experienced manifold sufferings. 72.
Formerly, you remained on this earth for four thousand years.
Once, a brāhmaṇa named Kulabhadra, who was a knower of all truths,
worshipped me with devotion through food offerings and other gifts on the bank of a river.
Having worshipped [me] along with the lord of the brāhmaṇas, he took those rice grains from my offering,
deposited them right there, and returned once more to his own home. Then, having come down from the tree, you, the bird, were overcome by hunger.
"O twice-born one, by eating even a single grain of rice from my offering, you have been instantly liberated from most terrible sins. When your time had come, you passed away, O Brahmin. (76-77)
I have sent my own messengers in every way to bring you here; then, having placed you— who are cleansed of all sin— upon a chariot,
all the hosts of messengers immediately arrived at the supreme abode.
"O best of Brahmins, you have remained in my presence for thousands of millions of aeons, enjoying all pleasures that are difficult even for the gods to attain;
thereafter, you have been born, O lord of Brahmins, into a pure lineage of Brahmins. (79-80)
Even there, O best of the twice-born, your devotion to me shall become exceedingly firm; by constantly propitiating me through the yoga of action,
at the end of your life, you shall attain my own abode through my grace.

"O Brahmin, when I am pleased, even one who is sinful becomes a partaker of liberation; but when I am angry with someone, even one who is virtuous becomes a partaker of sin. Therefore, O auspicious Brahmin, may you have well-being; you are my devotee, O observer of noble vows. (82-83)
"I shall grant you that supreme station which is unattainable even by the gods.
The Brahmin said: "O Lord, through your grace, I have heard the account of my own former history. (84)
Now, O Lord, I wish to hear whatever you may say; O Indra among gods, with whom are you pleased, or with whom are you angry, O Lord?
Out of your great compassion, you ought to tell me all of this.
The Blessed One said: O best of Brahmins, I shall describe in brief all those actions by which satisfaction arises in my heart, as well as those that provoke anger. 86.
O best of the twice-born, I am always pleased with that person who is free from ego toward all beings; and he who, endowed with righteousness and devotion, performs actions for my sake. (87-88)
"O you two, tell me: I am always pleased with that man who, having obtained a delicious object, gives it away;
I am always pleased with him who remains equal in honor and dishonor. (89)
I am always pleased with that man who knows me as residing within the bodies of all beings, who is free from harming others,
and who performs his actions after repeated and careful reflection. (90–91)
I am always pleased with him who desires the welfare of cows and Brahmins;
I am always pleased with him who diligently protects the word that has been personally uttered by me. I am always pleased with him who makes an effort to assist one who has sought refuge.

O best of the twice-born, I am always pleased with him who gives gifts even to those who cannot reciprocate, and whose mind is ever fixed on me; that by which I am satisfied through action has thus been briefly explained. 93–94.
I am angry because of a certain action; O Brahmin, listen as I tell you what it is:
he who delights in harming others and is merciless toward all living beings, who is always egoistic and wrathful—he brings me into the state of enmity. (95)
One who speaks untruth, one who is cruel, one who is intent on censuring others,
one who destroys the works of poets, and one who finds fault with their parents, wife, brothers, and sisters— even without visible cause— brings me into enmity. (96-97)

The deluded man who, out of ignorance, abandons [his father], and the man of foolish intellect who subjects his father to reproach, brings himself to a state of enmity equal to that of a foe. He who shows contempt for his guru brings himself to a state of enmity equal to that of a Brahmin.

Those who destroy groves, those who despoil reservoirs of water, and those who bring about the ruin of a village—they bring me enmity. Likewise, those people who fall into despair upon seeing another's wife [bring me enmity]. 99–100.
I am always angry with those who listen to talk of sin;
I am always angry with those fools who hate their Lord, those who seize the property of the helpless, and those who are betrayers of trust. 101.
I am forever enraged with those who kill cows, those who are husbands of low-caste women, and those who destroy the holy fig tree;
and with those who create divisions among Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa.

I am forever enraged with those who are excessively attached to the wives of others, and with those sinful-minded men who eat on the eleventh day [of the lunar fortnight] out of greed; I am forever enraged with those who revile the Vedas. 104.
I am forever enraged at those who delight in evil intent, those who betray their friends, and those who destroy the Dhātrī tree (105). And I am enraged at those who,
deluded by lust, engage in sexual intercourse during the day (106).
I am always enraged at those who approach a menstruating woman,
O best of beings, and those fools who, out of delusion, approach a woman whose menses have not yet appeared,
or one who is constantly engaged in a vow; they bring me into enmity.
O twice-born ones,
I am always angry with those who eat two meals on the day of the new moon (amāvāsyā), and especially those who consume meat, engage in sexual intercourse, or use oil at night on that day. (108–109)
"O best of Brahmins, I am always enraged at those who do not follow this [path].
What is the use of saying more? I shall tell you in brief:
I am always enraged at those who indeed revile the Vaiṣṇavas."
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu suddenly became invisible. That brahmin, his sleep abandoned, arose from there and praised him.
By these words spoken by Keśava, that brāhmaṇa became a devotee of Hari;
having abandoned all other duties, he became intent on the yoga of ritual action.
Even for one who eats the *naivedya* (food offerings) of Nārāyaṇa, this indeed is the fruit.
I do not know what might happen for those men who perform the worship of Hari; I shall tell you briefly, so listen, O most excellent Jaimini.
By performing the worship of Hari even once, the supreme state is attained.
Human birth is difficult to obtain in this world,
and even therein, devotion to the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu) is honored as being even more difficult to attain, O best of Brahmins.
That man in whose mind there exists the desire to cross the ocean of worldly existence, which is filled with all manner of suffering— [verse 117 follows].
With devotion, the noble one should constantly perform the worship of Vāsudeva as the culmination of all his actions.
(117) Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Essence of Kriyā-yoga," in the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Twenty.
Vyāsa said: O Brahmin, the fruit of the worship of Viṣṇu has been briefly described by me; now I shall speak of gifts—listen with a concentrated mind. 1.

Between the two—charity and austerity—charity alone is remembered as supreme. It is said that through austerity one removes sin, but there is no sin in the act of giving. Austerity was considered best in the Kṛta age, and meditation in the Tretā age.
In the Dvāpara age, worship was supreme; in the Kali age, giving is supreme.
Therefore, in the Kali age, the wise who desire the highest state should constantly perform acts of giving for the pleasure of the Lord of Kamalā.
O best of the twice-born, just as the moon increases its digits little by little, so too has the wise declared the proper course for charity and austerity; therefore,
one should accumulate wealth even bit by bit.

A wise person should apply accumulated wealth toward the act of giving. That mortal who, though possessing wealth, neither eats nor gives, should be known as poor, for he is devoid of both giving and enjoyment.
"O twice-born one, who has gone with this wealth?
And who has come from that city? It has been given here once he had met his death.
Having given and having given, men always give; yet they become poor. (8)
Those who do not give should be known as poor, yet they are lords of great wealth in the next world. Those who guard their wealth out of miserliness should be known as deeply miserable;
for, O Jaimini, having abandoned all that at the end, they depart in despair.

O best of the twice-born, that which is not given does not follow one to the next world; it does not accompany one who is destitute and friendless. O lord of brahmins, even if it be little by little, [a gift] offered with devotion and faith [yields great fruit].
Vaiṣṇavas should always give gifts out of their own devotion.
O best of the twice-born, among all gifts, the gift of food and the gift of water are proclaimed by the knowers of truth to be the most excellent. 12–13.

Without food, the life-breaths do not remain within the bodies of embodied beings; therefore, the giver of food should be known as the giver of life, and the giver of life is the giver of everything. (14) Consequently, the giver of food obtains the fruit of all possible gifts.
O Jaimini, there is no gift equal to the gift of food, nor is there a gift equal to the gift of water;
for without water, there can be no food, and therefore water is bestowed.
O best of Brahmins, hunger and thirst are proclaimed to be equal.
Therefore, the wise have declared that water is the best gift; it is the life of men, yet it is not merely life. Thus, for the sake of preserving life, a wise man should give the gift of water.
O best of Brahmins, by him who has given food and water upon this earth, all gifts have been bestowed;
of this there is no doubt.
Now hear the majesty of the gift of food and the gift of water.
In that very city of Hastināpura, there lived a courtesan named Surasundarī, who was as wealthy as Kubera;
she was renowned for her skill in the arts of love and endowed with every auspicious mark. (20)
There, a Brahmin woman named Akṣemaṅkarī, born of a noble lineage, was a daughter of a twice-born man; she was endowed with all virtues and was not a widow.
That Brahmin woman’s mind was enamored with the paramour of an excellent twice-born man.
Abandoning her discernment by performing forbidden acts, that Brāhmaṇa woman, though she was not a prostitute, became associated with one;
out of affection, she entered into friendship with her, adopting the lifestyle of a courtesan.
O Jaimini, that courtesan and the Brāhmaṇa woman— both of them— daily committed countless sins together with affection; thereafter,
that most clever woman reached old age.

O best of Brahmins, once that unchaste and extremely sinful Brahmin woman, having grown old as a chief courtesan, spoke thus with humility and wonder to her own friend: (26) "The words of the Brahmin have [struck me] with amazement. (27)
Ratividagdha said:
"O friend, along with you, a single terrible sin was committed;
even now, my vision regarding that sin remains intensely active."
"Both my beauty and my strength—indeed, everything of mine has been seized by old age.
(28) Thus, though it constantly causes ill health, hope cannot be abandoned;
yet I, having committed sins, have attained this vast state of immobility. (29)
Death now appears as if it has arrived; indeed, those [wealth] which were acquired by me through sin have been lost. When I have died childless, who will protect those [possessions] of mine? 30.
"Therefore, O friend, if you agree, I wish to give all my wealth— even that acquired by unjust means— to the Brahmins. The Brāhmaṇī said:
"Whatever wealth I have seen accumulated by me has been constantly given away to unworthy recipients;
therefore, being destitute of riches, what shall I give to the twice-born? (32-33)
"If you have any wealth, give it away in charity immediately. Hearing these words of hers, that prostitute was exceedingly delighted and gave away food with her entire fortune.
The eminent brahmin Hariśarman, possessing great wealth, constantly worshipped the Blessed Lord Janārdana with extreme devotion;
he had conquered his senses, restrained his anger, and was free from violence and hypocrisy.
For the sake of pleasing the Lord of Kamalā, they performed great penance,
worshipping Janārdana, the Lord of Gods, constantly with perfumes, flowers, offerings, ghee-incense, and lamps. 37.

Although that brahmin was wealthy, he was constantly anxious about the depletion of his riches. O best of the twice-born, ants, mice, and other creatures were perpetually hungry in the house of that miser.
O best of Brahmins, he himself consumed all the wealth he had acquired day after day, completely devoid of the act of giving;
never did he share it with his friends, Brahmins, or kinsmen. 40.
Fearing that he might request wealth, he did not even engage in conversation;
disregarding his own vast riches at home and considering himself as one of the most eminent, that best of brahmins rejoiced. 41–42.

Once, O twice-born one, when his time had come, that Brāhmaṇa who possessed immense wealth died at the same time as a courtesan and a Brāhmaṇa woman. Then, most terrifying messengers arrived to lead them away.
O Jaimini,
those messengers, Caṇḍa and the others, with nooses and mallets in their hands, took them along and immediately departed for the City of Dharma by a path that was difficult to traverse.
Caṇḍa said:
"O Lord of Life, by your command Hariśarman has been brought here, as well as that prostitute and the Brāhmaṇa woman; behold them standing before you. (46)
Beholding them, O best of the twice-born, the Lord of Life (Yama) laughed and spoke thus to Citragupta, who is expert in all affairs.
Yama said:
"O wise Citragupta of great intellect, examine from the very beginning all these deeds of theirs, whether auspicious or inauspicious.
Then, by the command of Yama, the discerning Citragupta [began his investigation].
He examined everything—the auspicious as well as the inauspicious.
Citragupta said: "O God, listen; I shall describe both merit and sin."
This prostitute and Brāhmaṇī caused Hariśarman to perform [these acts]. This courtesan named Ratividagdhā was exceedingly evil-minded; she committed such sins that they cannot be described.
O son of the Sun, this courtesan, having reached the prime of her youth, gave gifts of food with all the wealth she had acquired through unjust means.
By the power of that gift of food, [she was spared] from those who provide residence in the houses of torment.
This [earth] is abandoned by all sins, even those accumulated over ten million births.
O Great King, those people on earth who perform the gift of food—even if they are sinners—go to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. 53-54.
As many grains of food as men offer on the circle of the earth,
so many sins of killing a Brahmin undoubtedly perish for him;
for those who offer food, their bodies and their sins are cast off.
The son of the Sun (Yama) arrives suddenly at the very moment those who accept the vessels [of food].
Therefore, the wise do not accept food from sinners;
those fools who accept it out of delusion are themselves partakers of that sin.
O Lord, you have described the auspicious and inauspicious deeds of a prostitute;
now hear of the auspicious and inauspicious deeds of a Brāhmaṇa woman.
This Brāhmaṇa woman named Kṣemakarī was born of a pure lineage.
O Lord, Bhadra committed every sin, O beloved of Kīrti;
having abandoned the conduct of her own stage of life and being proud of her youth, she became exceedingly wicked, longing for union with a paramour. 59–60.
Once, O King, while playing with other children in her childhood, she dug a square-shaped pit in the street. On that very day, the clouds poured down water.
O Lord, that trench was filled with water by her as she had constructed it.
Then, O King, at the time of midday, a certain thirsty bull,
tormented by the heat of the sun, drank the water there.
By the power of her gift of water, O wise son of the Sun, all those great sins were indeed destroyed;
liberated from all evils, she shall go to the abode of Nārāyaṇa.
"O Lord of Gods, this Brahmin woman was of evil intent and had committed sins;
yet she has been liberated from all her misdeeds through the power of giving water.
This Brahmin is a great devotee of the Discus-wielder, the God of gods. (65-66)
Then, above him, the one Lord Acyuta, the master of all living beings, was remembered.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of Citragupta, the wielder of the staff [Yama]— 67.
I prostrated before that prostitute, that brahmin woman, and that brahmin as well,
honoring them with divine golden ornaments and various kinds of garments. O Jaimini, Yama heard of this worship performed by those householders.
Laughing, he spoke these words with great affection and gentle syllables.
Yama said: "You are all high-souled ones, whose every sin has been destroyed."

Then Yama placed those [disciples] upon a divine, golden seat yoked with royal swans— the abode of the Lord Śrīpati, which bestows all happiness— and dispatched them to that place of the Wielder of the Discus.
Then, mounted upon a divine chariot and adorned with all ornaments, they all, their sins having been destroyed, went to the city of the Blessed One;
and that prostitute, the Brāhmaṇī, her entire impurity likewise vanished.
Having obtained the presence of the Lord, he remained there for a long time in happiness.
Seeing Hariśarman approaching, Janārdana affectionately offered him an excellent seat made of gold.
Having honored that best of the twice-born with water for the feet, the arghya offering, and water for sipping,
and seeing him seated upon an excellent seat, Hari joyfully addressed him thus. (75) The Blessed Lord said:
"O twice-born one, tell me what is auspicious for me, since you, the foremost of my devotees,
remain for a long time in my abode which is free from all calamities. (76) The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O Lord, even by merely remembering you, a person attains well-being;
I have attained your very presence—what could be more auspicious than this?
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words spoken with affection, the Blessed One, being pleased, granted his own likeness to that twice-born man;
the Lord of Kamalā bestowed upon him every happiness that is difficult to attain.
Remembering that meanness, the Lord gave only a mere morsel of food. After two days had passed, the Brahmin, deprived of food and overcome by hunger,
stood bowed in humility and spoke to Viṣṇu, the Lord of Gods.
The Brahmin said:
"O Lord, this station has been attained by you through the fruits of manifold austerities;
yet even here, O Lord, I am constantly hungry—how is it that I am fruitless? (81)
He was fanned even upon his couches by divine hosts of celestial maidens in the bloom of youth with the breeze of white chowries;
he was adorned with great garlands of fragrant flowers.
