O Lord, O Supreme King, with all their limbs anointed with sandalwood paste by excellent women,
those lovely-limbed amorous maidens always dance and sing before me at your command, O Nārāyaṇa. 83–84.
All the gods, beginning with Vāsava, constantly bear the dust from my feet upon their heads, adorning their crowns;
so too do the divine sages and the ṛṣis, O Lord of the World. (85)
They constantly praise me with hymns at all times, like my servants;
I appear four-armed, dark-complexioned, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, with eyes like full-blown white lotuses, clad in yellow garments, and wearing beautiful earrings. 86–87.
Wearing a golden sacrificial thread, a crown, and earrings,
you appeared like a second Garuḍa-bannered Lord (Viṣṇu) before the gods today.
O Lord, these rare pleasures have been bestowed upon us by you.
"O Supreme Lord, why do you not give me food?
My body is being greatly scorched by the fire of hunger,
just like a tree ablaze from within its hollow."
"O Keśava, this happiness has been taken by you; it does not please me, for my limbs are distressed and the fire of my stomach is blazing.
Without you, the Lord of the World, [I cannot endure] through action, mind, or speech."

"No one worshipped by the hosts of gods has been left unpurified by me (92). O Lord of the World, I have not failed to offer devotion even in my dreams; for what fault, O Master, do you not grant me food? (93)
Vyāsa said:
Then the blessed Lord Viṣṇu, full of curiosity, spoke to him: "Go quickly, O Brāhmaṇa, may it be well with you, toward Brahmā. (94)
Having heard these words, the Brahmin quickly went to Brahmā; Brahmā spoke to him, displaying his own wretchedness.
Brahmā said:
Whatever karma has been acquired through suffering that is given away to one who is not a god, and which one does not enjoy oneself—that is surely lost; there is no doubt.
Thus, I have explained to you the entire cause of your suffering.
"Go, O Brahmin; may it be well with you. He has arrived here without a doubt.
The Brahmin said:
"This ripening of my own karma has been heard by me in its entirety through your grace."
"Now tell me, what gifts are to be given by men?
Brahmā said:
"There are many gifts; it is not possible to describe them all."
It is being told in brief; listen with a concentrated mind, O best of the twice-born. The gift of land is the most excellent of all gifts.
He by whom this has been performed is to be known as one who has given all possible gifts, O virtuous soul. (99-100)
O best of the twice-born, he who gives a plot of land even the size of a cow's hide shall go to the supreme abode,
liberated from all sins. He who,
being poor, gives land together with its crops to a member of the twice-born [attains the same].
O best of Brahmins, listen to the merit of one who gives [this]:
liberated from all sins, he shall go to the city of Nārāyaṇa; there he enjoys every happiness for as long as the fourteen Indras endure. 102–103.
Having repeatedly attained the earth, he becomes a sovereign emperor;
after enjoying the entire world for a long time, that man shall become Nārāyaṇa.
For this reason, land should be accepted by the twice-born, even setting aside hundreds of other gifts.

The giver of land and the leader to that land—both of these go to heaven. O best of Brahmins, that dull-witted twice-born man who abandons the gift of land shall be exceedingly miserable in every birth. 105–106.

Viṣṇu is exceedingly pleased with one who practices the gift of land by taking it from others and bestows upon him the supreme state. He who grants a village to a poor Brāhmaṇa of the twice-born caste [attains great merit]. 107.
Or listen further to the merit that one causes another to obtain:
for as many particles of dust as there are on the earth, and for as many drops of rain as there are, for that many *manvantaras* shall the wise person dwell in the world of Viṣṇu. 108–109.
O twice-born one, I shall describe the merit of that high-souled person who gives away a milch cow together with her calf; listen to it.
Whatever fruit one might obtain by giving the entire earth, consisting of seven islands, filled with crops—[that fruit he obtains]. (110)
A mortal obtains that same fruit which he gains by giving a cow to a twice-born man.
But he who gives a bull to a Brāhmaṇa who maintains a household,
being liberated from terrible sins, goes to the world of Rudra.
As many hairs as there are on the body of that bull, for so many thousands of kalpas he rejoices together with Rudra.
Furthermore, he who gives a "two-faced" cow to one learned in the Vedas [attains the same].
O Rudra, there is never again a return from that world for one who bestows a black bull joined with sesame seeds;
he shall dwell in the abode of Rudra for as many years as there are sesame seeds. 114–115.

Even one who gives gold the size of a sesame seed to a member of the twice-born caste goes to the abode of Viṣṇu, accompanied by ten million members of his lineage. He who, out of devotion, should give silver to a poor member of the twice-born caste [attains the same].
Having reached the world of Candra, he partakes of the nectar of immortality. O best of the twice-born, he who gives diamonds, pearls, coral, and likewise gems, goes to the world of Śakra.

O best of the twice-born, that noble-minded person who makes a gift of a horse attains the sovereignty of the king of the Gandharvas; of this there is no doubt. He who gives an elephant that is young and free from defects [attains the same].
O twice-born one, he who becomes a sharer in the kingdom of the gods shall become like Indra;
and he who gives a palanquin to a Brāhmaṇa along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) shall also attain the station of Indra and dwell there for four kalpas.

O twice-born one, listen as I describe in brief the merit of that person who gives a Śāligrāma stone to a member of the twice-born class— merit equal to that of one who has given the entire earth with its seven continents, along with its mountains, forests, and groves. (122)
The giver of a Śālagrāma stone obtains that very fruit.
(123) By bestowing a Śālagrāma stone, one obtains ten million times more fruit than the fruit that is attained by men through the gift of their own weight in gold (tulāpuruṣadāna). (124)
O best of the twice-born, by him who has offered a Śālagrāma stone,
the fourteen worlds have truly been offered. O foremost of men, he who performs the Tulāpuruṣa gift [attains the same merit].

That lord of the earth, wearing divine garments, shall remain so for a long time; there shall be no further birth for him in a mother’s womb. Furthermore, that best of men who gives away a maiden adorned with ornaments [attains this same state]. 126–127.

That foolish man who, out of delusion, sells his daughter shall go to the terrible hell known as Purīṣahrada (the Pit of Excrement), whereas he who [gives her away] goes to the abode of Viṣṇu, free from rebirth. 128.
O twice-born one, the son born of a girl who has been sold is to be known as a Cāṇḍāla, excluded from all religious duties;
a knower of the scriptures should not even look upon the face of the man who sells a daughter. 129–130.

O twice-born one, whatever auspicious rite may be performed before a seller of a maiden— even if one should look upon him out of ignorance or perform the ritual of beholding the sun— all that merit shall go to fruitlessness. (131)
For the seller of a daughter, there is no escape from hell;
for the giver of a daughter in marriage, there is no returning from heaven. What is the use of speaking much here? I shall tell you in brief. 133
The merit for one who gives shoes and an umbrella on this earth shall be more than a hundredfold that of [giving] diamonds and the daughter of the Earth (the goddess Śrī).
Listen, I shall tell you its great merit in brief.
In this world, he shall live for a hundred years endowed with all prosperity.
Having died and reached the city of Śakra, he shall remain there for four hundred kalpas; he who gives a new garment attains the supreme goal.
O Brahmin, that man who cuts an old garment, likewise [steals] a cow or silver,
or [marries] a girl who has reached her menses, shall always go to hell;
whereas a man who gives fruit goes to the abode of the gods.

There, for thousands of kalpas, he enjoys a fruit that is like nectar. O Brahmin, the giver of vegetables goes to the abode of the Lord Śambhu; there, for two kalpas, he enjoys milk-rice (pāyasa) which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
The man who gives milk, ghee, clarified butter,
and curd attains the drinking of nectar in the presence of the Lord Hari. O Brahmin,
the man who offers flowers and incense goes to the abode of the gods.
O best of the twice-born, he who gives a bed remains adorned with flowers and perfumes for thousands of yugas; O most excellent of brahmins,
having reached the world of Brahmā, he dwells there for a long time upon a couch.
The giver of a lamp and the giver of a seat is freed from all sins;
seated upon a divine throne and surrounded by rows of lamps, O King, the giver of betel-leaf enjoys every auspicious thing on earth. 143.
O best of the twice-born, that supreme man who eats betel while sleeping on the lap of a woman, and who bestows the gift of knowledge,
shall remain in the presence of Viṣṇu for two hundred yugas.
Then, O best of the twice-born, having attained knowledge right there through the grace of the Lord of Kamalā, he obtains liberation which is otherwise difficult to attain.
Furthermore, he who teaches the Veda to a helpless Brāhmaṇa who is in extreme distress—

One always goes to the abode of Viṣṇu, from which a return is difficult to obtain. Even a twice-born man of noble lineage does not shine without knowledge; therefore, those who cause a twice-born man to study reach the supreme state. 147-148.
Even a Brāhmaṇa who is a god manifest on earth and a refuge for the deities,
being the teacher of all castes, does not shine if he is devoid of learning. Whatever gifts there are in this world, such as gold and the like—
O best of the twice-born,
I shall briefly describe to you the merit of that man who, endowed with devotion, makes a gift of a book to a Brāhmaṇa by whom he has been taught through this [scripture]. (150–151)
In that regard, for as many syllables as there are on each leaf and in the book,
one shall obtain the merit born from the gift of ten million Kapila cows for every single syllable.
For as many days as those twice-born ones continue to recite that book, [they shall likewise obtain that merit].
The giver of a manuscript shall remain in Vaikuṇṭha for as long as a Manvantara. O Brahmin, there are many such gifts;
who in this world, even with two hundred years, would be capable of describing them all correctly? (153-154)
Whatever sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are committed by men, those sins are destroyed; therefore, one should practice charity.
Whatever gift is given through one's own merit is shared by three generations of people.
One obtains as much fruit from that gift as there is substance [in it].
Whatever gift is given by people for the pleasure of the Lord of Kamalā, one obtains ten million times that merit; of this there is no doubt. 156–157.
Therefore, a wise man, endowed with devotion and service toward the Brahmins, should practice charity as a means to please Nārāyaṇa;
for charity has been declared by the seers of truth to be even superior to austerity.
Therefore, a wise person should perform the act of giving even with effort. O Brahmin, there is no one equal to that best of men who performs both charity and austerity in this world. 159–160.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Greatness of All Gifts," in the Kriyāyoga-sāra of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Twenty-one.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard the words of Brahmā, Hariśarman, the best of the twice-born,
bowed to him once more with devotion and spoke thus, O Jaimini. Hariśarman said:
"O Lord, you have described those gifts that yield great happiness; you ought to tell me to whom those gifts should be given.
Brahmā said:
Among all the social classes, the Brāhmaṇa is the supreme guru;
gifts should be given to him by those endowed with devotion and faith.
The Brāhmaṇa is the refuge of all the gods; he is the visible manifestation of the deities upon this earth.
"The giver causes the donor to cross over the difficult-to-cross ocean of worldly existence.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O best of gods, you have stated that the Brāhmaṇa is the preceptor of all castes."
"Among them, who is the most excellent? To whom should a gift be given?
Brahmā said:
"All Brāhmaṇas are indeed always excellent and worthy of worship."
O best of Brahmins, these Brahmins are tormented by the defects of theft and other sins;
they are our enemies and never those of others.
Though lacking proper conduct, these twice-born ones are worthy of worship, yet the Śūdras, though their senses are conquered, are not.
Those who eat what is not fit to be eaten are considered the mothers of the worlds.
O best of the twice-born, out of affection for you, I shall now describe specifically the majesty of the gods of the earth (Brāhmaṇas); listen with a concentrated mind.
For Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, the twice-born are their gurus; likewise, the Brāhmaṇas are mutual gurus to one another, and these earth-dwellers are worthy of worship.
O best of men, he who worships a Brāhmaṇa with the understanding that he is Viṣṇu [attains the highest state].
His life, sons, fame, and prosperity increase (verse 10).
Keśava desires to strike off with his Sudarśana the head of that foolish man on earth who, being deluded in intellect, seeks to harm a twice-born (Brāhmaṇa) (verse 11).

O Jaimini, a wise man should not bow to a Brahmin who has flowers in his hand, water in his hand, or who is holding an offering for a deity; nor to one who has just applied oil as an unguent, or who is standing in water, or staying in a temple, or whose mind is absorbed in meditation.
A wise man should not bow to a Brāhmaṇa who is performing worship of the gods,
nor to one who is performing exclusionary rites, nor to one who is eating, O best of the twice-born,
nor likewise to one who is chanting the Sāman hymns. 13–14.

O best of the twice-born, when many Brahmins are standing together, a wise person should offer a salutation to each one individually. One who has performed a respectful greeting to a Brahmin should not fail to greet him with devotion.
He should be known as equal to a Cāṇḍāla and must never be saluted. Parents do not bow down to a son who has already offered his prostration;
likewise, all twice-born men who have offered their prostrations are to be saluted by other twice-born men.
The wise do not hate twice-born Brahmins or cows even when they have committed faults;
yet, if one hates them out of delusion, Hari is always enraged with them. He who looks upon begging Brahmins with an angry eye—
Yama causes needles to be thrust into the eyes of that person. Yama indeed places a heated iron rod into that mouth with which a fool reviles a Brahmin.
In whatever house a Brāhmaṇa eats, Keśava himself, along with all the deities, the ancestors, and the celestial sages, resides in that house.
A wise person who carries even a single drop of the water from a Brāhmaṇa’s feet [attains great merit].
All the sins residing within his body perish instantly.
Whatever holy places (tīrthas) exist indeed within the midst of millions of cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas), all those holy places reside in the right foot of the Brahmin. 22–23.
He whose head is constantly sprinkled with the water from the feet of a Brahmin has effectively bathed in all sacred fords and been initiated into all sacrifices;
he is cleansed of all terrible sins, including even the murder of a Brahmin.
All diseases such as consumption and others that cause extreme suffering perish instantly by holding the water from the feet of a Brahmin. (25–26)

Whatever water is offered at the feet of the Brahmins for the sake of the ancestors, the ancestors, satisfied by it, remain in heaven as long as the moon and stars endure. 27. The wise man who, having washed the feet of the Brahmins, worships them with dūrvā grass—
By him was worshipped Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World and the best of all gods.
(28) That mortal who bears upon his head the foot-washings and the floral remains (nirmālya) of the brāhmaṇas—truly, truly do I say this—his liberation shall indeed be eternal. (29)
That best of men who, having circumambulated a Brahmin, offers salutations,
has thereby circumambulated the earth with its seven continents.
He who gives fruits and betel-leaves to Brahmins after washing their feet [attains great merit].

The sick shall be liberated from disease, and the sinner shall be released from sin. One who is bound shall be freed from bondage by pouring water at the feet of Brahmins. And those noble women who are childless, as well as those wives whose children have died— [shall likewise find release]. 31–32.
Formerly, there was a Brāhmaṇa named Kriya, born of a pure lineage;
he was devoted to the service of Viṣṇu, a knower of the Vedas, compassionate, peaceful, and dedicated to the worship of his ancestors. (34-35)
Having performed worship for his guests and likewise honoring his kinsmen,
that best of the twice-born once went to a lake to bathe, having anointed his body with oil and taken his bathing garments.
Having performed his bath according to the prescribed rites, including the libations and other ceremonies, that lord of brahmins—
learned in all the scriptures and devoted to the welfare of all the world— concluded the bathing rituals while chanting the names of Hari.
He returned to his own home and became intent upon the worship of Hari;
he washed his feet with very cool water. Having washed his feet and hands, that brāhmaṇa, who was devoted to the worship of brāhmaṇas, [proceeded].
O best of the twice-born, he placed all the bathing requisites at the entrance; then a certain dog, tormented by the heat of the midday sun which was like fire, arrived there. 40-41.
Having fallen asleep upon that extremely cool water from the Brahmin’s feet,
that most sinful dog was liberated from all his sins, even those committed over ten million lifetimes, by the touch of the Brahmin’s foot-water. 42.
At the door of the temple, a dog, distressed by thirst, lay fast asleep;
he begged for water, but being struck by the servants of the twice-born, that dog-demon instantly met his death right there.
From the touch of the water used for washing the feet of the twice-born, the dog was cleansed of its impurities;
beholding that high-souled one who was like the Lord incarnate, this Brahmin, whose wealth was his asceticism, spoke while bowing low with humility. 45.
The Brahmin said:
"Who are you? Tell me, O highly fortunate one, by what karma have you become so sorrowful, born into the lineage of a dog amidst various miseries? (46)
Having heard the words of that brahmin-sage, the highly illustrious Brahmā related his entire account from the very beginning. 47.
I was a sovereign ruler of the whole earth named Śaṅkha, possessed of great strength; for four thousand years I protected the entire world.
By my command all were made to act, and all enemies were conquered in battle.

All gifts have been given by me, and those born of unknown wombs have been protected. (49) Once, O illustrious one, pierced by the arrows of Love, I forcibly carried off a certain woman of great beauty from among the wives of common folk. (50)
By the power of that sin, my prosperity fell into doubt;
consequently, even though I was possessed of great strength, I was cast out by all the worlds. Then, deprived of my kingdom, I took up residence within the depths of the forest.
Exhausted by hunger and thirst, I once met my death; having gone to the city of Antaka, I suffered misery for a long time.
O best of Brahmins, hearing this causes pain to the hearts of those who listen. (52-53)
He took delight in that earth made of molten copper, filled with heated iron weapons and extremely terrifying with its blazing tongues of fire.
Then, by the command of Yama, he [approached] a most fearsome pillar of iron.
I stood there embracing a blazing fire that scorched me;
then, I was sprinkled by the servants of Yama with streams of cold sugarcane juice.
Furthermore, I experienced other great sufferings there in the abode of Yama.
Thereafter, having repeatedly attained births in the remaining hells,
I experienced for a long time the great suffering of sinful wombs;
yet, through contact with the water from your feet, I have been liberated from the rope of sin.
"I am going to the supreme abode, which is difficult even for yogis to attain.
You are my guru, O best of the twice-born; salutations to you, the Great-Souled One.
By your grace, I am liberated from sins and shall go to the city of Hari. (58-59)
Bhadrakriya said: "O King, in the human realm, such a thing never occurs in a previous birth; therefore, having abandoned that son, one should always practice righteousness. (60)
That king who grasps political ethics indeed faces no calamity;
he enjoys the earth, long free from thorns.
But for that evil-souled king to whom political ethics do not appeal—
One will lose one's fortune even before long; there is no doubt about this.
(62) A king who desires long life, strength, fame, friends, victory, and happiness must always appoint learned men as his ministers. (63)

Despised by the king, the wise abandoned him with respect; for in an assembly devoid of the wise, political strategy (nīti) does not prevail. Then, when political strategy had perished, [the calamity] of the lord of the earth suddenly occurred.
Royal fortunes perish along with their treasuries, armies, and vehicles. Kings who desire their own welfare should never harbor hatred toward Brahmins, astrologers, physicians, or kinsmen. 65–66.
One who hates astrologers loses their fortune; one who hates physicians is deprived of long life;
one who hates kinsmen becomes familyless; and one who hates Brahmins suffers from all manner of afflictions. Kings are said to be the fathers, and likewise, the subjects are the sons.
Therefore, kings protect their subjects as they would their own biological sons. One should act toward the people of the city just as one has affection for one's own child.
Those kings who cause suffering to their subjects are exceedingly sinful.
The long-sighted should recognize that those kings who protect their subjects like discerning judges have the Goddess of Sovereignty resting upon their heads;
likewise, Hari, the Lord of Gods, protects them incessantly.
Both the protection of subjects and the administration of punishment are conducive to the welfare of a king.
Those kings who are devoid of these two should be known as the lowest of monarchs;
[namely,] the punishing of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous.
By acting thus, the protectors of the earth rejoice for a long time upon the surface of the world;
a lord of the earth should diligently protect wealth acquired through righteous means. For a king of wicked conduct does not expand his influence when faced with calamity.

O best of Brahmins, kings desiring their own welfare should constantly observe the auspicious and inauspicious state of their kingdom with the eyes of spies; as long as the fear of an enemy army has not arrived, they should remain vigilant regarding that threat.
O King, even when faced with both [types of] dangers, one should act fearlessly toward a kinsman,
a friend, a son, or a minister (76).
One should maintain a profound demeanor with the mouth, while harboring only pure affection in the mind.
Ministers, kinsmen, sons, subjects, and likewise brothers, do not regard a king who is devoid of gravity as being truly a king;
they first remain at a distance and do not stand before him. (77-78)
O King, those who have abandoned their depth of character do not desire that which is the refuge of the world; therefore,
a king who desires to rule his kingdom for a long time must appoint a single minister over the entire realm for the sake of its prosperity, O Brāhmaṇa.
One should remove the position of servants who possess excessively arrogant dispositions.
Therefore, in the assembly, the king should appoint another servant; for a king who is defeated by fools and women, and who is always devoted to song and instrumental music, [is lost]. 80-81.
Deprived of his mounts and horses, he would suddenly fall into calamity; O best of the twice-born,
the adoption of proper conduct, truthfulness, the fulfillment of one's own word, and profundity— these are the characteristics of kings.
How can he be called a king who is devoid of majesty? How can he be called a king by whom the enemy's land has not been conquered?
For as long as the king has conquered the enemy's land, he should march forward even a single step. (83–84)
By walking on foot, one obtains the inexhaustible fruit of the horse-sacrifice;
even one slain by kings in battle while desiring victory over enemy lands shall then go to the supreme abode, liberated from all sins.
A king who attains victory in battle reaches the supreme state;
or one who meets death in combat, O lord of gods, shall obtain prosperity.
[But he who has] cast away his weapons, abandoned his courage, and is intent on flight—[does not attain these]. 86–87.
O best of the twice-born, that king who kills a warrior in battle goes to a downward state, while the one who is intent on fleeing from the fight is the killer of him;
both of them shall remain in a hell that is exceedingly difficult to endure.

O best of the twice-born, he who fights against these warriors and slays them shall dwell in heaven as long as the moon and sun endure. What need is there for much speaking here? I shall state it in brief. 89–90.
"O King, one who performs the protection of his subjects never comes to grief.
Brahmā said:
"While that king was speaking thus, his impurities had dissolved away. (91)
O twice-born one, a great rain of flowers fell from the sky upon him; then, celestial messengers arrived for the sake of the high-souled Keśava,
bringing a beautiful, divine chariot yoked with royal swans.

Having ascended a divine chariot fashioned of gold, that king, with his sins entirely removed, went to the abode of Viṣṇu. Thus has the greatness of the water from a Brahmin’s feet been proclaimed to you. 93–94.
Having heard that with a spirit of devotion, a man shall attain liberation.
Thus everything has been told to you, which you desired to hear. Go, O Brāhmaṇa, may it be well with you, toward the abode of the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu).
Hariśarman said:
"My body is being consumed by a great fire of hunger.
O Blessed One, by what means may my hunger be pacified?"
"O Lord of Gods, you are devoted to me and affectionate toward your devotees;
[yet] I constantly experience great suffering, scorched by the fires of hunger.
Brahmā said:
"O best of the twice-born, eat the flesh of that very body which was constantly nourished by you with food;
for those who satisfy themselves with the food of another [are as such]. (98)
"Indeed, they shall eat their own flesh in the next world.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these harsh words of Brahmā, that best of the twice-born [replied].
Once again, he praised that God with words of tender syllables.
The Brahmin said:
"Be gracious, O Lord of the gods, O protector of those who have come for refuge."
Forgive all my faults, O best of gods; salutations be unto you.
(101) For men who carry bodies scattered with impurities and roots of sin, all [their efforts] are merely defects; there are no virtues at all. (102)

O Brahman, you ought to forgive this fault committed out of delusion; for the virtuous do not look upon the faults of those who have sought refuge. It is impossible, O Brahman, to eat the flesh from one's own body.
"From whatever [practice] contentment arises for embodied beings, that alone is what is fitting for them.
When these words had been spoken with devotion by that twice-born man,
the compassionate, omniscient Brahmā, who is dear to the brāhmaṇas, spoke.
Brahmā said: "O best of Brahmins, do not grieve; listen to these auspicious words regarding the manner by which one may obtain food here at present. (106)
A son is born from one's own self; as is the self, so is the son. Therefore, the ancestors indeed receive the fruits of the actions performed by their sons.
You have stayed for a long time in this exceedingly beautiful abode of the god.
Having been addressed thus by him, that brahmin, distressed by hunger, was shown a vision in a dream, and his son spoke these words. The brahmin said:
"You are initiated, O best of sons; likewise, let there be supreme auspiciousness for you. This is your father, gentle one; listen to me without sorrow.
O son, through the power of my asceticism, I have attained the supreme abode."
"Tormented by the fire of hunger, I am constantly perishing there; O twice-born one, if you still possess paternal affection for me now, my son,
then let food and water be given for my sake."
Whatever is given by sons on the surface of the earth for the sake of their ancestors, the ancestors receive that, for sons are born from the bodies of the ancestors.
Formerly, the Blessed One was worshipped by me with supreme devotion. (112–113)
With songs, instrumental music, dances, and beautiful recitations of hymns;
with perfumes, incense, food offerings, and lamps filled with ghee;
with water for the feet, respectful offerings, water for sipping, meditations, and the rites of invocation and so forth—114.
O son, out of my miserliness, I have never offered even a single morsel of cooked food as an oblation to the Lord of the World, the destroyer of sins;
nor have I ever worshipped a guest with water or other offerings. (115–116)
Because I did not provide satisfaction to my kinsmen and to those who came as supplicants, by that very karma, O son Nārāyaṇa,
I am tormented by the fire of hunger and perish day after day, even within your own home.
Therefore, O Lord, by giving food and water to a poor member of the twice-born, quickly provide protection for the life of this best of gods;
otherwise, you will be acting out of cruelty. || 118-119 ||
"Then, in the temple of Viṣṇu, I shall eat my own flesh. Having spoken thus, that hungry Brahmin, whose throat, lips, and palate were parched,
suddenly became invisible before his son, the initiated Dīkṣita.
Then, when the clear dawn had arrived and the sun had appeared, the initiated one reflected upon what his father had said in the dream:
"Due to the fault of my own actions, even in the next world, my father [is suffering]. (121-122)
With all my limbs consumed by hunger, I languish day after day. Fie on me, a person of dull intellect and the foremost among the wretched!
Even by means of the merit of my ancestors, nothing at all is being given away by me.
Having thus reflected in many ways, O best of the twice-born, though he had already been initiated,
he gave gifts to the Brahmins, endowed with faith and devotion.
By the power of that merit, he became free from thirst and hunger.
Listen to this: he remained in the abode of Nārāyaṇa for as long as a day of Brahmā is proclaimed to last—consisting of a thousand cycles of four yugas.
Within that very day, there arise fourteen Manus.

On that very day, fourteen Indras are said to exist; they, the best of Brahmins, enjoy their own respective domains individually. Having enjoyed their own auspicious domains on that single day of Brahmā, [they depart]. (127–128)
While Hariśarman remained in that exceedingly radiant world of Viṣṇu, fourteen Indras and Cāmanavas perished,
and a day of Brahmā passed in that place which bestows all happiness and is so beautiful.
Having enjoyed such delightful pleasures there for this long period of time,
he attained supreme knowledge and entered the body of Hari.
Vyāsa said:
O Jaimini, in this cycle of existence, there is no gift equal to food and water (131).
Indeed, the fruits of all gifts are attained through the giving of food and water; nor is there ever any requirement for examining the recipient or any restriction regarding the time (132).
The seers who perceive the truth have declared this regarding the giving of food and water:
"Indeed, the giving of food and water must always be performed. Those men who recite with supreme reverence this greatness of food, water, and likewise of the twice-born;
Having obtained the fruit of giving food and water, they then go to the bliss-bestowing abode of Nārāyaṇa.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Gift of Food and the Gift of Water," in the *Kriyāyogasāra* of the glorious *Padmapurāṇa*.
The twenty-second chapter. Jaimini said:
[I shall describe] the auspicious majesty of the Gaṅgā, as well as the fruit of the worship of Viṣṇu.
I have heard from you, O Guru, through your grace, the entire greatness of the gift of food and the supreme greatness of the gift of water,
as well as the sin-destroying greatness of the water used for washing the feet of Brahmins,
all accompanied by its historical accounts.
Now, O tiger among sages, I desire to hear with reverence the entire fruit of Ekādaśī, which destroys all sins. Why is Ekādaśī the most excellent, and what is its prescribed procedure?

When is it performed, or what is its fruit? Tell me that, O ocean of virtuous qualities. Who is the most worshipful deity there? And what fault would accrue to one who does not perform it? You ought to tell me this here. (4–5)
Vyāsa said: O brahmin-sage, no one other than Nārāyaṇa is able to describe the entire fruit of Ekādaśī; therefore, I shall speak of it in brief.
Having first created the world of moving and non-moving beings, that best of men,
for the sake of subduing them all, created the Person of Sin (Pāpapūruṣa),
whose head was the killing of the twice-born and whose eyes were the drinking of liquor.

The theft of gold is the face; violating the teacher’s bed is the ears; the killing of a woman is the nose; the sin of killing a cow is the arms; the misappropriation of a deposit is the neck; and likewise, the killing of an embryo is the throat. (8–9)

The tip of the penis represents adultery with another's wife; the belly, the killing of a friend or a member of one's community; the region down to the navel, the murder of those who have sought refuge and so forth; the hips, the reviling of one's guru; the thighs, the sale of a daughter; and the penis, [the aforementioned acts].
He spoke words that betrayed his trust; he had the anus as his organ of pleasure and feet for killing.
(11) He had downy hair like minor offenses, a massive body, and was terrifying;
he was black in color with tawny eyes, causing extreme suffering to those who took refuge in him. (12)
Seeing that most terrible person of sin, the Lord, the Supreme Person who removes the afflictions of his subjects, thought with compassion:
"This wicked and cruel man has been created; he brings suffering to those who depend upon him."
For the sake of subduing living beings, I shall create the cause for this.
Then that Lord Viṣṇu himself became the Ender (Death) and created the hells, such as Raurava, which inflict suffering upon the wicked.
The fool who practices evil does not attain the supreme state,
where, by his command, one must go to hells such as Raurava and the like.
Once, Lord Viṣṇu, the destroyer of the suffering of living beings, [appeared].
Having mounted Vainateya, he went to the abode of Yama.
Seeing that Lord of the worlds, the flawless Nārāyaṇa,
Bhāskari, with a satisfied mind, worshipped him with incense and other offerings.
Worshipped by Yama, Viṣṇu, the sole leader of all the worlds,
sat upon a golden throne, O tiger among the twice-born.
Seated there, the Blessed One, the slayer of the Daityas, remained together with Yama.
O Lord, he heard a sound of wailing in the southern direction.
Then, his mind filled with wonder, that beloved of Kamalā said this to Yama: "From where does this sound of lamentation come?"
Yama said: "O God, mortals who are sinners fall into the hell that causes extreme suffering; yet, due to the fault earned by their own hands, they also suffer in my abode. (22)
"O Viṣṇu, the fruit of the tree of evil is extremely painful to consume;
therefore, the sinners weep, and this is the great sound of them.
Thus was the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa addressed by the son of the Sun.
While those evildoers were crying out loudly, he went there suddenly. Seeing those sinful mortals situated in the Raurava and other hells,
the Lord, the Sovereign, felt compassion arise within his heart and began to reflect.
"Even while I abide within them, all creatures created by me suffer in hell, which yields nothing but absolute misery, due to the fault of their own actions.
O best of Brahmins, having reflected upon this and other matters, the Compassionate One [acted].
Suddenly, the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) itself appeared there;
then, as it was heard, she caused all those sinners to perform [the rite], and they all, their impurities dissolved, went to the supreme abode. 27–28.
Therefore, O Viṣṇu, know Ekādaśī to be the form of the Supreme Self,
the best among all vows and the most excellent of observances,
which purifies the three worlds by observing the lunar day of Ekādaśī. 29.
Apprehensive, the personification of sin approached Viṣṇu to offer praise (30).
Then, O twice-born one, with palms joined in devotion, that personification of sin praised the Lord Janārdana, the beloved of Kamalā (31).
Having heard his hymn of praise, the Supreme Lord was pleased and said, "I am gratified; tell me what you desire. 32.
The Personification of Sin said:
Created by Lord Viṣṇu as a source of suffering for his own devotees,
I am now brought to destruction by the power of Ekādaśī. When I have died, all embodied beings in this world [will likewise perish].
Embodied beings will become liberated from the bonds of worldly existence.
When all these best of embodied beings have been liberated, O Lord, with whom will you play in this theater-house of saṃsāra? 34-35.
O Keśava, if you desire to sport as it were in this temple of the world’s curiosity, then summon me out of fear for the Ekādaśī day;
indeed, I cannot be overcome by thousands of other meritorious deeds. (36)
"May you, the Giver of Boons, be able to destroy the sin of the meritorious Ekādaśī.
[Grant this] for humans, animals, insects, and other living beings;
on mountains, in trees, in places, and in waters. (37-38)

Out of fear of the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī), Viṣṇu fled from rivers, oceans, forests, and wildernesses; from heaven, the mortal world, and the netherworld (Pātāla); and from the gods, Gandharvas, and birds. (39)

There is no place anywhere where I may remain free from fear, nor by that [means] anywhere at all. O eternal God of gods, within the midst of millions of cosmic eggs, I have found no place to stay on this eleventh lunar day.
"O Lord, where shall I dwell on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) free from fear? Tell me that, O Lord of Gods; I have been created by you without cause.
Vyāsa said:
Having spoken thus, the personification of sin fell prostrate upon the ground before Acyuta, the destroyer of afflictions, his eyes streaming with tears.
Then the Blessed One, the crusher of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, laughed.
Terrified by the fear of Ekādaśī, he spoke to the Personification of Sin (Pāpapuruṣa).
The Blessed Lord said: "Arise, O Personification of Sin! Cast off your grief and rejoice."
I shall tell you where your abode is on the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī).
When the Ekādaśī arrives, purifying the three worlds, you, O personification of sin, must remain there, taking refuge in food. 45–46.
"O Brahmin-sage, this Ekādaśī tithi, which is my own form, shall slay you— the sinful person who stands there depending upon food. Having said this, even the Lord vanished right there.
The personification of sin (Pāpapuruṣa), having accomplished his purpose, departed just as he had come.
Therefore, those excellent persons who desire their own welfare should never consume food when the day of Hari has arrived. 48–49.

By the command of the glorious Nārāyaṇa, all those sins that exist in the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) reside specifically on the day of Ekādaśī, taking refuge in food; for those who [refrain from eating],
there shall be liberation from hell for all their sins.

And those who eat food here [at this time] should be known as the worst among sinners. (51) Again and again, I speak firmly: listen, listen, O people! It must not be eaten, it must not be eaten, it must never be eaten. (52)
O best of the twice-born, the Ekādaśī vow, which bestows the fruits of the four aims of life, must be observed by all— Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and others as well.
(53) Eighteen nimeṣas have been declared by the wise to be one kāṣṭhā.
Thirty *kāṣṭhās* are said to be one *kalā* by those who perceive all things;
thirty *kalās* constitute a *kṣaṇa*, and twelve *kṣaṇas* make a *muhūrta*.
Thirty *muhūrtas* are proclaimed as a day and night for the people of the world. (54–55)
O best of the twice-born, a fortnight (pakṣa) is to be understood as consisting of those fifteen days; a month is defined by means of the two fortnights, the bright and the dark.
O foremost of the twice-born, within that month there are the two fortnights, the bright and the dark.
Even one burdened with great sins, if he observes Ekādaśī, shall be liberated from all evil and attain the world of Viṣṇu;
for the Ekādaśī lunar day is indeed called "Mātā" (the Mother). 57–58.
In this very world, the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) protects one everywhere like a mother;
yet he who, having abandoned the Ekādaśī vow, performs another vow,
is like a fool who discards a jewel held in his own hand to grasp a clod of earth.

By those who have observed the Ekādaśī vow endowed with devotion, all sacrifices and all religious observances have been performed. And as for those sinful men who, out of delusion, eat on the day of Ekādaśī— 61.
Whether it be on the bright or the dark fortnight, Hari is always angry with those by whom that guest is transgressed,
and by whom all the duties have been violated.
Just as Viṣṇu is proclaimed to be the foremost among all the gods, so too is he [the guest].
Likewise, among all vows, the Ekādaśī vow is the most excellent.
Just as the sun is among the Ādityas and the moon is among the stars,
so too the Ekādaśī vow is declared to be the best of all vows.
Just as the Aśvattha is declared the best among trees and the Sāman among the Vedas,
so too the Ekādaśī vow is proclaimed the most excellent of all vows.
Just as Uśanas is the best among poets and the Brāhmaṇa among the social classes, [so is this vow].
Likewise, the Ekādaśī vow has been declared the best of all vows. Vyāsa is the foremost among sages, and Nārada among divine seers;
similarly, the Ekādaśī vow is the most excellent of all vows. (66–67)
Just as the gift of food is remembered as the best among all gifts,
so the vow of Ekādaśī is declared the most excellent of all vows.
(68) Just as there is no friend equal to merit, so there is no teacher equal to the scriptures.
In the same way, there is no vow equal to the Ekādaśī in the three worlds (69).
Just as the mind is declared by the wise to be the most excellent of the senses,
so Kārttika is the best of months, just as Arjuna is the best among the Pāṇḍavas (70).
Just as the Vedas are proclaimed to be the best among all scriptures,
so too is the Ekādaśī vow remembered as the most excellent among vows.
O twice-born one, [this is declared] in the Vedas, Āgamas, Purāṇas, and other treatises.
The wise have declared that no vow anywhere is equal to Ekādaśī.
When all human beings on the face of the earth remain fearless by observing the Ekādaśī vow, what will the son of the Sun (Yama) do? 72-73.
What can Yama do against those who properly observe each Ekādaśī?
Therefore, the Ekādaśī vow, which bestows auspiciousness, must indeed be performed.
(74) I shall now describe the procedure for the Ekādaśī vow in brief.
O Jaimini, best of beings, listen with a concentrated mind:
on the tenth day, having risen in the morning, one should perform the cleansing of the teeth;
thereafter, one should bathe without using oil and abstain from food. (75–76)
Then, having worshipped Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Universe, with water for the feet and other offerings,
one should take a single meal while remaining intent on meditation upon Hari. [One should avoid] meat, salt, as well as flesh and masūra lentils.
One should likewise avoid large beans and leafy vegetables on the tenth day (78).
One should also avoid eating twice a day, food from others, honey, sexual intercourse, and eating from vessels of bell-metal on the tenth day (79).

One should avoid neem leaves, eggplant, burnt food, and citron; likewise, one should avoid cow's products that are deficient in ghee on the tenth lunar day (daśamī). One should also avoid eating excessively and eating too little.

One should also completely avoid chewing betel leaf on the tenth day (daśamī). O best of the twice-born, whatever items are forbidden on the tenth day are likewise forbidden on the twelfth day (dvādaśī); of this there is no doubt.

O tiger among brahmins, on the tenth and also on the twelfth day, a devotee of Viṣṇu who desires to obtain the full fruit of the vow should not eat at night. Therefore, on the tenth day, the observant person should quickly prepare sacrificial food (haviṣya).
In the afternoon, one should again perform the cleansing of the teeth according to the prescribed rite (verse 84).
Having gone to the temple in the evening and taken a handful of flowers while meditating upon Keśava in the mind, one should utter this mantra (verse 85).

"O Govinda, this vow has been undertaken by me before you; may it reach fulfillment without obstacle through the compassion of your feet. For man is exceedingly fickle-minded, consisting as he does of greed, delusion, and pride. (86)
"Am I able to perform this vow without your grace?
(87) Having recited these two mantras and offered that very handful of flowers to Nārāyaṇa, one should then prostrate on the ground like a staff. (88)
In that very house, intent on the remembrance of Viṣṇu,
one should spread a bed of *kuśa* grass upon the ground and perform the act of lying down. Then, at dawn, one should perform the cleansing of the teeth with pure [materials].
The wise man should perform the purification of the mouth with twelve waves [of water],
and then perform his daily rites, such as the worship of Viṣṇu and other ceremonies;
thereafter, O chief of Brahmins, at night, he should do so together with all the people observing the vow.

In one place, together with his mother, his wife, his brother, and likewise his father, as well as his sons and friends, he should keep a vigil before the Lord of the World, Hari. 92. Thus he performs the vigil for Hari.
O twice-born one, the performer of the vow shall dwell for a long time in the abode of Viṣṇu (93).
Janārdana removes the sins committed over many births by him who draws the various marks of the conch, the discus, and so forth in the temple of Viṣṇu (94).
Listen to the fruit of one who draws various wonderful images in the temples of Viṣṇu using rice-powder paste, or with other forest-born materials:
he enjoys all auspiciousness through his sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons. (95)
Having gone to the city of Viṣṇu on the remaining [day], one shall attain liberation there.
On the day of the Lord of Kamalā, the man who performs the raising of the banner (dhvajāropaṇa) shall deliver ten million ancestors and go to the city of Nārāyaṇa.
O protector of the earth, a person who adorns the temple of Viṣṇu with rows of fluttering banners shall obtain [merit] in every birth,
for as long as those banners continue to wave in the wind. 98.

All the sins of the one who performs that [act] are destroyed right then and there. (99) Wise people desiring the supreme abode should place banners of various colors at the temple of Hari on the day of Hari (Ekādaśī). (100)
O brahmin-sage, that person who holds a most beautiful parasol over the head of Viṣṇu becomes a kṣatriya on earth in every birth;
and the man who creates a pavilion of flowers for Vāsudeva [attains the same].
For every flower [offered], one shall obtain merit exceeding that of a hundred horse-sacrifices.
On the day of Vāsudeva, the wise man, adorning [the deity] with fragrant flowers, should diligently perform this rite for the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life.
O brahmin sage, he who constructs a cloth-house on the day of Hari becomes a resident of a celestial mansion in the abode of the gods.
Having constructed a cloth-mansion there, a person binds [himself] within it.
Whether it be white, red, or black, the devotee who is dear to Acyuta should,
with devotion, bathe the Śāligrāma stone or an image of the Lord of Śrī there with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and then install it. 105–106.

At the outset, the wise man should perform an auspicious rite (*svastyayana*) as well as the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*); this must be performed with effort for the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life (*caturvarga*). O Brahmin, he should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and his own [mantra-]installation according to the injunctions spoken in the scriptures.
Then, becoming single-minded and taking an excellent flower,
he meditated upon the god Nārāyaṇa, who dwells within the lotus of the heart and is seated upon a golden throne as well as one made of jewels. 108–109.

I worship Him who sits upon a golden throne adorned with blazing jewels, wearing a playful attire; whose body is beautiful with the luster of a cloud illuminated by lightning; who shines eternally with four long arms holding all manner of weapons; and who, with lotus-like eyes, gazes with a sidelong glance at His own glorious face to dispel its weariness incessantly. 110
"Come, O Blessed One, accompanied by the gods; O Lord of Śrī,
O Teacher of the World, you who are endowed with all auspicious marks, this worship of yours must be performed by me with devotion during this vow, together with Lakṣmī."
"Remain upon this excellent seat while I perform your worship.
O Lord Nārāyaṇa, whose fame is renowned throughout all the worlds, is all well with you? Tell me everything, O you who are worshipped by the gods. (112-113)

"O Lord of Gods, O Nārāyaṇa, accept this fragrant water for washing the feet, which is exceedingly cool, pure, and which removes the dust from your two feet. O Viṣṇu, I offer you this *arghya* water, joined with sprouts of *dūrvā* grass."
O lotus-eyed one, I offer you this most pure water for sipping, accompanied by unbroken grains of rice;
please accept it, O increaser of supreme bliss. (115-116)

O destroyer of Jarāsandha, may your body be adorned by me with this fragrant scent, O Lord of Lakṣmī, with this sweet-smelling perfume. I offer it for the sake of purification, as the primordial cause of the worlds.
"O Lord of the Asuras, accept this water for sipping (ācamana).
Created by me previously according to the prescribed rite for the increase of the gods' satisfaction, this incense is now offered by me to you, O best of the Suras. (118-119)

O Janārdana, destroyer of the wicked, may this lamp, filled with ghee and the collector of the hymns of darkness, be for Your pleasure; O Janārdana, here is this garment with its upper cloth, beautiful upon the hips and the waist. 120.
"I give to you, O Lord of Gods, O Teacher of the World, this sacred thread (sopavīta).
Accept, O Supreme Lord, this fourfold food offered by me with devotion, endowed with the six delicious tastes. (121-122)

"O high-minded one, accept this betel leaf, endowed with camphor and khadira wood, which removes foul breath from the mouth and bestows liberation; O Govinda, worship Him with these unsurpassed offerings according to this rite. 123.

One should worship with devotion during all four watches of the day; whoever offers various offerings on the day of Hari must not practice stinginess regarding wealth if he desires the fruit of his actions. 124–125.

Then, O best of the twice-born, all those observers of vows who are devoted to Nārāyaṇa should perform a night vigil with dancing, singing, hymns of praise, and so forth; they should also perform circumambulations while reciting the names of the Lord of Kamalā.
Those devoted to the vow should remember these [names] which destroy all sins.
People who hear the sound of the name of Hari resonating from every mouth shall be liberated from great accumulations of sin. 127–128.
One should not engage in conversation with heretics on the day of Hari;
by merely conversing with heretics, all dharma is destroyed. (129) The song of Nārāyaṇa’s glory issued forth from every throat.
Having heard it, the deluded are not satisfied, just as dogs are not satiated by the sound of a lute.
The virtuous attain great joy upon hearing the song of the Lord of the Universe,
just as deer rejoice at the sound of a lute that destroys all sins.
Singing the songs of Hari and performing the most excellent dance, the observers of vows are satisfied upon seeing the Lord of Kamalā;
O twice-born one, they are satisfied by that very act in the temple of Viṣṇu. 132.
For them, this state of being like cattle shall be eternal, as if it were their very nature in every birth.
(133) Those who do not sing the Gītās on the day of Hari while observing their vows wander through birth after birth, deprived of sacred words. (134)
They play musical instruments such as the mṛdaṅga drum before Hari,
because the Lord Madhusūdana becomes pleased by such instrumental music;
they keep a vigil for Viṣṇu and perform the excellent study of the Vedas.
Or rather, the recitation of Purāṇas should be performed by Vaiṣṇava people.
On the day of Hari, the Rāmāyaṇa, the Bhāgavata, the Mahābhārata spoken by Vyāsa, and other Purāṇas should be read. (136–137)

Those who recite before Viṣṇu and those who listen to Hari during the day obtain the fruit born of the gift of a tawny cow for every single syllable. A Vaiṣṇava person should joyfully keep a vigil at night.
As long as one remains awake, one should meditate correctly on Keśava within the heart;
throughout the day, one should repeatedly perform circumambulations of Hari and prostrate before Janārdana, falling upon the ground like a staff.

Then, at the clear dawn, having performed the five great sacrifices, the devoted observer of the vow should bathe Hari with milk and worship Him. He should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a brahmin according to his own capacity. 141.
Therefore, one observing the vow should perform the *pāraṇa* (concluding meal) in the middle of the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*).
For he who performs the *pāraṇa* after having transgressed the twelfth lunar day, the merit acquired over ten million lifetimes is utterly destroyed. (142–143)
The wise who desire the fruit of their vow must perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) during the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), never on the thirteenth day (trayodaśī). O Brahmin,
even on the night of the fasting day, the Vaiṣṇava...

One who desires the fruit of the fast should avoid sleep with great effort. Indeed, without staying awake, the fast is surely useless; therefore, one should perform the vigil during both fortnights. 145–146.
O best of the twice-born, those who perform the Ekādaśī vow according to this prescribed rite— truly, truly, they all go to liberation.
It is the sole cause for removing birth and death, and it must be performed even by the hosts of gods led by Indra.
O Jaimini, perform with constant effort and care the essence of the Vāsudeva-day vow. 148.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Greatness of Ekādaśī," in the Kriyāyogasāra of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Twenty-three.
Vyāsa said:
Formerly, there was a king named Kocaraśa on the circle of the earth;
he was peaceful, supremely knowledgeable in dharma, and the best among those who know the science of royal policy.
He was a speaker of truth, one who had conquered anger, and one who had subdued the entire host of his enemies;
he was devoted to the worship of Nārāyaṇa and supremely intent on the service of Hari.
His queen, named Suprajñā, was a woman of excellent wisdom and spoke with endearing words.
Endowed with all auspicious marks, devoted solely to the service of her husband,
intent on the Ekādaśī vow, and desiring the welfare of all living beings—
she was a noble woman of great fortune, possessing excellent character and a beautiful complexion, and capable of recollecting her past lives.
Having observed the tenth day (Daśamī) along with his wife, the king, who knew the supreme truth,
prepared to perform the vigil on the night of the eleventh day (Ekādaśī). In the meantime, O lord of the earth, a certain Brahmin named Śaureya arrived before the monarch.
The one of great splendor arrived at his vigil-pavilion (6). As he was approaching, the king, who was devoted to Nārāyaṇa,
together with his wife and exceedingly joyful, honored him with water for the feet and other offerings (7).
Seated in their midst, that brahmin, who knew all truths, saw there many practitioners of vows intent on the worship of Viṣṇu;
some were worshipping Hari with various beautiful flowers.
With perfumes, incenses, lamps, and unsurpassed offerings, some,
adorned with the clay of the Gaṅgā and garlands of tulasī leaves, dance joyfully before Hari as observers of their vows. 10.
Some, devoted to their vows and dear to the Blessed One, sang charming songs of Hari while taking up cymbals; others praised the flawless Nārāyaṇa with unsurpassed hymns. 11.
Some praise the Lord of the worlds with divine meanings and tender syllables;
likewise, some fan the Lord of the world, Hari, with the cool breeze of white whisks, thereby bringing him great delight. 12–13.
Some high-souled ones played lutes and other musical instruments that were charming, pure, and auspicious; others sang of Keśava.
Both the king and the queen-mother were exceedingly joyful. 14.
As that noble couple performed their excellent singing and dancing with charming grace,
Śauri, the best of brāhmaṇas, laughed at them with sweet words. 15–16.
Śauri said:
"O protector of the earth, you are blessed, and your queen is blessed; this conduct of yours both is auspicious and difficult to find on this earth. (17)
I shall tell you this: since no supreme devotee of Viṣṇu has ever been seen by you, O protector of the earth, this world is blessed by you; of this there is no doubt.
This Ekādaśī vow is pure and dear to the Blessed Lord.
Therefore, O King of the Kurus, you are indeed the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas along with your wife;
O best of kings, you are the sole lord of the seven continents together with your wife, for you dance and sing out of love before Nārāyaṇa. 19–20.
"The conduct of you two, a husband and wife, has been seen to be wonderful. From what cause has this exceedingly pure intellect arisen in you both?
Vyāsa said:
Having heard these words of that twice-born man named Śauri, she,
with a slight smile upon her face, then spoke to the wise brahmin.
Suprājñā said:
O best of the twice-born, by the power of Ekādaśī, we two, who were formerly great sinners, were liberated by the high-souled son of the Sun;
through the power of the recollection of our former births, we performed the divine vow of Ekādaśī.
"O best of Brahmins, we are acting now out of a desire for the supreme station.
Śauri said:
"If indeed, O lady of noble form, you [remember] your own previous birth,"
A curiosity arises in my heart to hear what has been told by you both:
who was the woman previously situated there, or who was the husband; and how were you two abandoned by the Son of the Sun, even though you were sinners? (25-26)
Suprājñā said:
"O best of the twice-born, although this speech is not to be disclosed, I remain here as a chief courtesan, skilled in the arts and proficient in the scriptures. (27)
"O Lord of Brahmins, in that birth, many terrible sins were committed by me which truly bestow the sufferings of hell. This Śūdra, named Nityodaya, is devoid of his own proper conduct."
He was a stealer of others' wives, cruel, and a plunderer of others' wealth;
he drank liquor, was a slayer of friends, a destroyer of embryos, and a constant harmer of others; he was possessed of excessive pride and always reviled the dharma.
Once, abandoned by all his kinsmen who were devoted to virtuous vows,
he came to my house, lusting after the charms of courtesans.
O best of the twice-born, seeing him to be young and handsome, [I took him in].

Even though I was satisfied by those amorous delights, O ascetic, I still felt a longing; then, having experienced love-making with me, he, bowing low in humility out of affection, spoke these words to me: 32–33. "O you whose wealth is penance, even after enjoying amorous pleasure with me, this man, bowing down in modesty out of love, addressed me with these words."
"I am an expert in the science of sexual pleasure, yet I have been abandoned by my own kinsmen;
if you think it right, I shall stay here with you.
The twice-born [Vasiṣṭha] heard these words as she spoke them, bowing with humility.
Having attained the state of a husband and wife, I remained with him. Once, O tiger among the twice-born, on the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) sacred to Hari,
I was afflicted by great maladies that strike at the very body.
O best of the twice-born, on that very day, her body shattered by fever,
she drank no water and ate no food out of supreme fear; yet,
on that same day, there arose in her an outpouring of love for me, Hari.
Dejected by birth, she abandoned both food and water.
Then, O best of the twice-born, at night, having lit a lamp with ghee, I kept a vigil while my mind was overcome by fever. 38-39.
By him as well, keeping vigil throughout the night was performed while repeatedly chanting, "Nārāyaṇa, Hare, Kṛṣṇa, protect me! through the power of fasting and the utterance of Keśava's name. 40.
"O Brāhmaṇa, all our sins were utterly destroyed. Then, at the clear dawn when the divine sun had risen, O best of Brāhmaṇas, I, afflicted by fever, passed away."
Then, seeing me who had met my death and was afflicted by disease, he, though pure, was censured by all people as one who had brought about his own demise.
Thereafter, by the servants of Sūryaja, whose eyes resembled blazing fire—
Having bound him with a firm noose and led him along a difficult path, Citragupta,
being highly discerning, examined everything from its very root— whether it were auspicious or inauspicious karma— in accordance with the command. 44-45.
Citragupta said:
"O mighty-armed one, although these two were the foremost among great sinners,
they have nevertheless been liberated from their sins by fasting on the Ekādaśī day."
"Even he who might perform the meritorious Ekādaśī vow without desire shall go to the supreme abode, freed from all sins.
Thus was the highly illustrious Dharmarāja addressed by Citragupta.
Rising suddenly from their seats, they both bowed down to him;
adorned with fragrant divine sandalwood, incense, flowers, and golden ornaments, they were freed from all sin by Mṛtyu. 48–49.
There, with various kinds of sweet fruits comparable to nectar,
Bhāskari affectionately provided a meal for the two of us.
Then, after praising us with divine hymns, the lord Yama himself [honored us].
Having mounted them upon a divine chariot, he spoke with palms joined in reverence.
Yama said:
"You two are the foremost among the meritorious, entirely free from all sins."
"Go now to that place where the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu has set.
When this was said by Dharmarāja, who was indeed bowed low with humility, we both prostrated at his lotus feet and spoke as follows: (52-53)

"O God, that supreme abode of Viṣṇu must not be gone to otherwise; rather, we have a desire to see hell situated within your house. Then, by the command of Yama, the two Brahmins ascended a beautiful chariot.
"O devoted wife, we have seen there at length those hells that are difficult to behold, which are the abodes of the sinful.
The Brahmin said:
"O you who are faithful to your husband, tell me what kind of state is experienced by those who possess sin."
O lady of beautiful hips, you ought to explain all those various paths in detail— by which meritorious souls go to the abode of Yama, and by which those of sinful nature do so. Tell me this in full.
"What kind of Lord Vaivasvata would a meritorious soul see there,
and what are the paths of the meritorious and the sinful that bestow happiness and suffering? Thus spoke Suprājña.
"I have described the path for meritorious men;
listen, O tiger among the twice-born, as it increases the joy of those who hear it.
It is bound together with broad slabs of stone and covered with divine garments. (59)
The path of those possessing merit shines forth, free from all calamities.
In some places, wonderful songs are sung by Gandharva maidens; in others, Apsaras with lovely bodies perform dances.
In some places they played the lute and various musical instruments that were enchanting to the mind;
in some places there was a rain of flowers, and in others a cool breeze.
In some places there were water-stalls with cool water, and in others dining halls.
In some places gods and gandharvas recite the supreme hymn of praise;
in various places there are beautiful long ponds with blooming lotuses,
and here and there are trees providing excellent shade, such as the flowering vañjula and others.
Then, O best of the twice-born, those meritorious men, having attained a peaceful death, proceed along the path endowed with happiness;
some, moreover, are mounted upon horses and adorned with various ornaments.
Some go covering their heads with tall, white umbrellas;
some go mounted on elephants, some on chariots, and some people go to the abode of Yama comfortably, mounted on vehicles. 66–67.
Some gods go along being fanned by the breezes from chowries held in the hands of celestial nymphs, while being praised by divine sages;
others carry divine weapons and are adorned with garlands and sandalwood paste.
While chewing betel-leaf, meritorious souls go to the abode of Yama;
some, illuminating the ten directions with the luster of their own bodies, proceed to the house of Śamana, those who dwelt in water-reservoirs. 69–70.
O best of beings, some go along eating divine rice-pudding (apūpa),
while others proceed happily on the path consuming excellent food. Some drink milk, and others likewise drink sugarcane juice.
Some go to my abode drinking buttermilk;
some, eating curds; some, various fruits; and some meritorious ones indeed go while drinking honey. 73.
Then, seeing those many who had arrived and were devoted to the Dharma,
Nārāyaṇa himself attained solar joy and became four-armed, dark-complexioned, with eyes like full-blown lotuses. 74.
Bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, with Garuḍa as his vehicle (75),
wearing a golden sacred thread, possessing a beautiful and great face,
adorned with a crown, earrings, and a forest garland (76).
The highly wise Citragupta and the servants of Yama, headed by Caṇḍa,
all assumed the form of Nārāyaṇa and spoke with sweet words. Then Dharmarāja himself addressed all those best of men.

O twice-born one, having attained supreme joy, he should honor them like friends with divine jewels and fruits; then the son of the Sun spoke to those meritorious men, saying, "Let them take their meal. 78-79.
Yama said:
"O you all, great-souled ones who fear the torments of hell, go to the supreme state by virtue of the absence of your own karma. (80)

"O best of the twice-born, when a man has attained birth in this cycle of existence (saṃsāra) and performs meritorious deeds, he is equal to his father, equal to his brother, equal to his kinsman, and equal to his friend. Having been addressed thus by Dharmarāja, all of them [listened].
Having ascended a divine chariot, they have gone to the city of Nārāyaṇa.
O best of the twice-born, the destination of the meritorious has been described by you in brief;
now hear in detail the destination of those with sinful souls, which I shall declare.
The width of the path for those of evil nature is said to be eighty-six thousand yojanas, and it is filled with every kind of suffering;
in some places there is a rain of fire, and in others a shower of stones.
In some places the sand was heated by the best of the gods;
in some places there were sharp rocks, and likewise in others, hot stones;
in some places there was a rain of weapons, and in others, a shower of glowing coals.
In some places, O twice-born one, there were winds of the final age, intensely heated like fire; in other places, there were deep, blinding darknesses with whirlpools of straw for their mouths;
and in some places, there was a rain of thorns consisting of iron arrows.
In some places there are rows of stones difficult to climb, inhabited by serpents;
there the sinners go with their throats, lips, and palates parched, amidst such manifold afflictions that are devoid of shade and water. 88-89.
O best of the twice-born, upon that path the sinners travel in misery;
they are named Vimuktakeśas, having the appearance of ghosts and being terrifying to behold.
Some are drenched in streams of blood, while others are smeared with mud.
Some sinners with blackened limbs travel along the path;
some wail in agony, their eyes clouded with flowing tears; and some sinners go along lamenting their own past deeds. 91-92.
For some sinners there was the binding of a leather noose upon the neck;
for some it was bound upon the skeleton, and for others upon both feet. Having pierced the neck with a needle, he fastened the noose firmly with great wrath.
These non-servants are dragged along by certain evildoers;
carrying heavy stones placed upon their ears and iron burdens upon the crowns of their heads, these sinners travel the path. 94-95.
Some sinful ones the servants of Yama lead away by their arms with nooses and arrows; others they lead by their necks with firm blows from their hands.
Thus the messengers of Yama lead them on, hurling them again and again before him.
Some go with their heads downward and others with their feet upward;
some go on their arms and some on one foot—thus they move in distorted forms, uttering cries of distress. 97–98.
Being beaten by the messengers of Yama, the sinners travel along that path;
when they have all arrived there, the sinful-souled Yama cast off his divine form and became exceedingly terrifying.
With eyes resembling a pond thirty yojanas long, smoke-colored, possessed of great luster, tall, with a gurgling voice,
a row of very long teeth, and a line of nails like winnowing baskets; 100–101.
Mounted upon a fierce buffalo, biting his lips,
staff in hand and holding a leather noose, with a face contorted by frowns—
Citragupta, the master of great illusion, his eyes reddened with rage. 102.
Uttering loud, terrifying laughter, Samavartin shone forth resplendent.
All the servants, Caṇḍa and the others, with nooses and mallets in their hands,
became as fierce and enraged as roaring clouds.
"Kill, kill the most sinful ones! Pierce, cut, and pierce them!
The servants of Yama are running and leaping from every direction!
(105) To all those sinners as they were falling, the Lord Dharmarāja spoke:
He should threaten them with the staff of Time while uttering the sound "Hum.
Yama said:
"O you sinners of wicked conduct, you who are devoid of discernment!"
"Alas! You have committed sins that cause you suffering even now. 107.
Even though I, the Lord of Life, am standing right here upon your heads, you did not perceive me; and despite knowing me, you committed these transgressions. 108.
"I am the kinsman of the virtuous and the enemy of the sinful"— have you not heard this anywhere with your own ears? (109) The hells are unbearable and filled with various miseries.
"It is well known that sinners eat these [roots];
thinking this was false, you of evil intent engaged in debate with me.
Today, let those who have committed such sins be seen by your own eyes. 111
"O you who are always intoxicated by words born of wealth-blindness, you have indeed constantly woven webs of sin;
O wicked ones, as you now enjoy the fruit of those sins, what is the use of your lamentation? (112)
Having spoken thus, the god Bhāskari, the highly wise one, said to Citragupta:
"O illustrious one, deliberate upon the evil deeds of these people. (113)
Having heard the words of Dharmarāja, Citragupta, being thus urged, then spoke of all the sins they had committed; thereupon,
O best of the twice-born, all those sinners began to wail.
Thus spoke the sinners, terrified and bound by the leather noose; they said to Śamana, "O son of Bhāskara, whatever sins have been committed by us... (116)

Who are the witnesses present there, and who have you been designated as such? Tell us what was seen here before us, whether it be inauspicious or auspicious, regarding that which was done by us in the past. (117)
Then, O twice-born one, the Blessed One, laughing with great wrath,
summoned all the witnesses and spoke these words.
Yama said:
"All of you are witnesses to what has occurred in my presence.
The sky, the earth, the water, and likewise the guests;
day and night, both twilights, and Dharma—these are the witnesses. (119–120)

They spoke of all the deeds, both auspicious and inauspicious, of those evil-minded ones; at whatever time and for whomever a particular action had been performed, Yama, in their presence, declared that very deed as a witness.
Having heard that, all the sinners stood with their minds drawn by terror and their hearts trembling, like deer upon seeing a cloud;
then [the executioner] made a clattering sound with his rows of teeth.

The King of Dharma struck each of those who had committed sins individually with his staff of Time (Kāladaṇḍa). Being thus beaten by the King of Dharma, they all cried out, lamenting their own deeds and overcome with terror.
Then, by the command of Yama, Caṇḍa and the other messengers, filled with rage, cast all those sinners into the hells such as Raurava and others;
they threw some who had committed heinous crimes into the Tāpana hell and others into the Avīci hell.
They cast them into Saṃghāta, Kālasūtra, Mahāraurava,
and likewise into Saṃtapta, Vālukākuṇḍa, Kumbhīpāka,
Nirucchvāsa, Mahāghora, and Pramardana.
In the terrible forest of sword-leaves (Asipatravana), the sinners were devoured by various beasts;
likewise, some servants of Yama threw them into the Vaitaraṇī river, while others cast them into a horrific pool of excrement filled with chaff, charcoal, and bone-thorns. 128–129.
The servants of Yama cast her, who was intensely tormented by the full [suffering],
into the smearing of excrement and likewise into the eating of excrement;
she was placed by the servants of Yama even into the eating of her own flesh.
Some consume phlegm, and some consume semen;
some drink urine, and some, being sinful, drink blood.
In the mouths of some there are leeches resembling serpents. 131–132.
O best of the twice-born, the serpents are filled [with their own tongues] by the terrifying messengers of Yama; having been produced by those who are intensely tormented,
these tongues are thrust into the ear-cavities and mouths of certain evildoers.
The merciless servants of Yama fill [the pits] with boiling oil;
they cut off the arms and likewise the feet, as well as the ears, noses, and so forth, of those wicked-souled ones. 134–135.
Some of the servants of Yama force them to lie down upon heaps of glowing embers,
some upon thorns like iron arrows,
and others upon heated mud.
They pull the sinners by their hair and cast them down, O best of the twice-born;
and into the mouths and the joints of the nails of some of those sinners, they repeatedly thrust thousands of red-hot needles. 137–138.
They indeed place some upon the points of heated iron spikes;
others, with their heads pierced by sharp thorns,
cry out in pain as they are seized by the hands and feet with the thorns of the *śālmali* tree.
Some, crying out piteously as they were being flayed with iron claws,
and others, having stones tied to their necks,
were cast again and again by the servants of Yama into pits of blood and pits of water.
The messengers of Yama violently crush the heads of sinful men with stones again and again;
they thrust clusters of iron spikes into the chests of some.

They cast [the sinners] into the worlds of those who cry out, O twice-born one; the eyes of some whose souls are evil are plucked out with hooks, while the noses of others are filled with scorpions. 143–144.

Having bound the feet of some with nooses to the branches of trees, the servants of Yama kindle a smoky fire upon the ground; there, those who have committed sins undergo the inhalation of smoke. 145. Their limbs... [are consumed].
With their faces turned downward and their feet upward, they remained there as long as the moon and stars exist.
Some, being struck again and again with clubs and mallets by the messengers of Yama, vomited blood, overwhelmed by agony.
O twice-born one, in houses filled with darkness and foul odors, some sinners suffer from gadflies and mosquitoes;
some consume ashes, while others consume worms. (148)
Some [are eating] foul-smelling flesh, and others putrid earth;
being devoured by dogs, tigers, jackals with vajra-like teeth and claws, and bears, some cry out, drenched in blood.

Others are being devoured by serpents of exceedingly fierce venom; still others, O twice-born one, have their chests pierced by the tips of buffalo horns and fall to the earth in a swoon, drenching the ground with blood.
Others, their entire bodies shattered by the terrible arrows released from the bows of Yama’s messengers—arrows resembling venomous serpents—roll upon the surface of the earth;
they fall upon glowing iron balls and likewise upon heated stones. (152–153)
With the weapon of their stings, some [demons] tear at the faces of certain beings, while others tear at their nostrils and the mouths of the messengers of Yama; indeed,
they pierce the nostrils for the purpose of obstructing the wind of the breath.
The limbs and skins of some are torn away by the powerful messengers of Yama with their uplifted, sharp-edged spears;
others are seized by the hair, cast down upon the surface of the earth.
Those who have committed sins are indeed constantly struck with spikes at their feet and other parts, and some, being tormented by streams of caustic water,
drink that caustic water while crying out in many ways, O twice-born one. (157)
Some unfortunate sinners are made to drink bile;
others, the worst of sinners, are made to drink the milk of the Snuhī plant.
While some lie upon the ground, their chests are pierced by the servants of Yama.
Heated stones as large as mountains are being placed upon them;
having fixed two pieces of wood upon their necks and throats,
they bind the faces of some upward with firm ropes.
Some they hang upon the branches of trees, while others they cast down to the ground; they repeatedly lift them up from the earth and throw them back down again.
Thus all those sinners remain there, both hungry and thirsty.
Crying out "Save us! Save us! they wail in the house of torment for as long as an eon or until the end of the world, having experienced the agonies of hell;
and when they have not yet fully exhausted their suffering, with a remnant of sin remaining, they are born into sinful wombs.
Those born from sinful wombs become afflicted by disease;
