they have deficient or redundant limbs, are miserable, and serve evil.
They are childless, exceedingly foolish, and devoted to harming others. 164–165.
Those of short lifespan and small intellect, as well as those who have wicked wives, constantly perform sinful deeds through action, mind, and speech; again,
by the power of their sins, they go to hell as before.
Therefore, sin must never be committed by the best of beings.
For men who have committed sins, there is no escape from hell.
In brief, O best of the twice-born, the suffering of sinners has thus been described.
Who is capable of correctly describing the ends of the miserable states of men who have committed sins, even in hundreds of tens of thousands of years? Having seen this,
we two ascended the celestial chariot and went to the city of Nārāyaṇa.
Having enjoyed pleasures in the abode of Hari for thousands of millions of kalpas,
O best of the twice-born, you have now been born in this pure lineage of King Vairaja;
having experienced all enjoyments endowed with every prosperity here.
Having attained a peaceful death, one must go to the supreme state;
there is no vow equal to the Ekādaśī vow in the three worlds.
Even by performing it unintentionally, such is the destination that we have reached.

"Those who observe the Ekādaśī vow with a spirit of devotion—I do not know what may become of them through the compassion of Vāsudeva. Thus, O best of Brahmins, everything you asked has been told to you. (173-174)
"What else do you wish to hear regarding the greatness of Viṣṇu’s day?
Vyāsa said: Having heard these words of his, that brāhmaṇa, who was a knower of the supreme truth... (175)
The king and the queen made their own minds very firm in the vow of Ekādaśī; having enjoyed the earth for a long time,
they went to the city of Viṣṇu at the end and attained the supreme state.

Those who hear and recite this greatness of the King of Vows (Vratarāja) are liberated from the webs of sin and attain the presence of Hari. Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Greatness of Ekādaśī," in the Kriyāyogasāra of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
Chapter Twenty-four.
Sūta said:
Having heard the fruit of Ekādaśī, Jaimini was then well-pleased.
With palms joined in reverence, he spoke thus to the Lord Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana. Jaimini said:
"By your grace, I have heard the majesty of the divine Viṣṇu."
The greatness of Tulasī destroys the sins of those who hear it.
Vyāsa said:
O Blessed Goddess Tulasī, by all the deities, including Indra and the others—
She who, when constantly served, bestows the fruits of the four aims of life; Tulasī is difficult to obtain for even the virtuous in heaven, on earth, or in the netherworld.
Indeed, devotion toward her brings about the attainment of the fruits of those four aims.
O best of beings, wherever a single tulasī tree stands, there indeed reside all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
Keśava dwells in the middle of the leaf, and Prajāpati at the tip of the leaf.
The auspicious Tulasī shall always indeed abide upon her leaves;
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Gāyatrī, and Caṇḍikā,
as well as all other wives of the gods, reside within those leaves.
Indra, Agni, Yama, Nairṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, and Kubera— these dwell upon that branch;
as do all the Ādityas, the planets, and the Viśvedevas at all times.
The Vasus, the Munis, and all the celestial sages likewise [dwell there].
Whatever holy places exist upon the surface of the earth within the midst of the millions of universes,
they indeed reside by taking refuge in a leaf of Tulasī.

He who serves the Tulasī endowed with a spirit of devotion has thereby served all sacred fords as well as the gods, beginning with Brahmā. Those who cut the masses of grass growing at the roots of the Tulasī [are likewise purified].
At that very moment, Hari destroyed the sin of Brahman-slaughter residing within his body.
O best of the twice-born, by sprinkling fragrant, cool water upon the Tulasī plant during the summer season, a man shall attain liberation.

He who gives a moon, a fan, or an umbrella to her— especially during the summer heat— is declared free from all sins. Furthermore, the person who [offers] Tulasī with streams of unbroken rice and water in the month of Vaiśākha...

He who sprinkles [water] upon the Tulasī daily obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha). Even he who sprinkles the Tulasī with merely a handful of water attains heaven, freed from all sins.

O brahmin sage, if that best of men should at any time sprinkle the *tulasī* with its own milk, prosperity shall remain steadfast in his house. He who performs the smearing of the root of the *tulasī* with cow dung—
O brahmin sage, hear now the meritorious fruit of that sweeping: O Jaimini, for as many particles of dust as are removed from there,
for that many thousands of kalpas he rejoices together with Viṣṇu.
He who places a lamp upon a tulasī leaf at twilight goes to the abode of Viṣṇu, accompanied by ten million members of his lineage.
He protects cows, dogs, donkeys, and human beings.
Keśava always protects that person who offers tulasī to children. That man who plants tulasī with devotion attains supreme liberation upon death; of this there is no doubt.
That best of men who, endowed with devotion, beholds Tulasī at dawn,
obtains the inexhaustible fruit of actually seeing Viṣṇu himself.
Furthermore, that man who, filled with devotion, bows down to Tulasī—
His lifespan, strength, fame, wealth, and progeny increase.
By the mere remembrance of Tulasī, all sins are destroyed;
by the mere touch of Tulasī, the diseases of men perish. 24–25.
Whoever eats an auspicious Tulasī leaf, which removes all sins,
the sin residing within that person's body perishes at that very moment.
(26) That man who wears a garland produced from Tulasī wood—
There is no sin in his body; this truth is spoken by me.
He who bears on his head the water dripping from a *tulasī* leaf obtains the merit born of bathing in the Gaṅgā; of this there is no doubt. 27–28.
A man who worships the auspicious Tulasī with devotion using dūrvā grass, unbroken rice grains, flowers, and food offerings, shall obtain the fruit of the worship of Viṣṇu.
By whomsoever the Blessed Tulasī has ever been honored with food offerings, flowers, excellent incense, and ghee lamps—

O Brahmins, what need have those who bestow the supreme nectar of dharma, artha, and kāma for the practice of worshiping the feet of Viṣṇu? O Brahmin, when they plant the tulasī— which delights Hari and is served by hosts of gods— in places free from defects, Hari, the enemy of Mura and lord of the three worlds, being pleased, swiftly grants them the supreme state.

Whatever sacrifice, vow, worship of the ancestors, adoration of Acyuta, charity, or any other auspicious rite men perform upon the faultless soil of Tulasi, all those indeed become inexhaustible. Whatever righteous deed a person performs on this earth without Tulasi, who is most dear to Narayana, [that too becomes fruitless].
O best of the twice-born, all that indeed becomes fruitless, and even the lotus-eyed God of gods is not pleased.

However, that man who, endowed with a spirit of devotion, beholds the auspicious and pure Tulasī during pilgrimages—by the grace of Hari, the entire fruit of his pilgrimage is swiftly accomplished; this word of mine is most firm. (33-34)
Having abandoned fragrant flowers such as the mandāra, kunda, and lotus, the Infinite Lord of the world,
out of joy, accepts even withered tulasī, which consists of pure virtues and provides protection by destroying abundant sins.
(35) But those of sinful intent uproot the tulasī, which resembles the vine of nectar and is the very source of all things, and cast it upon the ground.
Lord Hari, who is fond of Tulasī, truly and constantly seizes the fortune of those men who do so out of ignorance.

(36) Furthermore, Hari swiftly takes away the wealth of those people who constantly void urine, feces, or other filth upon the ground of a Tulasī plant—the very abode of the gods—thereby accumulating sins against that sanctuary. (37)
"I gather you for the sake of worshipping Nārāyaṇa; salutations to you!
For Keśava is not satisfied by flowers such as the pārijāta, nor even by perfumes and the like, without you. Therefore, O auspicious one, I gather you."
"O illustrious one, without you every action is fruitless. Therefore, O Goddess Tulasī, I choose you; be the bestower of boons.
O Goddess, whatever suffering arises in your heart from this [act of] choosing..."
"O Lord of the World, forgive that; I bow to you, Tulasī.
Having recited these mantras with palms joined in reverence, the Vaiṣṇava person claps his hands twice and plucks a leaf of Tulasī.
O best of the twice-born, just as a tree does not shake when its branches are unharmed, so too, O lord of Tulasī,
whenever a leaf is plucked from a branch that has been broken,
pain arises in the heart of Viṣṇu.

Even with an old leaf fallen from the tip of a branch onto the ground, Govinda, the crusher of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, is worthy of worship; how much more so for one who worships the Lord Acyuta with tender tulasī leaves! 44.
"One quickly obtains everything that one desires with the mind.
Jaimini said:
"O bull among the twice-born, what tree is equal to the Tulasī tree?"
"I desire to know that; speak, O son of Satyavatī. Vyāsa said:
"O twice-born one, just as Tulasī is eternally most dear to Viṣṇu,"

Likewise, O best of the twice-born, all the deities who reside at the foot of the Tulasī tree, which is most beloved and the destroyer of all sins, dwell there at the base of the Āmalakī tree as well. 47–48.
O best of the twice-born, the Gaṅgā and other sacred fords (tīrthas) are located right there,
where the purifying Dhātrī tree, most dear to Viṣṇu, stands; whatever action, whether auspicious or inauspicious, is performed at the foot of the Amalaka tree—
Whatever is performed by men for the sake of the twice-born shall become true and inexhaustible.
(50) One who worships Hari with pure, fresh leaves of the dhātrī tree is liberated from the web of sins and attains sāyujya with Hari. (51)
O Jaimini, that place where the Dhātrī and the auspicious Tulasī do not stand would be impure, and one would not obtain the fruit of one's ritual actions (kriyā).
That hermitage in which the Dhātrī and the auspicious Tulasī do not stand [is likewise impure].
Everything performed by that person surely goes to waste;
O Brahmin, in whose house there is no dwelling place for the Dhātrī and Tulasī, misfortune, all sin, and even the Kali age are satisfied by him. 53-54.
O best of the twice-born, that place where there is neither the *dhātrī* nor the *tulasī* should be known by the seers of truth as being equal to a cremation ground.
Wherever the *dhātrī* and the *tulasī* may stand, there all the gods reside.
There, no sin whatsoever remains for one who wears a garland of *dhātrī* fruits, which destroys all evil;
Viṣṇu, together with Śrī, always dwells within his body. (56-57)
The wise man who wears a garland made of dhātrī wood has all the deities residing within his body. Whatever action a man performs while wearing a garland of dhātrī fruit, [it becomes efficacious].
All that, whether auspicious or inauspicious, is declared to be inexhaustible.
But for that man who knows the entirety of reality and eats the dhātrī fruit, all sin residing within his body is destroyed. 59-60.
O best of the twice-born, listen as I describe the supreme majesty of one who wears a garland made of dhātrī fruits, which removes all sins.
Even if, by the turn of fate, his death should occur in a cremation ground, [he shall attain liberation]. 61.
One attains the merit born of dying in the Gaṅgā; of this there is no doubt.
Upon seeing him, all sinners are instantly liberated from their most terrible webs of sins, even those accumulated over hundreds of millions of births.

O best of Brahmins, he who daily takes the mud from beneath the *dhātrī* tree obtains merit day after day; of this there is no doubt. Those who destroy the *dhātrī* tree, which is the refuge of all the hosts of gods, [commit a grave offense].
There is no doubt that she always bestows great bliss upon the limbs; there is no doubt in this. (65) The Earth is composed of all the gods and is especially dear to Keśava;
even Brahmā is not able to fully describe her virtues. (66)
The man who, having realized all truths, offers devotion to the nurse Tulasī, enjoys all pleasures and thereafter attains liberation at the end through the grace of Hari.
(67) Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Tulasī," in the Kriyāyogasāra of the glorious Padma Purāṇa. (24)
Chapter Twenty-Five. Jaimini said:
O highly fortunate one, [listen again] to this sin-destroying [account] concerning Tulasī.
"Tell me also in detail the greatness of honoring a guest.
Sūta said:
"O best of the twice-born, thereafter the greatly effulgent Vyāsa [spoke] concerning Tulasī..."
He began to describe the majesty that destroys the sins of those who hear it. Vyāsa said:
This Tulasī is Mahālakṣmī herself, the beloved of Bhava.
Therefore, O Jaimini, mortals do not perceive this Tulasī with the same knowledge they have of other trees, even though they constantly serve her on earth;
likewise, Indra and the gods serve her in the abode of the immortals.
Wherever this Tulasi, whose very nature is the Supreme Brahman, resides, there everything is declared by me to be firmly established as auspicious.
Even one who is a sinner, if he receives water [from her] at the time of death, [attains liberation].
One who, with the desire for the proximity of Hari, carries at the time of death a tilaka made of Tulasī clay mixed with water dripping from a Tulasī leaf,
is liberated from all sins and goes to the city of the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu).

O best of the twice-born, at the time of death, the Sun-god becomes the master of that man who has a tulasī leaf in his mouth, on his head, or in his ears. Sumati, whose name was Pavitra, became a knower of the supreme truth.
He had a Brāhmaṇa wife named Bahulā,
who was born of a noble lineage, virtuous, and devoted to the service of her husband.
There lived a certain excellent Brāhmaṇa there whose name was Anapatya.
Then that most excellent man, Pavitra, who was devoted to the twice-born, sat upon a single excellent seat out of affection with his friend Anapatyapati, who was eager for conversation. 11.
In the meantime, a virtuous twice-born man named Lomaśa, possessed of great luster,
arrived and beheld those two as they were recounting various wonderful stories.
Then, rising from their seats, the two brahmins [honored] that brahmin Lomaśa.
With water for the feet, the arghya offering, water for sipping, and other honors, those two worshipped him;
Lomaśa, who was devoted to Nārāyaṇa, was well-pleased with them. That best of Brahmins sat upon a seat, glorifying Hari.

To the high-souled Lomaśa, who was seated with his hands joined in reverence, those two sages, the sons of Atri, spoke with devotion: "O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, by the touch of your pair of feet, men [attain purity]. (15-16)

"By being accepted by the virtuous, this hermitage has surely been purified; indeed, all those sins that we two previously committed out of delusion have been destroyed by the sight of your pair of feet. (17)
"You are Nārāyaṇa himself, worthy of worship even by the immortals.
How could we two mere mortals be capable of performing their worship properly? We have offered this hospitality to our guest according to our own limited power. (18-19)
"Delighted by this, O Bhava, forgive our fault," having said this, those two high-souled ones— the householder and his friend, the best of the twice-born— fell at the two feet of that guest. 20.
Vyāsa said: Then Lomaśa, the best among the wise, being well-pleased by their devotion, spoke:
"O foremost of the twice-born, you two are the best among the humble and are devoted to dharma."
I have been exceedingly gratified by your words of humility;
for the wise declare that a guest is none other than Brahmā, Śiva, or Viṣṇu in person.
May there be auspiciousness for you both, who possess such great devotion toward him.
"I have been properly honored as a guest with abundant food.
Vyāsa said: Then, O Brahmin, having risen, he [placed his head] at the two lotus-feet of that [sage].
Having bowed down once more, those two Brahmins spoke to the sage Lomaśa. The two Brahmins said:
"O Brāhmaṇa, you ought to speak of the greatness of honoring a guest."
By performing which even men attain liberation, though it is difficult to obtain— 25—
who is called a guest in this world, and what is his worship? What two goals do the host and the guest respectively attain?— 26.
Lomaśa said:
"Because of the honoring of these— the forest-dweller, the student, and the mendicant— among all four stages of life, the householder's stage is declared to be the most excellent."

Among the four stages of life, householders are considered the foremost; they, endowed with devotion, must perform the worship of guests. The supreme duty of householders is declared to be the honoring of guests.
Those who have not fallen away from the conduct prescribed for their stage of life (āśrama) are therefore considered true householders.
If householders possess dexterity in honoring guests, then what need have they for any other meritorious deeds? 29–30.
He whose name, lineage, and residence are not known,
and who arrives at the house unexpectedly— he is called a guest by the wise.
(31) Whether they be Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or likewise Śūdras—
Those who have come to one's home should be honored like Viṣṇu by those who perceive the ultimate truth (tattvadarśibhiḥ). Others as well, including Cāṇḍālas and those born of low castes,
should be honored like Viṣṇu with water for the feet (pādya), respectful offerings (arghya), and abundant food.

When guests have arrived, even a householder who is about to depart should quickly offer them water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), and so forth; the twice-born host should also inquire after their welfare with words of gentle syllables.
The wise man, having joyfully accepted [the guest], should provide him with a meal consisting of divine gems (35).
He should arrange for a comfortable bed in his dwelling; however, seeing that the guest wishes to depart in the morning, he should let him go as he returns. (36)
O best of beings, I shall tell you this: if one becomes a wealthy householder as a result of the ripening of karma, then a guest must be honored with hospitality.
When guests have arrived, one should devotedly offer them even grass and other such necessities.
One should say with devotion, "O Earth, please be seated," as if there were no grass available;
then one should offer excellent water for the purpose of washing the feet, and inquire after his well-being and so forth with sweet words. (38–39)
Then, for the sake of his meal, he should devotedly offer fruit and other items;
in their absence, the wise man should joyfully announce it to the Brahmin.
And he should say: "O guest, I am a great sinner and the most wretched of the poor."
I desire to offer devotion to you; [yet] this system of the gods is a source of contradiction.
(41) By this method, even a poor man who has abandoned the worship of guests and fallen from his own conduct may obtain the aforementioned fruit, provided there is no other [obstacle]. (42)
If a guest departs unhonored from the house of a householder,
the merit accumulated by that person over ten million lifetimes goes to ruin.
By him who honors even a single guest with a spirit of devotion, [merit is gained].
Hari shall instantly take away his sin arising from ten million births.
(44) I speak the truth, I speak what is beneficial, and I speak firmly with effort: for a householder, there is no path or goal without the honoring of guests. (45)

"Truth, truth, and again truth: for householders, there is truly no other path, none at all, none at all, except through the honoring of guests. Known as the duty toward kinsmen, this was the beloved practice in the Dvāpara age."
He became a knower of all dharmas; his wife was named Śrīvallabhā. 47. All deeds were performed by him while serving his kinsmen, and he made his residence in Saurāṣṭra together with that wife. 48.
O twice-born ones, because the movement of the clouds was obstructed there, Indra did not send rain for twelve years; consequently, a very great famine occurred.
During that great famine, the people residing in that region—
They all became sorrowful and even abandoned their moral boundaries (maryādā).
In the age known as Dvāpara, the great yogi Jñānabhadra,
his wealth having been seized by famine, became exceedingly miserable.
Seeing his sons and wife distressed by hunger, he, who was honored by the twice-born,
went to the foot of the mountain to seek fruits and roots; at the edge of the mountain's base, that long-lived one remained hungry.
The two best of Brahmins obtained a single kūṣmāṇḍa fruit (53). Taking that fruit, the illustrious Jñānabhadra, the lord of Brahmins, went with joy and great speed to his own home (54).
In the meantime, while the sky was covered by clouds resembling dark blue lotuses, a rain of great torrents fell;
and the sage, his entire body drenched by that rain, [remained there].
A certain forest-dweller, afflicted by the cold, came from the forest to the house.
Seeing that guest was distressed by the cold, he then saluted him with his head bowed; thereafter, out of devotion, he offered him a seat of grass, water for his feet, and other honors.
Then, with a sweet voice, he stood together with that very guest, his mind at ease, engaging in conversation with wisdom;
while Gopī, who was highly skilled in serving her master, remained with the housewife.

Then, having obtained a fresh, ripe kushmanda gourd with great effort, that virtuous woman was delighted; she divided it into portions and gave him his share. Thereupon, that cowherd became weak from fasting for twenty days.
Then that virtuous housewife, devoted to her husband, joyfully gave her husband’s portion to that noble guest. (61) She gave him his allotted share with great delight.
Then,

having eaten there, that best of brahmins became exceedingly well-pleased; he was honored by that high-souled couple with firm devotion like Viṣṇu himself, and the guest received two portions of food.
Having rested there for the night, she bathed in the morning and traveled for a long time;
thus, twenty-one days passed in fasting.
Then those two high-souled husband and wife met their death.
By the power of that merit, that noble-minded couple attained union with Viṣṇu, which is difficult even for yogis to achieve;
this was brought about by the power of their merit through the performance of hospitality toward guests.
In that kingdom, famine was then destroyed; consequently,
the people became exceedingly happy, free from grief and disease,
and they became devoted to righteousness, endowed with wealth, grain, and other necessities.
After that [lineage] was destroyed, there arose there a king who was a protector of the world (68).
The people were devoted to their own traditional conduct, and the clouds rained according to their desires; such were his ancestors numbering ten million, as well as those born after them (69).
By that very act, they attained liberation, freed from sin;
endowed with faultless wealth, they were uniquely honored by all the world. Devoid of sorrow and disease, their progeny flourished.
Lomaśa said:
O brahmins, I have recounted to you the greatness of honoring guests along with its ancient history. What else do you two, who are pleased, wish to hear?
Vyāsa said:
While Lomaśa, the storehouse of asceticism, was speaking thus,
a black rat, seized by Time (Death), emerged from its own burrow right there.
As the black mouse rose from the pit, Pavitra, overwhelmed with anger, stood up there and said repeatedly:
"This wicked mouse of sinful intent has come to the hermitage at night! (73-74)
With its rows of sharp teeth it tears apart the house-demon;
compassion is proclaimed as the highest virtue for all social classes alike. That compassion, moreover, should be practiced toward all beings, but not toward those who are wicked.
Having spoken thus, he struck that mouse,
the committer of sin, with an exceedingly sharp iron arrow at the appropriate moment;
the mouse’s limbs were drenched by streams of flowing blood.

Struck in his heart by grief, the brahmin-sage fell to the ground; when that mouse had fallen, the most excellent of the twice-born, being compassionate, cried out "Alas! Alas! and then rose up with speed.
He brought an excellent *tulasī* leaf from his own ear and placed it upon the head and ears of that rat, saying:
"O Mother, O Goddess Tulasī, you who bring delight to the Lord of the cows! (79-80)
"O you who have performed this horse-sacrifice, grant the highest destination to this horse that has committed sin.
Having spoken thus, that best of the twice-born, the benefactor of all the worlds, raised a loud cry, "Hare! Nārāyaṇa! Ananta! (81)
By the touch of a *tulasī* leaf, the mouse was freed from its impurities;
and by hearing the name of Hari, it was liberated from the bondage of worldly existence.
Then, messengers of Mahāviṣṇu, endowed with all auspicious marks, [arrived].

O best of the twice-born, having mounted a divine chariot and surrounded by hosts of Viṣṇu’s messengers, they arrived swiftly on excellent chariots to lead that man, whose sins had been destroyed, to the supreme abode; thus did the mouse depart.
Having remained in the hermitage of Nārāyaṇa for thousands of millions of yugas,
he attained knowledge there and, having reached liberation, he departed as a mouse.
Vyāsa said:
The majesty of the goddess Tulasī has been told to you, O best of the twice-born. Now tell me, O highly fortunate one, what do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the *Kriyāyogasāra* of the glorious *Padma Purāṇa*.
Chapter Sixty-six. Jaimini said: O highly fortunate one, when the most dreadful Kali age has arrived,
"Tell me, what will all the people of the future be like? Vyāsa said: "They say that the first age is the Satya Yuga; therein, the people, beginning with the Brahmins,"
Devoted to the worship of Nārāyaṇa, they were free from grief and disease; all spoke the truth, were compassionate, long-lived,
and endowed with wealth, grain, and other riches, while remaining free from violence and hypocrisy.
O best of the twice-born, in the Satya Yuga all people were devoted to helping others and were likewise learned in all the scriptures;
and the kings, protectors of their subjects, adhered to the duties of royalty.

In the age of *ahosatya*, there was no one capable of explaining his virtues or fame. When the *tretā* age arrived, people did not utter even a word of unrighteousness, and Dharma had reached its three-quarter state.
Some people were possessed of little sorrow, while others were the refuge of sin; some people were devoted to the meditation on Viṣṇu, and others were intent upon sacrifice and charity.
They were all engaged in the conduct of their respective castes and stages of life, happy, and composed in mind.
The Śūdras there were all devoted to the Brāhmaṇas, having been established by the Brāhmaṇas on their lands.
And the Brāhmaṇas were high-souled, masters of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, abstaining from accepting gifts, true to their word, and having conquered their senses.
Constantly devoted to penance and vows, charitable, and worshippers of Viṣṇu [they shall be] at the end of the Tretā Yuga when the Dvāpara Yuga arrives. At that time,
Dharma will be deficient by two feet, and human beings will be possessed of both pleasure and pain.
Some are devoted to evil, while others are righteous;
some are devoid of virtues, while others possess great virtues;
some are exceedingly miserable, and likewise, some are happy.

Sometimes a Brāhmaṇa develops a desire for receiving gifts, and sometimes the subjects are oppressed by kings out of greed for wealth. The Brāhmaṇas were devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu, and the Śūdras served the twice-born.

O twice-born one, whenever in age after age Dharma has fallen to three-quarters, then Vyāsa, who is a form of Viṣṇu, divided the Veda. And in the Kali age, O best of brahmins, that abode of every kind of sin, [he did so].
In the Kali age, Dharma will exist on only one foot; all people, including Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, will be devoted to sin. They will be excessively lustful and cruel. 16.
In the Kali age, there will be those who revile the Vedas, as well as those who engage in gambling and theft; some will be immersed in unions with widows,
and certain Brahmins, for the sake of a livelihood, will be practitioners of great deceit.

All women will become consumers of intoxicants, always devoted to the female womb, and they shall steal the property of others. They will be constantly greedy for the food of others and forever averse to austerity and vows. 19.
In the Kali age, people will be bound by association with heretics; Brāhmaṇas will wear red garments and follow the dharma of Śūdras.
In the Kali age, even the most excellent, having lost their composure, will sink to the lowest state.
People who are currently low-born and destitute will ascend to high positions,
and all people will bestow gifts upon those who have helped them.
Even with great effort, the Śūdras will not allow the Brāhmaṇas to perform their religious duties.
In the Kali age, people will give false testimony out of affection for their friends (23). With unrighteous intentions, they will speak with unrighteous intent;
cruel and backbiting behind one's back, they will speak pleasant words to one's face (24).
In the Kali age, unchaste women will speak words of praise to their husbands;
likewise, there will be those who harm the wives of others and twice-born men who sell their own lineage,
as well as those who sell their daughters.
All men will be conquered by women, and women themselves will be exceedingly fickle. In the Kali age, mortals will be of evil intent;
likewise, the earth will yield little grain, and the clouds will hold but scant water.
Furthermore, O Jaimini, in the Kali age cows will rain out of season; they will consume dung and yield very little milk.
And that milk will be devoid of ghee—of this there is no doubt.

In the Kali age, people will be intent on praising themselves and devoted to censuring others; they will have stunted limbs and children will consume vast amounts of food. Furthermore, Brahmins will perform ancestral sacrifices merely for the sake of hypocrisy.
Everyone will be affectionate in speech only as long as their purpose has not been accomplished;
but upon seeing men devoted to dharma, everyone indeed mocks them. Consequently, people become intent on sin, and the worlds increase in unrighteousness.

In ten or twelve years, even with their very roots, they will go to destruction. Just as increases of water occur during the rainy seasons, so too will people come to have their youth dissolved by the *kalī* age. 32–33.
In the fifth or even the sixth year, women will conceive,
yet men will have many offspring and become exceedingly miserable. Everyone will be desirous of taking, and no one at all will be desirous of giving.

In the Kali age, there will be Mleccha kings who are devoted to sin; for the sake of sensual objects, the people of the Kali age will become of a single caste. During the first twilight of the Kali age, human beings will revile Hari.
In the midst of the Kali age, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras will not perceive the pure names of Hari; in the Kali yuga, all four varṇas will become a single varṇa.
O best of the twice-born, whenever there is a decline for the virtuous and an increase for sinful men, that should be known as the progress of the Kali age;
even though this Kali has been described by me as terrible, O most excellent of the twice-born. (38–39)
Nevertheless, O best among the virtuous, there is a great quality of this Mahānasa:
in the Kṛta age, the accomplishment of merit may take twelve years;
in the Tretā, half of that; and in the Dvāpara, it may be accomplished in a month. 40.
In the Kali Yuga, that same result may be achieved in a single day and night;
therefore, for men in the Kali Yuga, the supreme goal is attained through mortal effort alone.
Whatever fruit is obtained by worshipping Hari for twelve years in another Yuga, [is gained here in a day]. 41-42.
A mortal obtains that fruit by uttering the name of Hari;
for in this Kali age, whatever man speaks even a single name of Hari, Kali does not afflict him—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. 43.
Jaimini said:
"Because of the absence of purity of mind, all action is fruitless"—this which was previously spoken by you has caused wonder in my mind. (44)
"In the Kali age, all will be devoid of purity of mind.
O Guru, tell me how their every action may come to pass.
Vyāsa said:
Whatever dharma-action a mortal performs during the Kali age,
he should offer that to Mahāviṣṇu, endowed with a spirit of devotion;
every action offered to Viṣṇu shall indeed become inexhaustible.
Vyāsa said:
O best of Brahmins, I have thus related to you everything that occurred, hearing which with a spirit of devotion a person may attain liberation. 48.
Sūta said:
Thus enlightened by that Supreme Self, Jaimini became devoted to the yoga of action and attained the supreme state. 49
Those people who, seeking liberation, read with devotion this *Kriyāyogasāra* spoken by the high-souled Vyāsa, and those who listen to it—
they all [are freed] even from terrible sins accumulated over many births.
Being liberated, they attain supreme liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Whatever is desired, those seeking liberation who read or hear this obtain that very thing quickly through the grace of the Lord of Kamalā. 51-52.
By reciting or hearing even half a verse, a single verse, or even a quarter-verse of this work, a person obtains their desired fruit. Furthermore,
whoever writes or causes this scripture to be written shall worship it.
A human being obtains the very fruit of the worship of Viṣṇu. This most secret [teaching], which has issued from the mouth of Vyāsa, is an exceedingly ancient Purāṇa that grants joy to the Vaiṣṇavas.
May it long be for the pleasure of Murāri—the wielder of the discus, the sustainer of all worlds, whose feet are worshipped by the foremost of the immortals. 55.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Purāṇas Preceded by the Exposition of the Duties of the Ages," in the *Kriyāyogasāra-khaṇḍa* of the glorious *Padmapurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Vyāsa and Jaimini.
